q_0001.stem: A nurse says that research is worthwhile only when it produces knowledge no one has had before. Which statement best corrects this using the text's definition of research?
options: Research is any careful observation of practice that is recorded and shared with colleagues
Research is limited to generating new knowledge through controlled experimentation
Research validates and refines existing knowledge and also develops new knowledge
Research is the appropriation of knowledge from other disciplines to guide nursing practice
q_0001.rationale: Research is a diligent systematic inquiry or study that validates and refines existing knowledge and develops new knowledge. The definition includes both functions, and diligent systematic study indicates planning, organization, and persistence.
q_0001.trap: (B) is the reflex because new knowledge is the memorable half of the definition; an option offering only that half is incomplete. (D) is the definition of borrowing.

q_0002.stem: Which phrase in the text's definition of nursing research is what distinguishes it from the general definition of research?
options: It generates knowledge that directly and indirectly influences nursing practice
It is conducted only by nurses prepared at the doctoral level
It uses numerical data to obtain information about the world
It validates existing knowledge but does not generate new knowledge
q_0002.rationale: Nursing research is a scientific process that validates and refines existing knowledge and generates new knowledge that directly and indirectly influences nursing practice.
q_0002.trap: The word indirectly is the part that gets dropped. Studies of nursing education or administration are still nursing research even though they do not change bedside care immediately. (C) is the definition of quantitative research.

q_0003.stem: A unit adopts a new pressure-injury protocol based entirely on one high-quality meta-analysis, without consulting the staff nurses who deliver the care or asking patients about their preferences. Why does this fall short of the text's definition of evidence-based practice?
options: A meta-analysis is not considered best research evidence
Evidence-based practice requires that the synthesis be a systematic review rather than a meta-analysis
Evidence-based practice requires that an expert consensus panel approve the evidence first
Evidence-based practice is the integration of best research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's circumstances and values
q_0003.rationale: EBP evolves from the integration of the best research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's circumstances and values to produce quality health outcomes. Applying research findings is only one of the three parts.
q_0003.trap: This is the single most testable idea in the chapter. Any option that calls applying research findings EBP by itself, or that names only two of the three parts, is the distractor.

q_0004.stem: According to the text and the QSEN evidence-based practice competency, which elements are integrated to produce evidence-based practice? Select all that apply.
options: The best current research evidence
The nurse's clinical expertise
The patient's or family's preferences, values, and circumstances
The institution's cost-containment targets
The consensus opinion of the nursing leadership team
q_0004.rationale: The QSEN competency is integrating the best current evidence with clinical expertise and patient and family preferences and values for delivery of optimal health care, which is the same three-part integration the text uses to define EBP.
q_0004.trap: (E) is tempting because leadership sets protocol, but the opinion of experts and authorities is the weakest level of evidence in Fig. 1.3, not a component of EBP.

q_0005.stem: The text defines best research evidence as which of the following?
options: The findings of the single most rigorous study available on a clinical problem
The empirical knowledge generated from the synthesis of quality health studies to address a clinical problem
The recommendations issued by a panel of experts after they review the literature
The accumulated clinical judgment of the experienced nurses on a unit
q_0005.rationale: Best research evidence is the empirical knowledge generated from the synthesis of quality health studies to address a clinical problem.
q_0005.trap: (A) is the reflex, but best research evidence is a synthesis product, not one study however strong. (C) describes evidence-based guidelines, which are built from best research evidence rather than being it.

q_0006.subtopic: tradition, borrowing, and trial and error
q_0006.stem: A new graduate asks why the unit changes IV tubing on a set schedule and is told, "It is in the policy manual; that is how this unit has always done it." Which way of acquiring knowledge does this represent, and what limitation does the text attach to it?
options: Authority; the authority may be influencing behavior without a basis in research evidence
Tradition; it can narrow and limit the knowledge sought for practice
Borrowing; knowledge taken from another discipline may not fit nursing's focus
Role modeling; imitating an expert transmits behavior without explanation
q_0006.rationale: Traditions are truths or beliefs based on customs and trends, carried in policy manuals and transferred from the past. The text says traditions can narrow and limit the knowledge sought for practice and often go unquestioned because they are supported by those with power and authority.
q_0006.trap: (A) is close because the text mentions power and authority in the same breath. Authority as a way of knowing requires a specific person with expertise and power influencing opinion and behavior; here the source is the custom itself.

q_0007.subtopic: tradition, borrowing, and trial and error
q_0007.stem: The text names a specific weakness of trial and error as a source of knowledge for practice. Which is it?
options: It cannot be used in situations of uncertainty
It produces knowledge that cannot be expressed numerically
It requires a person with expertise and power to interpret the result
The knowledge gained is often not shared, so ineffective interventions continue to be used
q_0007.rationale: Trial and error is an approach with unknown outcomes used when other sources of knowledge are unavailable; the chapter's stated problem is that the knowledge gained is frequently not shared, so ineffective interventions persist.
q_0007.trap: The reflex is to call trial and error simply unscientific. The text actually accepts it as legitimate under uncertainty and faults it for nondissemination.

q_0008.stem: An expert nurse tells a colleague she "just knew" a patient was deteriorating before any vital sign changed. How does the text characterize this?
options: Trial and error, because the outcome of acting on the feeling was unknown
Intuition, which is a lack of knowing and therefore must be set aside in favor of objective data
Intuition, which is not a lack of knowing but is instead a result of deep knowledge
Borrowing, because the insight originates in psychology rather than nursing
q_0008.rationale: Intuition is an insight into or understanding of a situation as a whole that a person usually cannot explain logically, often described as a gut feeling or hunch. The text is explicit that intuition is not the lack of knowing but a result of deep knowledge.
q_0008.trap: (B) inverts the chapter's own sentence and is the option a student picks when trying to sound scientific. Benner's work is the citation behind the correct reading.

q_0009.stem: A nurse consistently views the patient as a whole and as a member of a family and community, and adjusts the plan of care to each patient's response. Which of Benner's five levels of experience does this describe?
options: Advanced beginner
Competent
Proficient
Expert
q_0009.rationale: The proficient nurse views the patient as a whole and as a member of a family and community and adjusts care to each patient's response. Benner's five levels came from a phenomenological qualitative study.
q_0009.trap: (D) is the reflex for any description of skilled holistic practice. Expert is defined by grasping a situation intuitively with accuracy and speed; competent is defined by conscious, deliberate, organized planning toward long-range goals.

q_0010.stem: Which of the following does the text list among the ways nursing has historically acquired knowledge? Select all that apply.
options: Traditions
Borrowing
Role modeling
Meta-analysis
Intuition
q_0010.rationale: The eight ways named are traditions, authority, borrowing, trial and error, personal experience, role modeling, intuition, and reasoning.
q_0010.trap: (D) is a synthesis strategy used to produce best research evidence, not a historical way of knowing. The historical ways are the ones research evidence is meant to improve on.

q_0011.stem: A doctoral student reviews the findings of 14 individual studies of early ambulation after surgery and combines them into a general statement about best practice. Which type of reasoning is this, and in which direction does it move?
options: Inductive reasoning, from the specific to the general
Deductive reasoning, from the general to the specific
Inductive reasoning, from the general to the specific
Deductive reasoning, from the specific to the general
q_0011.rationale: Inductive reasoning moves from the specific to the general, combining particular instances into a larger whole. Synthesizing multiple studies into a best practice is the logic behind building an evidence-based practice.
q_0011.trap: (C) and (D) attach the right label to the wrong direction, which is how this pair is usually missed. Fix the cue: synthesis of many studies is inductive.

q_0012.stem: A nurse begins from the premises that all humans experience loss and that all adolescents are humans, and concludes that all adolescents experience loss. Which type of reasoning is this?
options: Inductive reasoning
Deductive reasoning
Intuition
Trial and error
q_0012.rationale: Deductive reasoning moves from the general to the specific, or from a general premise to a particular situation or conclusion. This is the chapter's own worked example.
q_0012.trap: This is the mirror image of the synthesis item. The chapter's inductive example runs the other way: a headache is stressful and a terminal illness is stressful, therefore all altered levels of health are stressful.

q_0013.stem: A researcher wants to describe the lived experience of parents who have lost a child. Which type of qualitative research fits this purpose?
options: Ethnographic research
Grounded theory research
Exploratory-descriptive qualitative research
Phenomenological research
q_0013.rationale: Phenomenological research is an inductive holistic approach used to describe an experience as it is lived by individuals; the chapter's own example is the lived experience of losing a child.

q_0014.stem: A researcher interviews nurses in order to formulate, test, and refine a theory explaining how they manage interruptions during medication administration. Which type of qualitative research is this?
options: Phenomenological research
Ethnographic research
Grounded theory research
Exploratory-descriptive qualitative research
q_0014.rationale: Grounded theory research is an inductive technique used to formulate, test, and refine a theory about a particular phenomenon.
q_0014.trap: (B) is the near-neighbor when a study takes place inside a work setting, but ethnographic research was developed by anthropology to investigate cultures through in-depth study of members of the culture. The target has to be the culture itself.

q_0015.stem: Box 1.1 classifies the research methods used in nursing. Which of the following does it list as types of quantitative research? Select all that apply.
options: Descriptive
Correlational
Quasi-experimental
Experimental
Exploratory-descriptive
q_0015.rationale: Box 1.1 names four types of quantitative research: descriptive, correlational, quasi-experimental, and experimental.
q_0015.trap: (E) is one of the four qualitative types. Descriptive and exploratory-descriptive qualitative are near-identical names sitting on opposite sides of Box 1.1.

q_0016.stem: In Table 1.3, which characteristics are attributed to qualitative research? Select all that apply.
options: Philosophic origin is naturalistic, interpretive, and humanistic
Basis of knowing is meaning, discovery, and understanding
Theoretical focus is developing theory
Analysis is statistical analysis
Researcher involvement is shared interpretation
q_0016.rationale: Table 1.3 gives qualitative research a naturalistic, interpretive, humanistic origin, a basis of knowing in meaning and discovery, a theoretical focus on developing theory, shared interpretation by the researcher, words as data, and text-based analysis.
q_0016.trap: (D) belongs to quantitative research. The theory direction is the other half of this trap: qualitative develops theory, quantitative tests it.

q_0017.stem: A study is grounded in logical positivism, measures its variables with scales and physiological instruments, and sets out to test an existing theory. Which method is this, and what is its basis of knowing?
options: Quantitative research; cause and effect relationships
Qualitative research; meaning, discovery, and understanding
Outcomes research; the results of care and changes in health status
Mixed methods research; complex health problems
q_0017.rationale: Table 1.3 assigns quantitative research a logical positivist origin, an objective researcher stance, numbers as data, statistical analysis, and a basis of knowing in cause and effect relationships. Quantitative research is a formal, objective, systematic process using numerical data.
q_0017.trap: This is the mirror of the qualitative item. Swapping logical positivism with naturalistic origins, or tests theory with develops theory, is the Table 1.3 reversal.

q_0018.stem: A researcher studying a complex symptom problem collects numerical symptom scores and unstructured interview data from the same participants within a single study. Which method is this?
options: Outcomes research
Meta-analysis
Mixed-methods systematic review
Mixed methods research
q_0018.rationale: Mixed methods research is an approach to inquiry that combines quantitative and qualitative research methods in a single study, and the text ties it to expanding understanding of complex health problems.
q_0018.trap: (C) has almost the same name and is the distractor to beat. A mixed-methods systematic review synthesizes studies that already exist; mixed methods research combines the two approaches inside one primary study.

q_0019.stem: Which statement matches the text's definition of a nursing-sensitive outcome?
options: A laboratory value that changes measurably after a nursing intervention
An individual, family, or community state, behavior, or perception that is measured along a continuum in response to nursing interventions
The financial result of care that can be attributed to nurse staffing levels
A patient satisfaction score collected after discharge
q_0019.rationale: A nursing-sensitive outcome is an individual, family, or community state, behavior, or perception measured along a continuum in response to nursing interventions. The Nursing Outcomes Classification standardizes this terminology across specialties and settings.
q_0019.trap: (D) is one of the four areas outcomes research investigates, not the definition of a nursing-sensitive outcome. Measured along a continuum is the phrase that identifies the key.

q_0020.stem: The text names the areas requiring investigation in outcomes research. Which of the following are among them? Select all that apply.
options: Patient responses to nursing and medical interventions
Functional maintenance or improvement of physical, mental, and social functioning
Financial outcomes achieved with the provision of healthcare services
Patient satisfaction with health outcomes, care received, and providers
Nurse job satisfaction and intent to remain in the profession
q_0020.rationale: Outcomes research examines the results of care and the changes in health status for the patient and family, and the four areas named are patient responses, functional maintenance or improvement, financial outcomes, and patient satisfaction.
q_0020.trap: (E) is plausible because outcomes data are used in staffing arguments, but all four areas the chapter names are patient- or system-facing, not workforce measures.

q_0021.stem: A team combines the results of previous quantitative studies of an intervention into a single statistical analysis in order to estimate its effectiveness. Which synthesis strategy is this?
options: Meta-analysis
Systematic review
Meta-synthesis
Mixed-methods systematic review
q_0021.rationale: A meta-analysis pools the results from previous quantitative studies into a single statistical analysis, and is strongest when pooling quasi-experimental and experimental studies.
q_0021.trap: (B) is the reflex because the two words are used loosely as synonyms. A systematic review is the structured, comprehensive process of identifying, locating, appraising, and synthesizing evidence for one healthcare question; many systematic reviews contain a meta-analysis, but the terms are not interchangeable.

q_0022.stem: A student proposes conducting a meta-analysis of ten phenomenological studies of living with chronic pain. Why will this not work, and which strategy fits instead?
options: The studies are too few in number to pool; a systematic review is the correct strategy
Qualitative studies cannot be appraised for quality; a mixed-methods systematic review is the correct strategy
Qualitative studies do not produce statistical findings and cannot be pooled; a meta-synthesis is the correct strategy
Qualitative studies rank below expert opinion on the evidence pyramid; an expert consensus panel is the correct strategy
q_0022.rationale: Because qualitative studies do not produce statistical findings, they cannot be included in a meta-analysis; meta-synthesis is the systematic compilation and integration of qualitative study results, and it focuses on interpretation rather than on combining results.
q_0022.trap: (D) inverts the pyramid. Expert opinion is the base, below descriptive and qualitative studies, not above them.

q_0023.stem: Which statements about the levels of research evidence in Fig. 1.3 are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of high-quality quasi-experimental and experimental studies sit at the top of the pyramid
Among individual studies, experimental studies such as randomized controlled trials provide the strongest research evidence
Descriptive and qualitative studies provide initial knowledge and a basis for further study
Replication of studies with similar methodology increases the strength of the evidence
The opinions of expert committees and authorities occupy the level just below systematic reviews
q_0023.rationale: The levels form a continuum with the strongest evidence at the top: syntheses of quasi-experimental and experimental studies, then meta-analyses of correlational, quasi-experimental, experimental, and outcomes studies, then mixed-methods systematic reviews and meta-syntheses, then individual correlational and cohort studies, then descriptive and qualitative studies, with expert opinion at the base.
q_0023.trap: (E) places expert opinion near the top. It is the weakest evidence at the base of the pyramid, which is the same idea as authority being a historical way of knowing that research evidence is meant to supersede.

q_0024.stem: A nurse proposes changing a unit protocol on the basis of one predictive correlational study. Using the levels of research evidence, what is the appropriate response?
options: Proceed, because correlational studies examine relationships and therefore establish intervention effectiveness
Proceed, because a single study conducted in a comparable setting counts as a synthesis
Decline, because correlational studies rank below the opinions of expert committees on the pyramid
Decline, because correlational, predictive correlational, and cohort studies provide direction for future research but are not ready for use in practice
q_0024.rationale: The chapter places individual correlational, predictive correlational, and cohort studies at the level that provides direction for future research but is not ready for use in practice.
q_0024.trap: (C) inverts the pyramid, since expert opinion is the weakest level and sits below correlational studies. (A) confuses examining relationships with determining effectiveness, which is the job of quasi-experimental and experimental studies.

q_0025.topic: the nurse's research role by education
q_0025.stem: A BSN-prepared staff nurse asks what her research role is. Which activities does Table 1.4 place at the BSN level? Select all that apply.
options: Reading and critically appraising studies
Using best research evidence in practice with guidance
Assisting with problem identification and data collection
Serving as primary investigator and obtaining research funding
Leading the development of evidence-based guidelines for the institution
q_0025.rationale: The BSN nurse reads and critically appraises studies, uses best research evidence in practice with guidance, assists with problem identification and data collection, and adheres to IRB guidelines.
q_0025.trap: (D) is the PhD role and (E) is the DNP role. The chapter's line that all nurses have a role in research invites overreach; the role expands with education rather than being identical at every level.

q_0026.topic: the nurse's research role by education
q_0026.stem: A nursing student is comparing doctoral options. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two degrees as the text describes them?
options: The DNP is practice-focused and translates scientific knowledge for use in practice, while the PhD is research-focused and generates nursing knowledge
The DNP is research-focused and generates nursing knowledge, while the PhD is practice-focused and translates it for use
Both degrees are research-focused, but only the PhD is permitted to conduct clinical studies
Both degrees are practice-focused, but only the DNP obtains research funding and coordinates research teams
q_0026.rationale: The DNP is practice-focused, representing the highest level of clinical expertise and translating scientific knowledge for use in practice; the PhD is research-focused, generating nursing knowledge as nurse scientists.
q_0026.trap: (B) is the straight swap and is the likeliest item off this table. Anchor it by the other duties: PhD nurses obtain funding and coordinate research teams of BSN, MSN, and DNP nurses, while DNP nurses develop and revise protocols, policies, and guidelines.

q_0027.stem: A study's variables include waist circumference, resting heart rate, and days of hospitalization for one aim, and perceived coping and depression for a second aim. Which classification of these variables is correct?
options: Both sets are direct measures, because both are recorded with standardized procedures
The first set require indirect measures; the second set are direct measures
Both sets are indirect measures, because some error is present in every measurement strategy
The first set are direct measures; the second set require indirect measures
q_0027.rationale: Direct measures determine the value of concrete factors such as waist circumference and heart rate, along with demographic variables such as days of hospitalization; abstract concepts such as coping and depression require indirect measures, which capture only some of the elements of the concept.
q_0027.trap: (C) mistakes the universality of measurement error for a statement about directness. Even direct measures contain error, and that does not make them indirect.

q_0028.stem: A researcher notes that the pain instrument chosen for a study might also be measuring aspects of anxiety and fear. Which characteristic of indirect measures does this illustrate?
options: Indirect measures produce systematic rather than random error
Indirect measures cannot be evaluated for reliability in the study sample
Indirect measures may capture elements that are not part of the concept being measured
Indirect measures are appropriate only when the concept can be measured concretely
q_0028.rationale: With indirect measures, the methods used may capture elements that are not part of the concept; the chapter's example is that pain measures might be measuring aspects of anxiety and fear in addition to pain.
q_0028.trap: (D) inverts the definition. Concrete factors are exactly what direct measures handle; indirect measures exist because abstract concepts cannot be measured concretely.

q_0029.stem: A researcher measures children's postoperative pain with the FACES Pain Rating Scale, structured observation, and physiological measures. Which statements reflect the chapter's reasoning for this approach? Select all that apply.
options: Using multiple measurement methods decreases measurement error
Using multiple measurement methods increases understanding of the concept
Physiological measures such as pulse, blood pressure, and respiration provide a more objective measurement
Observation of pain includes rubbing or guarding the area, facial grimacing, and crying
Using all three methods together measures the entire concept of pain
q_0029.rationale: Rarely, if ever, can a single measurement strategy measure all aspects of an abstract concept, so multiple methods are needed; this decreases the measurement error and increases the understanding of the concept. Physiological measures give a more objective measurement, and observation covers guarding, grimacing, and crying.
q_0029.trap: (E) is the reflex that more methods equals full coverage. The chapter states that even with all three, the entire concept of pain is still not completely measured.

q_0030.stem: A study protocol specifies how blood pressure will be obtained so the recorded value is as accurate and precise as possible. What does the chapter describe as the usual practice?
options: A single reading taken by the same nurse at every visit
Three BP measurements are taken and averaged
Two readings compared between two observers for interrater agreement
Readings repeated until two consecutive values match
q_0030.rationale: For blood pressure, three measurements are usually taken and averaged to determine the most accurate and precise reading.
q_0030.trap: (C) is a real chapter concept but belongs to observational data requiring judgments by two or more data gatherers, not to averaging out random error in a physiological reading.

q_0031.stem: A researcher codes each participant's admitting diagnosis as kidney stone, gastric ulcer, or cholecystitis and enters the codes 1, 2, and 3 into the dataset. What level of measurement is this variable?
options: Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio
q_0031.rationale: Medical diagnoses are nominal: the categories are exclusive and exhaustive but cannot be ordered, because a kidney stone cannot be rated higher than a gastric ulcer. The categories differ in quality but not in quantity.
q_0031.trap: The numeric codes are what pull students upward to ordinal or interval. Codes assigned to categories are labels, not quantities, and nothing about 1, 2, 3 makes the diagnoses rankable.

q_0032.stem: A demographic form offers Single, Married, Divorced, and Widowed. A participant who was widowed and has since remarried cannot decide which box to mark. Which nominal rule is violated, and what fix does the chapter give?
options: Exhaustiveness; add an "Other" category
Exhaustiveness; redefine the variable as Current Marital Status
Exclusiveness; redefine the variable as Current Marital Status
Orderability; rank the categories by duration of the current status
q_0032.rationale: The exclusive rule requires that each datum fit into only one category, and the chapter's remedy for this exact example is to redefine the variable as Current Marital Status.
q_0032.trap: (B) pairs the correct fix with the wrong rule. Two categories a person could legitimately claim is an exclusivity failure; a person for whom no category exists is an exhaustiveness failure.

q_0033.stem: A "Cardiac Medical Diagnoses" item lists only Hypertension, Heart Failure, and Myocardial Infarction, leaving a participant with cardiomyopathy nowhere to be recorded. Which statement about adding an "Other" category is accurate?
options: It makes the categories exclusive and improves the analysis
It raises the variable from the nominal to the ordinal level
It has no effect unless the categories are also rank ordered
It makes the categories exhaustive, but the resulting data are difficult to analyze and interpret
q_0033.rationale: Adding "Other" makes the categories exhaustive so that all data fit somewhere, but the chapter notes that these data are difficult to analyze and interpret.
q_0033.trap: Adding "Other" reads like a free fix. It is a trade-off, and an option presenting it as pure improvement overstates what the chapter actually says.

q_0034.stem: Which statements about nominal-level measurement are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The categories must be exclusive, so each datum fits into only one category
The categories must be exhaustive, so all data fit somewhere
The categories can be rank ordered from lowest to highest
The categories differ in quality but not in quantity
Gender, race and ethnicity, marital status, and medical diagnoses are examples
q_0034.rationale: Nominal categories must be exclusive and exhaustive and are not orderable; they differ in quality but not quantity. The chapter's examples are gender, race and ethnicity, marital status, and medical diagnoses.
q_0034.trap: (C) imports the ordinal rule. Ranking is precisely what nominal data cannot support, and it is the single rule separating nominal from ordinal.

q_0035.stem: Participants rate their shortness of breath on a 0-to-4 dyspnea scale. What level of measurement does this produce, and why?
options: Nominal, because the numbers function only as labels for categories
Ordinal, because the ranks are ordered but the intervals between them are unequal
Interval, because the numerals 0 through 4 are equally spaced on the form
Ratio, because 0 on the scale represents the absence of dyspnea
q_0035.rationale: The 0-to-4 dyspnea scale is ordinal: the ranks are ordered, but a smaller difference may exist between the ranks of 1 and 2 than between the ranks of 3 and 4. The same logic applies to pain ranked excruciating, severe, moderate, mild, none, where a greater difference may exist between mild and moderate than between excruciating and severe.
q_0035.trap: (C) is the reflex because the printed numerals look evenly spaced. Equal spacing of the numerals is not equal spacing of the underlying attribute, and that is the entire ordinal-versus-interval distinction.

q_0036.stem: A study records each participant's body temperature in degrees Fahrenheit. What level of measurement is this, and why?
options: Ordinal, because temperatures can be ranked from lowest to highest
Ratio, because a temperature of 0 degrees Fahrenheit indicates the absence of temperature
Interval, because the intervals are equal but there is no absolute zero
Interval, because temperature values can be multiplied and divided
q_0036.rationale: The difference between 70 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit is the same as the difference between 30 and 40 degrees, so the intervals are equal; but 0 degrees Fahrenheit does not indicate the absence of temperature, so there is no absolute zero.
q_0036.trap: (D) attaches the wrong permission to the right level. The chapter's level table gives interval data addition and subtraction, and reserves multiplication and division for ratio data.

q_0037.stem: A researcher reports that "Medication container A holds twice as much as medication container B." What property of the measurement level justifies that statement?
options: Equal intervals between values, which is the defining addition of interval data
Exclusive and exhaustive categories, which nominal data require
Ranked ordering of values, which ordinal data provide
An absolute zero point, which ratio data have
q_0037.rationale: Ratio-level data have an absolute zero, and that is what permits ratio statements such as one container holding twice as much as another; weight, length, and volume are the chapter's ratio examples.
q_0037.trap: (A) is the near-miss. Equal intervals let you say participant A weighs 25 more pounds than participant B; only an absolute zero lets you say A is twice B.

q_0038.stem: Which statements about interval-level measurement are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The intervals between values are equal
There is an absolute zero point
Values can be added and subtracted
Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is the chapter's example
Interval data can be analyzed with statistical techniques of greater strength than ordinal data
q_0038.rationale: Interval measurement adds equal intervals to the ordinal rules but has no absolute zero, and temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is the chapter's standing example. Interval and ratio data support statistical techniques of greater strength for determining significant relationships and differences.
q_0038.trap: (B) is the ratio rule, and the absence of an absolute zero is the only thing keeping interval data from being ratio. Note the chapter's own internal tension here: its level table gives interval data only addition and subtraction, while its summary sentence says interval- and ratio-level data alike can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided. Answer from the table when a stem asks about one level in isolation.

q_0039.stem: A researcher redesigns a study so that a variable previously collected as ordinal ranks will now be collected at the interval level. According to the chapter, what does this change buy her?
options: The data can be analyzed with statistical techniques of greater strength to determine significant relationships and differences
The instrument no longer requires reliability testing in this sample
The data will no longer contain measurement error
The results can be reported as percentages rather than as frequencies
q_0039.rationale: Interval- and ratio-level data can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided, so they can be analyzed with statistical techniques of greater strength to determine significant relationships and differences.
q_0039.trap: (C) is the reflex that a higher level means a better measurement. Level of measurement governs which analyses are permitted; some error is always present regardless of the level.

q_0040.stem: A research team is assigning levels of measurement to its study variables. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Weight in pounds — ratio
Level of mobility, ranked from bedbound to independent — ordinal
Race and ethnicity — nominal
Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit — ratio
Pain rated as mild, moderate, severe, or excruciating — ordinal
q_0040.rationale: Weight is a ratio variable because it has an absolute zero; levels of mobility and pain categories are the chapter's ordinal examples; race and ethnicity is nominal.
q_0040.trap: (D) is the most repeated misclassification in this chapter. Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is interval precisely because zero does not mean the absence of temperature.

q_0041.stem: During data entry a research assistant occasionally transposes digits, and a few participants mark the wrong column on the answer sheet. The resulting values fall above and below the true values with no pattern. What type of error is this, and what does the chapter recommend?
options: Systematic error; recalibrate the measurement instrument
Random error; average multiple values, because a mean is a closer estimate of the true measurement
Systematic error; average multiple values to cancel out the bias
Random error; discard the affected cases before analysis
q_0041.rationale: In random measurement error the difference between the measured value and the true value is without pattern or direction; an average value such as the mean is a closer estimate of the true measurement.
q_0041.trap: (C) pairs the right remedy with the wrong error. Averaging works only because random errors fall in both directions and cancel one another.

q_0042.stem: A digital scale used in a weight-loss study reads 0.5 lb high for every participant at every visit. How should this error be classified?
options: Random error, because the deviation is small relative to body weight
Random error, because weight is a direct measure and direct measures are precise
Systematic error, because the variation from the calculated average is primarily in the same direction
Systematic error, because the sample was too small to detect the difference
q_0042.rationale: Systematic measurement error is variation in measurement values from the calculated average that is primarily in the same direction, and a consistent flaw in the instrument or process produces it.
q_0042.trap: Taking and averaging more readings will not help here. Every reading carries the same 0.5 lb bias, so the mean is biased by the same amount. This is the mirror image of the random-error item, where averaging is the fix.

q_0043.stem: A reviewer argues that a study's physiological measures cannot contain measurement error because they are direct measures. How does the chapter answer this?
options: Direct measures are error-free once the equipment has been calibrated before data collection
Direct measures contain systematic error only, never random error
Direct measures contain error only when more than one data collector is used
Some error is always present in any measurement strategy, including direct measures
q_0043.rationale: Some error is always present in any measurement strategy; the chapter's own examples include a scale inaccurate by 0.5 lb, calibrated BP equipment that loses accuracy with use, and a tape measure held at different tensions.
q_0043.trap: (A) is the reflex, but the chapter specifically names calibrated BP equipment losing accuracy with use as an error source, which is the counterexample to calibration as a guarantee.

q_0044.stem: Which statements about measurement error are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Measurement error is the difference between the true measure and what is actually measured
As the number of random errors increases, the precision of the estimate decreases
In random error, the difference between the measured and the true value is without pattern or direction
Systematic error is corrected by averaging repeated measurements
Even direct measures such as weight and blood pressure are subject to error
q_0044.rationale: Measurement error is the difference between the true measure and what is actually measured; random error has no pattern or direction, and as random errors accumulate the precision of the estimate decreases. Some error is present in every measurement strategy.
q_0044.trap: (D) borrows the random-error remedy. Averaging cannot remove a bias that pushes every value in the same direction, which parallels the rule that a larger sample fixes random but not systematic variation.

q_0045.stem: A researcher administers the CES-D to the same participants on two occasions 4 weeks apart and correlates the two sets of scores. Which reliability is being examined?
options: Stability, determined by test-retest
Equivalence, determined by alternate forms
Equivalence, determined by interrater comparison
Internal consistency, determined by the Cronbach alpha
q_0045.rationale: Stability reliability is concerned with the reproducibility of scores with repeated measures of the same concept over time and is determined by test-retest; the CES-D shows r = 0.51 to 0.67 at 2- to 8-week intervals, which the chapter calls very solid.
q_0045.trap: Nothing in the stem involves two versions or two raters. Repeat administration to the same people over time is the signature of stability, not equivalence.

q_0046.stem: What assumption underlies test-retest reliability testing?
options: The two administrations use parallel versions of the instrument
The attribute remains the same at the two testing times, and any change in the score is a consequence of random error
The instrument yields interval- or ratio-level data
The interval between administrations is long enough for the attribute to change
q_0046.rationale: Test-retest assumes that the attribute to be measured remains the same at the two testing times and that any change in the value or score is a consequence of random error.
q_0046.trap: (C) is the constraint on the Cronbach alpha, not on test-retest. (D) inverts the assumption outright, since real change would confound the estimate.

q_0047.stem: Two trained observers independently rate the same infant feeding sessions and their ratings are compared. Which reliability is this, and what benchmark does the chapter give?
options: Alternate forms reliability; values below 0.80 are a serious concern
Internal consistency; 0.70 is acceptable for a relatively new tool
Interrater reliability; values below 0.80 are a serious concern and reliability is best at 0.90 or higher
Interrater reliability; 0.70 is acceptable for a relatively new observation tool
q_0047.rationale: Comparison of two observers or two judges is interrater reliability, one of the two forms of equivalence; the chapter states that a value below 0.80 is a serious concern and that reliability is best at 0.90, or 90 percent, or higher.
q_0047.trap: (D) borrows the Cronbach alpha leniency for new scales. The 0.70 standard belongs to internal consistency of a relatively new scale, never to interrater agreement.

q_0048.stem: A researcher compares participants' scores on two paper-and-pencil versions of the same anxiety instrument. Which reliability is being tested?
options: Interrater reliability
Stability reliability
Internal consistency
Alternate (parallel) forms reliability
q_0048.rationale: Equivalence is the comparison of two versions of the same paper and pencil instrument or of two observers measuring the same event; comparing two paper and pencil instruments or scales is alternate, or parallel, forms reliability.
q_0048.trap: This is the mirror of the interrater item and both live under equivalence. Two observers gives interrater reliability; two instruments gives alternate forms.

q_0049.stem: A newly developed 15-item scale yields a Cronbach alpha of 0.74 in the study sample. How should this value be interpreted?
options: Acceptable, because 0.70 is acceptable for a relatively new scale
Unacceptable, because an alpha of at least 0.80 is required of every scale
Unacceptable, because values below 0.80 are a serious concern for interrater reliability
Perfect internal consistency, because 1.00 indicates none and 0.00 indicates perfect
q_0049.rationale: A Cronbach alpha of 1.00 indicates perfect reliability and 0.00 indicates none; 0.80 is strong for an established scale, and 0.70 is acceptable for a relatively new scale.
q_0049.trap: (B) applies the established-scale standard to a new one. The benchmark shifts with the maturity of the scale, and (C) drags an interrater benchmark into an internal consistency question.

q_0050.stem: A researcher wants to estimate internal consistency for a screening tool whose items are all answered yes or no. Which statistic applies?
options: The Cronbach alpha, since it is the most commonly used measure of internal reliability for multi-item scales
The Kuder-Richardson formula (K-R 20)
A test-retest correlation over a 2-week interval
An interrater reliability coefficient between two scorers
q_0050.rationale: The Cronbach alpha can only be calculated for interval- and ratio-level data; for dichotomous yes/no data the Kuder-Richardson formula (K-R 20) is used.
q_0050.trap: (A) is the reflex precisely because the alpha is the most commonly used measure for multi-item scales. Dichotomous items disqualify it no matter how common it is.

q_0051.subtopic: reliability as a property of the use
q_0051.stem: A published report states, "The instrument has established reliability, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.89 in prior research," and reports no reliability testing in the current sample. Which statements apply? Select all that apply.
options: Estimates of reliability are specific to the sample being tested
High reliability values reported for an established instrument do not guarantee satisfactory reliability in another sample or population
Researchers need to perform reliability testing on each instrument used in a study
A previously published alpha of 0.89 is sufficient evidence of reliability for this study
Reliability exists in degrees and is usually expressed as a correlation coefficient
q_0051.rationale: Estimates of reliability are specific to the sample being tested, and high values reported for an established instrument do not guarantee that reliability will be satisfactory in another sample or with a different population, so researchers must perform reliability testing on each instrument used in a study.
q_0051.trap: (D) is the reflex a published alpha invites. Reliability is a property of the use of the instrument in this sample, not a permanent attribute of the instrument.

q_0052.subtopic: reliability as a property of the use
q_0052.stem: Which statements about reliability testing are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Internal consistency testing is used primarily with multi-item scales, in which each item is correlated with all other items
Correlation coefficients closer to 1.0 indicate less random error and a more reliable scale
Studies collecting observational data or requiring judgments by two or more data gatherers must report interrater reliability
There is an absolute value below which interrater reliability is always unacceptable
Reliability testing determines the measurement error in an instrument or scale used in a study
q_0052.rationale: Internal consistency correlates each item with all other items on a multi-item scale; stronger coefficients closer to 1.0 indicate less random error and a more reliable scale; observational studies and those requiring judgments by two or more data gatherers must report interrater reliability; and reliability testing determines the measurement error in an instrument.
q_0052.trap: (D) hardens a guideline into a rule. The chapter gives 0.80 and 0.90 as benchmarks but states explicitly that there is no absolute value below which interrater reliability is unacceptable.

q_0053.stem: Before using a newly written adherence scale, a team compares the items against how the concept is described in the literature, asks content experts to rate the relevance of each item, and reviews study participants' responses to the items. Which statements about this validity work are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: All three activities are sources of evidence for content validity
Comparing items against the description of the concept in the literature is face validity
The content experts' evaluation may be reported as an index
Face validity is a fourth type of validity, separate from content validity, in this chapter
Content validity examines whether the scale includes all the major elements relevant to the construct
q_0053.rationale: Content validity examines the extent to which the measurement method or scale includes all the major elements or items relevant to the construct, and its evidence comes from three sources: how well items reflect the description of the concept in the literature, which is face validity; content experts' evaluation of item relevance, which may be reported as an index; and study participants' responses to the items.
q_0053.trap: (D) is imported from other texts. In this chapter face validity is one evidence source inside content validity, not a separate type of validity.

q_0054.stem: A researcher administers a new depression scale and the existing Hamilton Rating Scale to the same participants at the same time and obtains correlations of 0.40 to 0.80. Which evidence is this?
options: Predictive validity
Divergent validity
Convergent validity
Content validity from participant responses
q_0054.rationale: Convergence involves administering a new instrument and an existing one that measures the same construct at the same time, with a strong positive correlation expected; the CES-D correlated 0.40 to 0.80 with the Hamilton Rating Scale.
q_0054.trap: Simultaneous administration also describes concurrent validity, so timing alone will not sort these. Convergence compares two measures of the same construct; concurrent validity estimates present performance on a different criterion.

q_0055.stem: A hope scale correlates -0.6 with a hopelessness scale administered at the same time. How should this result be interpreted?
options: The hope scale lacks reliability, so the correlation cannot be interpreted
Validity is not supported, because validity evidence requires positive correlations
Convergent validity is supported, because the magnitude exceeds 0.4
Divergent validity is supported, because instruments measuring opposite concepts are expected to correlate negatively
q_0055.rationale: Divergence involves administering instruments that measure opposite concepts, such as hope versus hopelessness or despair, and expecting a negative correlation, for example in the range of -0.4 to -0.8.
q_0055.trap: (B) is the reflex that a minus sign means failure. This is the mirror of the convergence item: the same construct gives a positive correlation, opposite constructs give a negative one, and both support construct validity.

q_0056.stem: Investigators administer the CES-D to a group of people diagnosed with depression and a group without that diagnosis, predicting the diagnosed group will score higher. Which evidence is this?
options: Construct validity from contrasting groups
Criterion-related validity
Content validity from expert review
Stability reliability
q_0056.rationale: Contrasting-groups evidence compares groups expected or known to differ; on the CES-D, the group diagnosed with depression is expected to score higher.
q_0056.trap: (B) is tempting because a clinical diagnosis sounds like a criterion. Criterion-related validity uses a participant's score to infer performance on another variable, not to separate two already-known groups.

q_0057.stem: Scores on a health-promotion-behaviors scale collected at enrollment are used to forecast participants' blood pressure, BMI, and minutes of exercise one year later. Which validity is being examined?
options: Concurrent validity
Predictive validity
Convergent validity
Content validity
q_0057.rationale: Predictive validity is the extent to which an individual's score on an instrument can be used to predict future performance or behavior on a criterion; the chapter's example is a health-promotion-behaviors scale predicting future BP, BMI, and minutes of exercise.
q_0057.trap: The distinguishing feature is timing alone. A criterion measured in the future makes it predictive no matter how strong or weak the resulting correlation is.

q_0058.stem: A researcher uses participants' current self-esteem scores to estimate their present ability to cope with illness. Which validity is this, and what distinguishes it from its counterpart?
options: Predictive validity; the two are distinguished by the strength of the correlation
Concurrent validity; the two are distinguished by whether a criterion standard was used
Concurrent validity; the two are distinguished by the timing of the measurement of the other criterion
Convergent validity; the two are distinguished by whether both instruments measure the same construct
q_0058.rationale: Concurrent validity is the extent to which an individual's score can be used to estimate her or his present or concurrent performance on another variable; the difference between concurrent and predictive validity is the timing of the measurement of the other criterion.
q_0058.trap: (A) invokes strength. Strength never separates these two, and this item is the mirror of the predictive-validity item: present versus future is the whole distinction.

q_0059.stem: An observation instrument used in a study achieves an interrater reliability of 0.55. What does the chapter conclude about that instrument's validity in this study?
options: Validity is unaffected, because reliability and validity are independent properties
Validity can still be established by adding more content experts to the review panel
Only stability is compromised; criterion-related validity may still be acceptable
If a measurement method does not have acceptable reliability, then it is not valid
q_0059.rationale: You cannot consider validity apart from reliability, and if a measurement method does not have acceptable reliability, then it is not valid.
q_0059.trap: The dependency runs one direction only. A reliable instrument is not automatically valid, but an unreliable one cannot be valid, and that one-way relationship is the testable point.

q_0060.stem: A team plans to use the CES-D, which was developed in mental health settings, with patients receiving cancer treatment. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Validity testing evaluates the use of an instrument for a specific group or purpose rather than the instrument itself
An instrument may be valid in one situation but not in another
Whether the CES-D is valid for this population should be established by pilot-testing in the new population
Validity is an all-or-nothing property that the CES-D already possesses
Readability is essential if an instrument is to be considered valid and reliable for a sample
q_0060.rationale: Validity varies from one sample to another and one situation to another, so validity testing evaluates the use of an instrument for a specific group or purpose; the chapter's own case is that the CES-D's validity for cancer patients must be established by pilot-testing in the new population. Readability is essential if an instrument is to be considered valid and reliable for a sample.
q_0060.trap: (D) inverts the chapter's statement that validity, like reliability, is not an all-or-nothing phenomenon but is measured on a continuum, and that no instrument is completely valid.

q_0061.stem: A screening tool detects 97.6 percent of adolescents who are truly at risk according to the criterion standard. Which property is being described, and what follows from a high value?
options: Sensitivity; the test has a low percentage of false negatives
Sensitivity; the test has a low percentage of false positives
Specificity; the test has a low percentage of false negatives
Specificity; the test has a low percentage of false positives
q_0061.rationale: Sensitivity is the proportion of patients with the disease who have a positive test result, the true-positive rate; a highly sensitive test is very good at identifying the disease in a patient and has a low percentage of false negatives.
q_0061.trap: (B) pairs the right term with the wrong error. Sensitivity is computed inside the diseased group, so the only mistake it can minimize is the false negative.

q_0062.stem: In the ASQ implementation study, only 43.3 percent of patients who were not at risk on the criterion standard screened negative. Which property is low, and what is the consequence?
options: Sensitivity is low, so a high percentage of true cases are missed
Specificity is low, so the test produces a high percentage of false positives
Specificity is low, so the test produces a high percentage of false negatives
Negative predictive value is low, so a negative screen cannot be trusted
q_0062.rationale: Specificity is the proportion of patients without the disease who have a negative test result, the true-negative rate; a very specific test has a low percentage of false positives, so a specificity of 43.3 percent means many false positives.
q_0062.trap: (C) swaps the error type. Specificity is computed inside the disease-free group, where the only possible mistake is a false positive. This is the mirror of the sensitivity item.

q_0063.stem: Developers revise a screening instrument so that it captures a larger proportion of true cases. According to the chapter, what usually happens to its other property?
options: Specificity usually increases in parallel
Specificity is unaffected, because the two are computed on different groups
The test usually becomes less specific
The negative predictive value usually falls below 0.1
q_0063.rationale: As a test becomes more sensitive, it usually becomes less specific.
q_0063.trap: (D) misuses the likelihood ratio cutoffs. A likelihood ratio greater than 10 rules the disease in and one less than 0.1 almost rules it out; 0.1 has nothing to do with predictive values.

q_0064.stem: Which statements about the ASQ (Ask Suicide Screening Questions) as reported in the chapter are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The ASQ has 4 items, and a "yes" to any item counts as a positive screen
In the development study against the SIQ criterion standard, sensitivity was 97.6 percent and specificity was 65.6 percent
In the implementation study, sensitivity was 93.3 percent and specificity was 43.3 percent
A high negative predictive value means the patient probably does not have the disease, which reduces the number of uncomfortable, costly treatments
In the implementation study, 53 percent of patients who screened positive presented with suicide-related complaints
q_0064.rationale: The ASQ is a 4-item screen used in a pediatric emergency department with patients aged 10 to 21, where a yes to any item is a positive screen; the development study reported sensitivity 97.6 percent, specificity 65.6 percent, and NPV 96.9 percent, while the implementation study reported 93.3 percent, 43.3 percent, and an NPV calculated at 98.98 percent.
q_0064.trap: (E) reverses the finding. It was 53 percent of patients who screened positive who did NOT present with suicide-related complaints, and they were more likely to be male, African American, and carrying externalizing behavior diagnoses.

q_0065.stem: Which statements about diagnostic test accuracy are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: A highly sensitive test is very good at identifying the disease in a patient
A highly specific test is very good at identifying the patients without a disease
Specificity is the true-positive rate
A likelihood ratio greater than 10 rules in the disease
A likelihood ratio less than 0.1 almost rules out the disease
q_0065.rationale: A highly sensitive test is very good at identifying the disease and a highly specific test is very good at identifying patients without it; sensitivity is the true-positive rate and specificity is the true-negative rate. A likelihood ratio above 10 rules the disease in and one below 0.1 almost rules it out.
q_0065.trap: (C) is the most common inversion in this section. Specificity is the true-NEGATIVE rate; the positive likelihood ratio is the ratio of true-positive to false-positive results and the negative likelihood ratio is the ratio of true-negative to false-negative results.

q_0066.stem: Using a CES-D cutoff score of 15 or higher, which values does the chapter report for older adults?
options: Sensitivity 89 percent, specificity 70 percent
Sensitivity 87 percent, specificity 92 percent
Sensitivity 70 percent, specificity 89 percent
Sensitivity 92 percent, specificity 87 percent
q_0066.rationale: At a score of 15 or higher, CES-D sensitivity is 89 percent in adults and 92 percent in older adults, and specificity is 70 percent in adults and 87 percent in older adults.
q_0066.trap: (A) gives the adult figures and (B) transposes the two properties, so match both the population and the direction. Note also that this benchmark cutoff of 15 is not the same number as the score of 16 or higher that the chapter names as the extensively used cutoff for depression.

q_0067.stem: A researcher plans to have participants select from an ordered series of categories of a variable that are assumed to be based on an underlying continuum. How does the chapter characterize this strategy?
options: It is the crudest form of measurement involving scaling techniques
It is the most commonly used scaling technique
It measures the strength, magnitude, or intensity of subjective feelings
It requires that interrater reliability be reported
q_0067.rationale: A rating scale lists an ordered series of categories of a variable that are assumed to be based on an underlying continuum, and the chapter calls it the crudest form of measurement involving scaling techniques.
q_0067.trap: (B) belongs to the Likert scale and (C) to the visual analog scale. Rating scales are also easy to develop, but the chapter warns against end statements so extreme that no participant will select them.

q_0068.stem: A 15-item Likert scale is scored by summing the item values into a single total. What does the chapter say about the level of measurement here?
options: Each item and the summed score are both ordinal
Each item is technically ordinal-level data, but the summed score is often analyzed as interval-level data
Each item is interval-level data, but the summed score must be treated as ordinal
Both the item and the summed score are ratio, because zero is a possible value
q_0068.rationale: Although the values of each item are technically ordinal-level data, the summed score is often analyzed as interval-level data.
q_0068.trap: Both halves of that sentence are true, and an exam item can test either half on its own. Do not resolve the tension by assigning one level to everything.

q_0069.stem: A Likert scale is written with six response options and no midpoint. What is this version called, and what is the argument against including a midpoint?
options: A parallel form; a midpoint lowers internal consistency
An evaluation-type scale; a midpoint biases responses toward agreement
A forced choice version; a middle "uncertain" option allows the participant to avoid making a clear choice
A forced choice version; a midpoint converts ordinal data into nominal data
q_0069.rationale: An odd number of options puts uncertain or neutral in the middle, which is controversial because it allows the participant to avoid making a clear choice; using four or six options with no midpoint is a forced choice version.
q_0069.trap: (A) borrows a reliability term. Parallel forms are two versions of an instrument used to test equivalence, not a response-option layout.

q_0070.subtopic: visual analog scales and the CES-D
q_0070.stem: A researcher wants to measure the intensity of patients' dyspnea with a visual analog scale. Which construction matches the chapter's description?
options: An ordered series of five declarative statements, each followed by a response scale
A 100-mm line whose anchors are set at the most commonly reported values to improve discrimination
A numeric rating scale from 1 to 10 read aloud to the patient
A line usually 100 mm long with right-angle stops at either end and bipolar anchors that span the entire range possible
q_0070.rationale: The VAS is a line usually 100 mm long with right-angle stops at either end, presented horizontally or vertically, with bipolar anchors beyond each end that must span the entire range possible, such as no pain and unbearable pain; participants place a mark through the line.
q_0070.trap: (A) describes a Likert scale, since declarative statements each followed by a scale is the Likert signature. (B) violates the rule that anchors must span the entire range possible.

q_0071.subtopic: visual analog scales and the CES-D
q_0071.stem: Which statements about the CES-D as described in the chapter are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It has four response options scored 0 through 3
The response "Occasionally or a moderate amount of the time" corresponds to 3 to 4 days
Total scores range from 0 to 60
Higher scores indicate more depressive symptoms
A score of 25 or higher is the extensively used cutoff for depression
q_0071.rationale: The CES-D's four options are rarely or none, less than 1 day, scored 0; some or a little, 1 to 2 days, scored 1; occasionally or a moderate amount, 3 to 4 days, scored 2; and most or all, 5 to 7 days, scored 3. Total scores range from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating more depressive symptoms.
q_0071.trap: (E) inflates the cutoff. A score of 16 or higher is the extensively used cutoff for depression, while 15 appears only as the cutoff used for the sensitivity and specificity benchmarks. Two different numbers, easy to merge into one.

q_0072.stem: A researcher comparing an intervention group and a control group begins from the assumption that both groups are components of the same population relative to the study variables. Which framework is being applied, and how is that assumption stated?
options: Probability theory, stated as the effect size
Decision theory, stated as the null hypothesis
Probability theory, stated as the research hypothesis
Decision theory, stated as the confidence interval
q_0072.rationale: Decision theory assumes that all of the groups in a study are components of the same population relative to the variables under study, an assumption expressed as the null hypothesis, which states there is no difference between or among the groups.
q_0072.trap: Probability theory is the other named framework, but it is used to explain the extent of a relationship or the probability that an event will occur or be accurately predicted. It is not the same-population assumption, and it is up to the researcher to provide evidence for a genuine difference.

q_0073.stem: An analysis reports p = 0.23. What does that value mean?
options: The two groups differ by 23 percentage points
23% of participants fell outside the confidence interval
There is a 23% probability that the outcome occurs
The result is significant at the 0.23 level
q_0073.rationale: Probability ranges from 0 to 1 and can be expressed as a decimal or a percentage; p = 0.23 means a 23% probability that the outcome occurs.

q_0074.stem: In a published study, which value reveals the risk of a Type I error in that particular study?
options: The effect size
The power level
Beta
The probability (p) value
q_0074.rationale: The chapter's summary is explicit: the probability (p) value reveals the risk of a Type I error in a particular study.
q_0074.trap: Students routinely attach p to Type II risk. Type II risk is the province of power and beta; p speaks only to the chance of calling something significant when it is not.

q_0075.stem: Which value, established before the study begins, reveals whether the probability value met the cutoff point?
options: The alpha (level of statistical significance)
The probability (p) value
The coefficient of determination
The standard deviation
q_0075.rationale: The alpha value, set before the study, reveals whether the probability value met the cutoff point; alpha is the probability level at which results are judged to indicate a statistically significant difference between groups.
q_0075.trap: This is the mirror of the previous item. Sort it by timing: alpha is chosen in advance and is a threshold; p comes out of the analysis and is a risk estimate.

q_0076.stem: Which statements about the alpha level in a nursing study are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is set before data collection begins
The level of significance selected for most nursing studies is 0.05
It is calculated from the sample data once the analysis is complete
If p is less than or equal to alpha, the groups are considered significantly different, that is, members of different populations
It reveals whether the probability value met the cutoff point
q_0076.rationale: Alpha is set before data collection, is 0.05 for most nursing studies, and functions as the cutoff: p at or below it means the groups are considered significantly different and therefore members of different populations.
q_0076.trap: (C) inverts the whole logic. Nothing about alpha is derived from the data; a cutoff chosen after seeing the results is not a cutoff.

q_0077.stem: A researcher set alpha at 0.05 and obtained p = 0.051. The report states the findings "approached significance." How should a consumer of research evaluate this statement?
options: Acceptable, because 0.051 rounds to 0.05
Acceptable, provided the sample was large enough for adequate power
Inappropriate; decision theory requires an absolute cutoff, so the groups are not significantly different
Inappropriate; the researcher should reset alpha to 0.10 and reanalyze
q_0077.rationale: Decision theory requires that the cutoff point selected for a study be absolute, and the chapter calls it inappropriate to state that findings approached significance at p = 0.051 when alpha was 0.05. Under decision theory that result means the groups are not significantly different.
q_0077.trap: "Approached significance" sounds like careful hedging, which is exactly why it survives in published abstracts. The chapter names this phrase specifically as the error.

q_0078.stem: A study set alpha at 0.05. One comparison yields p = 0.001 and another yields p = 0.05. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Both comparisons are statistically significant
The p = 0.001 comparison is more significant than the p = 0.05 comparison
The level of significance is dichotomous, so there are no degrees of significance
From a probability standpoint, the chance the groups are from the same population is 1 in 1000 at p = 0.001 and 5 in 100 at p = 0.05
The p = 0.05 comparison should be reported as approaching significance
q_0078.rationale: Once alpha is set at 0.05, a result of 0.001 is not considered more significant than 0.05 — the level of significance is dichotomous, with no degrees of significance. From a probability-theory perspective the two still differ in Type I error risk: 1 in 1000 versus 5 in 100.
q_0078.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because the two p values genuinely do differ in Type I risk. The distinction the chapter draws is that they differ in risk, not in significance. And p = 0.05 with alpha at 0.05 is significant, not "approaching" anything.

q_0079.topic: type I and type II error
q_0079.stem: A study concludes that a fall-prevention bundle significantly reduced falls. In fact the null hypothesis was true and there is no difference between the groups. What has occurred?
options: A Type I error
A Type II error
A correct decision, because the p value met alpha
A power failure, because power fell below 0.80
q_0079.rationale: A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is rejected when it is true — saying something is significant when it is not.
q_0079.trap: The tell is which hypothesis was true and what the researcher did with it. Rejecting a true null is Type I; the significance of the p value is irrelevant to naming the error.

q_0080.topic: type I and type II error
q_0080.stem: A study reports no significant difference in pressure injury rates between two turning schedules. A later, larger trial establishes that a real difference does exist. Which error did the first study make, and by which symbol is it represented?
options: Type I error, symbolized by alpha
Type I error, symbolized by beta
Type II error, symbolized by alpha
Type II error, symbolized by beta
q_0080.rationale: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is regarded as true but is in fact false — saying something is not significant when it is. It is symbolized by beta.
q_0080.trap: This is the mirror of the previous item. Alpha belongs to Type I, beta to Type II; pairing the right error name with the wrong Greek letter is the standard half-credit trap.

q_0081.topic: type I and type II error
q_0081.stem: In 5% of statistical tests, the value of one of the groups can be expected to fall outside the 95% range and yet still belong to the same population. What is this situation called?
options: A nondirectional result
A Type I error
A Type II error
An effect size of zero
q_0081.rationale: If groups come from the same population their values fall within the 95% range; a value outside it leads to concluding they belong to different populations. In 5% of tests that conclusion is wrong while the groups still belong to the same population, which is a Type I error.
q_0081.trap: The 5% here is the same 5% as alpha = 0.05. That is why the level of significance is what indicates Type I risk.

q_0082.topic: type I and type II error
q_0082.stem: A researcher changes the level of significance from 0.05 to 0.01 to be more conservative. What is the consequence?
options: Both Type I and Type II risk decrease
Both Type I and Type II risk increase
Type I risk decreases and Type II risk increases
Type I risk increases and Type II risk decreases
q_0082.rationale: The risk of a Type I error is greater at 0.05 (5 in 100) than at 0.01 (1 in 100), while the risk of a Type II error is greater at 0.01 than at 0.05. Tightening alpha trades one error for the other.
q_0082.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because "more conservative" sounds like it should be safer in every direction. Any option claiming a stricter alpha reduces both errors is wrong.

q_0083.topic: type I and type II error
q_0083.stem: Compared with an alpha of 0.01, an alpha of 0.05 carries which risk profile?
options: Less Type I risk and more Type II risk
More Type I risk, at 5 in 100 rather than 1 in 100, and less Type II risk
More Type I risk and more Type II risk
Identical risk, because significance is dichotomous
q_0083.rationale: At alpha = 0.05 the chance of a Type I error is 5 in 100, versus 1 in 100 at 0.01; Type II risk moves in the opposite direction and is greater at 0.01.
q_0083.trap: This is the same tradeoff run backward from the previous item. (D) misapplies a true statement — significance is dichotomous, but that says nothing about error risk across different alpha levels.

q_0084.topic: type I and type II error
q_0084.subtopic: type II risk in nursing research
q_0084.stem: The chapter concludes that the risk of a Type II error is often high in nursing studies. Which reasons does it give? Select all that apply.
options: Many nursing studies are conducted with small samples
Instruments frequently do not accurately and precisely measure the variables
Multiple variables interact, and examining only a few can let small differences between groups be overlooked
Type II errors are often caused by flaws in the research methods
Nursing studies conventionally set alpha at 0.001 rather than 0.05
q_0084.rationale: The chapter attributes Type II errors to flaws in research methods, and names small samples, imprecise instruments, and multiple interacting variables of which only a few are examined as the reasons Type II risk is often high in nursing studies.
q_0084.trap: (E) is false on its own terms — 0.05 is the conventional nursing alpha — and it also reverses the tradeoff, since a stricter alpha would raise Type II risk rather than being an argument against it.

q_0085.stem: Which elements are the four parameters of a power analysis, any three of which allow the fourth to be calculated? Select all that apply.
options: Power
Level of significance
Effect size
Sample size
Level of measurement
q_0085.rationale: Cohen's four parameters of a power analysis are power, level of significance, effect size, and sample size; if three of the four are known, the fourth can be calculated.
q_0085.trap: (E) is a real and heavily tested concept in this chapter, but it belongs to test selection, not power analysis.

options: The probability level at which results are judged to indicate a statistically significant difference
The probability that a statistical test will detect a significant difference that exists
The degree to which the phenomenon is present in the population
The probability that the null hypothesis is rejected when it is true
q_0086.rationale: Power is the probability that a statistical test will detect a significant difference that exists.
q_0086.trap: Every distractor is a real chapter definition attached to the wrong term — (A) is alpha, (C) is effect size, (D) is a Type I error.

q_0087.stem: A researcher planning a nursing intervention study can expect only a small effect size. What sample size does the chapter indicate is often needed to detect a significant difference?
options: 30 or more
50 or more
100 or more
200 or more
q_0087.rationale: In many nursing studies only small effect sizes can be expected, and with a small effect a sample of 200 or more is often needed to detect a significant difference.
q_0087.trap: Small effect sizes themselves arise from small samples, weak study designs, and instruments that measure only large changes — so the fix is not simply to accept the small effect and proceed.

q_0088.stem: A study fails to reject the null hypothesis and reports a power level of 0.65. How should a consumer of research respond?
options: Question the validity of the nonsignificant findings, because power is below 0.80
Accept the nonsignificant findings, because power above 0.50 is adequate
Conclude that a Type I error occurred
Conclude that alpha was set too low
q_0088.rationale: The power level should be discussed in studies that fail to reject the null hypothesis, and if power is below 0.80 you need to question the validity of the nonsignificant findings. The minimum acceptable power is 0.80.
q_0088.trap: (C) inverts the error. A nonsignificant finding that may be wrong is a candidate Type II error, not a Type I error.

q_0089.stem: A student claims that the height data collected from one nursing class "fits the normal curve exactly." Why is that claim inaccurate?
options: The normal curve is a theoretical frequency distribution of all possible values in a population, and no real distribution exactly fits it
The normal curve applies only to nominal-level data
The normal curve requires a sample of at least 200 before it can be applied
The normal curve describes samples rather than populations, so populations fit it less well
q_0089.rationale: The normal curve is a theoretical frequency distribution of all possible values in a population; however, no real distribution exactly fits the normal curve. It was developed by Johann Gauss in 1795 at age 18.
q_0089.trap: Because so much of inferential statistics depends on the normal curve, students treat it as a description of real data. It is a model, not a measurement.

q_0090.stem: Which statements about the normal curve and standard deviations are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Approximately 68% of values fall within 1 SD above and below the mean
Exactly 95% of values fall within 2 SDs above and below the mean
95.5% of values fall between -2 and +2 SDs
99% of values fall within 2.58 SDs
Each tail beyond 1.96 SDs from the mean contains 2.5% of values
q_0090.rationale: The landmarks are 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 1.96 SDs, 95.5% within 2 SDs, and 99% within 2.58 SDs; the tails below -1.96 and above +1.96 SDs hold 2.5% each.
q_0090.trap: (B) is the fine-grained inversion. 95% goes with 1.96 SDs, not 2 SDs; a full 2 SDs captures 95.5%. Both numbers are in the chapter and the exam can use either.

q_0091.stem: A researcher hypothesizes that anxiety scores will differ between two groups but does not predict which group will score higher. Which test is indicated, and where does the 5% lie?
options: One-tailed, with all 5% in the upper tail
One-tailed, with all 5% in the lower tail
Two-tailed, with 2.5% in each tail
Two-tailed, with 5% in each tail
