q_0091.rationale: A two-tailed test is the analysis of a nondirectional hypothesis, and the 5% is split across both tails at 2.5% each.
q_0091.trap: (D) doubles the alpha without meaning to. Splitting 5% across two tails yields 2.5% per tail, not 5% per tail.

q_0092.stem: A researcher predicts specifically that the intervention group will have lower anxiety scores than the control group. Which statement about the appropriate test is accurate?
options: A two-tailed test is required, because comparing two groups always splits the 5% across both tails
A one-tailed test is indicated, but it carries less power than a two-tailed test
A one-tailed test is indicated, and it increases the possibility of a Type II error
A one-tailed test is indicated, and it is more powerful, decreasing the possibility of a Type II error
q_0092.rationale: A one-tailed test is used when the hypothesis is directional, with all 5% in a single tail; one-tailed tests are uniformly more powerful than two-tailed tests, decreasing the possibility of a Type II error.
q_0092.trap: (B) and (C) both assume that concentrating the alpha in one tail is a concession. It is the opposite — the cost of a one-tailed test is that the researcher must have sufficient knowledge of the variables to predict which tail the difference will fall in.

q_0093.stem: A researcher summarizes the blood types of a sample. Which measure of central tendency is appropriate?
options: The mode
The median
The mean
The standard deviation
q_0093.rationale: The mode is the numerical value or score that occurs with greatest frequency and is the appropriate measure for nominal data.
q_0093.trap: The mode does not necessarily indicate the center of the data set, which is why students reject it — but for nominal categories no other measure of central tendency applies.

q_0094.stem: A study's income data contain several extreme outliers. Which measure of central tendency is the research report most likely to present, and why?
options: The mean, because it uses every score in the data set
The median, because it is not affected by extreme scores or outliers
The mode, because outliers cannot be the most frequent value
The mean, because outliers cancel out above and below
q_0094.rationale: If the study has outliers, the mean is most affected by these, and the median might be the measure of central tendency included in the research report.
q_0094.trap: (A) is true as a description of the mean and is exactly why it fails here — using every score is what lets a handful of extreme values drag it.

q_0095.stem: Which statements about measures of central tendency are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: In a perfect normal distribution the mean, median, and mode are equal
The median is the 50th percentile of an ungrouped frequency distribution
The mean is the measure least affected by extreme scores
With an even number of scores the median is the average of the two middle scores and may not be an actual score in the data set
A distribution with more than two modes is described as bimodal
q_0095.rationale: All three measures coincide in a perfect normal distribution; the median is the exact center, or 50th percentile, and with an even number of scores it is the average of the two middle scores, so it may not be a member of the data set.
q_0095.trap: (C) reverses the outlier rule — the mean is the measure most affected by extreme scores. (E) misnames the count: two modes is bimodal, more than two is multimodal.

q_0096.stem: A sample has a mean score of 5.28 with an SD of 2.22. Approximately 68% of the sample falls between which two values?
q_0096.rationale: One SD below the mean is 5.28 minus 2.22 = 3.06 and one SD above is 7.50, so about 68% of the sample falls in that interval. Two SDs would give 0.84 to 9.72.
q_0096.trap: (A) is the 2 SD interval, which holds about 95.5%, not 68%. Match the percentage in the stem to the number of SDs before computing.

q_0097.stem: A report gives a mean pain score of 5.28 with an SD of 2.22. What does the standard deviation tell the reader?
options: The distance between the highest and lowest scores in the sample
The proportion of participants who scored above the mean
The interval within which the population mean falls 95% of the time
The average deviation of a value from the mean, indicating the degree of error that would result if the mean alone were used to interpret the data
q_0097.rationale: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and is the average difference or deviation value; it indicates the degree of error that would result if the mean alone were used to interpret the data.
q_0097.trap: (C) describes the 95% confidence interval, which is a different reported statistic even though both accompany a mean.

q_0098.stem: Which statements about confidence intervals and z-scores are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: A 95% CI indicates that 95% of the time the population mean would fall within that interval
A 95% CI indicates that 95% of the participants' scores fall within that interval
Confidence intervals can be calculated around parameters such as correlation coefficients and t-test values
The mean expressed as a z-score is 0
A z-score of -2 indicates a score 2 SDs above the mean
q_0098.rationale: The 95% CI indicates that 95% of the time the population mean would fall within this interval; CIs are usually calculated for 95% and 99% and can be built around any population parameter, including correlation coefficients and t-test values. A z-score expresses deviation from the mean in SD units, so the mean itself is 0.
q_0098.trap: (B) is the standard misreading of a CI — it is a statement about where the population mean sits, not about where participants sit. (E) drops the sign: values above the mean are positive z-scores, below are negative.

q_0099.stem: A study reports r = -0.72 between hours of sleep and perceived fatigue. How should this be interpreted?
options: A weak relationship, because the coefficient is negative
A moderate relationship in which both variables change in the same direction
A strong relationship establishing that sleep loss causes fatigue
A strong inverse relationship, in which high scores on one variable occur with low scores on the other
q_0099.rationale: Strength is judged by the absolute value: below 0.3 is weak, 0.3 to 0.5 moderate, and above 0.5 strong. A negative correlation is inverse, meaning a high score on one variable occurs with a low score on the other.
q_0099.trap: (A) is the single most common correlation error — reading the minus sign as weakness. Strength decreases as r approaches 0 from either direction, so -0.72 is strong.

q_0100.stem: Which statements about the Pearson product-moment correlation are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It examines the relationship between two variables measured on a single sample
It indicates both the nature and the magnitude of the relationship
It establishes whether variable A leads to or causes variable B
Its values range from -1 to +1, with 0 indicating no relationship
It is symmetrical, giving no indication of the direction of the relationship
q_0100.rationale: Pearson correlation is an inferential technique for bivariate correlations, giving the nature (positive or negative) and the magnitude of a relationship between two variables measured on one sample, with values from -1 to +1.
q_0100.trap: (C) is the causal reading. Because correlational outcomes are symmetrical, it is not possible to establish whether A causes B or B causes A — the analysis gives no indication of direction at all.

q_0101.stem: A study reports r = 0.6 for anxiety and depression. What percentage of the variance is explained by the relationship between the two variables?
q_0101.rationale: Explained variance is indicated by r squared and expressed as a percentage: r = 0.6 gives r squared = 0.36, or 36% explained variance.
q_0101.trap: (C) reads r itself as a percentage. The correlation and the proportion of variance it explains are different numbers, and the second is always the smaller for any r between 0 and 1.

q_0102.stem: A regression model is reported with R squared giving 26% and model significance tested by ANOVA, F(4,79) = 7.051, p < 0.001. What does the 26% represent?
options: The percentage of variance in the dependent variable explained by the model
The percentage of participants whose outcomes the model predicted correctly
The correlation between the predictors and the outcome
The probability that the model result reflects a Type I error
q_0102.rationale: In regression, R squared multiplied by 100% gives the percentage of variance explained; the chapter's worked example reports 26%, with the model tested for significance by ANOVA at F(4,79) = 7.051, p < 0.001.
q_0102.trap: (D) confuses the model's explanatory power with the p value. Type I risk here is carried by p < 0.001, not by R squared. Standardized beta coefficients, not R squared, identify which individual predictors are significant.

q_0103.stem: Which judgments determine which statistical analysis is appropriate for a study? Select all that apply.
options: Whether the question focuses on differences or on relationships and associations
The level of measurement of the data
How many groups are being compared
Whether the samples are independent or paired
The alpha level the researcher selected
q_0103.rationale: Four judgments determine the appropriate analysis: differences versus relationships, level of measurement, number of groups, and independent versus paired samples.
q_0103.trap: (E) matters enormously for interpreting the result but plays no part in choosing the test. Alpha is set before data collection regardless of which test will be run.

q_0104.stem: Body weight in kilograms is measured for all participants, but the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shows the values are not normally distributed. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Parametric, because weight is ratio-level data
Parametric, because the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test checks only for outliers
Nonparametric, because parametric analysis requires interval or ratio data and a normal distribution
Nonparametric, because ratio-level data are always analyzed nonparametrically
q_0104.rationale: Parametric analyses are conducted when variables are at the interval or ratio level and the values are normally distributed; both conditions are required. Nonparametric analyses are conducted when variables are at the nominal and ordinal levels.
q_0104.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because level of measurement is the criterion students memorize first. Interval or ratio data that are not normally distributed do not automatically qualify for parametric analysis.

q_0105.stem: Each participant's pretest score serves as the control for that same participant's posttest score. How are these observations classified?
options: Independent, because each participant contributes one score to each condition
Independent, because no randomization to separate arms occurred
Paired, but only if the participants were also randomly assigned
Paired (dependent), because the observations are related to one another
q_0105.rationale: Paired or dependent groups exist when participants or observations are related in some way to the selection of other participants or observations, which includes a participant serving as their own control with the pretest as the control.
q_0105.trap: Misclassifying a pretest-posttest design as independent samples changes the correct test. Paired designs also include matched pairs and twins with one in each group, and groups sometimes matched on age and severity of illness.

q_0106.stem: Participants are randomly assigned to either a treatment group or a control group, and no participant appears in both. How are these samples classified?
options: Independent, because the selection of one participant is unrelated to the selection of the others
Paired, because both groups were drawn from the same recruitment pool
Independent, only if the groups are also matched on age and severity of illness
Paired, because random assignment produces equivalent matched groups
q_0106.rationale: Independent groups exist when the selection of one study participant is unrelated to the selection of other participants, as when participants are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups.
q_0106.trap: This is the mirror of the pretest-posttest item. (C) and (D) both treat matching as something random assignment accomplishes; matching is a deliberate pairing procedure and is what makes groups dependent.

q_0107.subtopic: matching the test to the comparison
q_0107.stem: Two independent groups are compared on mean serum sodium, a ratio-level variable that is normally distributed. Which test is appropriate?
options: Chi-square test of independence
t-test
ANOVA
Post hoc analysis
q_0107.rationale: The t-test is used to examine differences between two groups with interval or ratio level data.
q_0107.trap: (C) is the reflex answer for anyone who has learned ANOVA as the general difference test. ANOVA is for three or more groups; using the wrong one of this pair is the classic error in both directions.

q_0108.subtopic: matching the test to the comparison
q_0108.stem: Three clinic sites are compared on whether patients did or did not return for follow-up, a yes or no outcome. Which test is appropriate?
options: t-test, because the outcome has two categories
ANOVA, because there are three groups
Chi-square test of independence, because the outcome is nominal
Pearson product-moment correlation, because two variables are involved
q_0108.rationale: The chi-square test of independence is used with three or more groups when the data are nominal or ordinal; ANOVA and ANCOVA require interval or ratio data.
q_0108.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because "three or more groups" points straight at ANOVA. Number of groups alone never settles the test — level of measurement has to be checked with it, and nominal data rule out the parametric options.

q_0109.subtopic: matching the test to the comparison
q_0109.stem: A researcher compares four groups using ANOVA and reports a significant F value. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: ANOVA tests for differences in variance, not in means alone
The significant F value identifies which specific pair of groups differs
Post hoc analyses are conducted to determine the location of the differences among groups
Bonferroni correction, Newman-Keuls, Tukey HSD, Scheffe, and Dunnett are post hoc options
Between-group variance is the variation of the group means around the grand mean
q_0109.rationale: ANOVA tests for differences in variance, partitioned into within-group variance and between-group variance around the grand mean; with more than two groups it is not possible to determine from the ANOVA where the significant differences occur, so post hoc analyses are conducted.
q_0109.trap: (B) is the single most tested misreading of ANOVA. A significant F tells you that the groups differ, not which ones — with only two groups the location would be obvious, which is precisely why post hoc tests exist for three or more.

q_0110.subtopic: what appraisal is and is not
q_0110.stem: A student's written appraisal of a published study concludes that the researcher lacks the expertise to conduct this kind of work. Why does this comment fall outside an intellectual critical appraisal?
options: It is directed at the creator rather than at the product that was created
It uses the word critique, which the chapter treats as a negative term
It reports a weakness without also reporting a strength
It was made before the entire study had been read
q_0110.rationale: Intellectual critical appraisal is associated with critical thinking and evaluation and is directed at the product that is created, such as a study, rather than at the creator, and it involves evaluating the quality of that product.
q_0110.trap: (C) names a real violation of the principles, but the fatal problem here is what the comment is aimed at, not how balanced it is. The chapter does examine author expertise as part of appraisal, which makes attacking the researcher feel permissible; the appraisal still belongs to the study.

q_0111.stem: Which characteristics identify a high-quality study as the chapter describes one? Select all that apply.
options: Focuses on a significant problem
Produces findings that can be generalized to all similar patient populations
Demonstrates sound methodology
Produces credible findings and indicates implications for practice
Provides a basis for additional studies
q_0111.rationale: A high-quality study focuses on a significant problem, demonstrates sound methodology, produces credible findings, indicates implications for practice, and provides a basis for additional studies.
q_0111.trap: (B) borrows quantitative sampling language and applies it as a universal quality marker. Generalizability is not one of the five markers, and for qualitative work the chapter rejects it outright in favor of transferability.

q_0112.stem: A baccalaureate student asks how much critical appraisal skill her program is expected to give her. Which response reflects the chapter's role expectations?
options: Appraisal skill is expected only after several years of clinical practice
Basic and advanced analytic appraisal skills are both acquired at the baccalaureate level
Appraisal is a doctoral competency, and prelicensure students are expected only to read findings
Basic research and appraisal knowledge is acquired in the baccalaureate program, with more advanced analytic skills at the master's and doctoral levels
q_0112.rationale: Basic research and appraisal knowledge is acquired in the baccalaureate program, and more advanced analytic skills are developed at the master's and doctoral levels.
q_0112.trap: (C) is tempting because beginners are told to focus on step 1 of the appraisal process, but QSEN identifies striving to base practice on evidence as a competency for associate and baccalaureate prelicensure students. Beginning is not the same as being excused.

q_0113.stem: Which statements about who critically appraises research, and why, are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: QSEN identifies striving to base practice on evidence as a competency for associate and baccalaureate prelicensure students
Evidence-based practice is essential in agencies seeking or maintaining Magnet status
Advanced analytic appraisal skills are the ones acquired in the baccalaureate program
Nurse educators appraise studies to expand their clinical knowledge base, update curriculum content, and serve as role models for students
Practicing nurses appraise studies so that practice rests on current research evidence rather than on tradition or trial and error
q_0113.rationale: Students, practicing nurses, educators, and researchers all appraise studies; QSEN names EBP a prelicensure competency, Magnet status depends on EBP, educators update curriculum and model the skill, and practicing nurses appraise so practice is not built on tradition or trial and error.
q_0113.trap: (C) inverts the levels. Baccalaureate preparation supplies basic research and appraisal knowledge; the more advanced analytic skills come at the master's and doctoral levels.

q_0114.stem: A unit council emails a current research article to staff each month and posts copies in the break room, and the manager reports this as the unit's critical appraisal activity. Which evaluation is accurate?
options: The activity qualifies as critical appraisal because staff are reading current studies
The activity increases awareness of study findings but is not sufficient for critical appraisal to occur
The activity qualifies as critical appraisal for quantitative studies but not for qualitative ones
The activity satisfies the requirement for evidence-based practice in an agency seeking Magnet status
q_0114.rationale: Reading research journals and posting or emailing current studies at work can increase nurses' awareness of study findings but are not sufficient for critical appraisal to occur; nurses must question the quality of the studies, the credibility of the findings, and the meaning for practice, as in a research journal club.
q_0114.trap: (D) is the plausible pull because EBP really is essential to Magnet status, so anything labeled EBP feels like it counts. Circulating articles produces awareness, not appraisal.

q_0115.stem: A nurse's appraisal of a study lists seven weaknesses, names no strengths, and concludes that the study is worthless. Which principle of critical appraisal does this appraisal violate?
options: Read and critically appraise the entire study
Indicate the type of study conducted and identify its steps or elements
Identify strengths as well as weaknesses, and avoid being overly critical
Discuss the usefulness of the findings for practice
q_0115.rationale: All studies have strengths and weaknesses, so attention must be given to all aspects, and the appraiser should try not to be overly critical in identifying weaknesses or overly flattering in identifying strengths.
q_0115.trap: Harshness reads as rigor, which is why this appraisal looks thorough. An appraisal made entirely of weaknesses is a failed appraisal, not a demanding one.

q_0116.stem: A second nurse appraises the same study, reports that it has no weaknesses at all, and recommends an immediate practice change. Compared with an appraisal that lists only weaknesses, how does this one rate?
options: Stronger, because it identifies strengths as the principles require
Stronger, because it discusses usefulness of the findings for practice as the principles require
Weaker, because recommending a practice change falls outside the scope of critical appraisal
Equally flawed, because being overly flattering is named as an error alongside being overly critical
q_0116.rationale: The principles state that all studies have strengths and weaknesses and that the appraiser should be objective and realistic, neither overly critical in identifying weaknesses nor overly flattering in identifying strengths.
q_0116.trap: (B) misuses a real principle. Discussing usefulness for practice is required, but it does not license skipping the weaknesses, and this is the mirror image of the only-weaknesses appraisal, not an improvement on it.

q_0117.stem: An appraisal of a study contains the single comment, "The sampling section is inadequate." Which principles of critical appraisal does this comment fail to satisfy? Select all that apply.
options: Provide specific examples of the strength or weakness identified
Examine the organization and presentation of the report
Provide a rationale for the comment, documented with sources from the current literature
Identify the study's strengths as well as its weaknesses
Appraise only those sections of the report that bear directly on practice
q_0117.rationale: The principles require identifying both strengths and weaknesses, providing specific examples of each, and providing a rationale for comments documented with sources from the current literature.
q_0117.trap: (E) inverts principle 1, which requires reading and critically appraising the entire study. (B) is a genuine principle but concerns the report's overall organization and presentation, which this comment says nothing about either way.

q_0118.stem: A journal club is appraising one quantitative study and one qualitative study. Which statements about the appraisal process are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The same three steps apply to both quantitative and qualitative studies
Quantitative and qualitative studies are appraised with the same detailed set of questions
The first step is identifying the steps or elements of the study
The second step is determining the study's strengths and weaknesses or limitations
The final step is evaluating the credibility and meaning of the study findings
q_0118.rationale: The same three steps apply to both study types: identify the steps or elements of the study, determine strengths and weaknesses, and evaluate the credibility and meaning of the findings.
q_0118.trap: (B) is the near miss. The steps are identical, but the detailed question sets are not — Box 12.2 supplies the quantitative questions and Box 12.3 the qualitative ones.

q_0119.stem: A student appraising her first research report is unsure where to concentrate her effort. Which step should she expect to occupy most of it?
options: Determining the study's strengths and weaknesses
Evaluating the credibility and meaning of the findings
Identifying the steps or elements of the study
Performing all three steps at the same time
q_0119.rationale: Because you are new to critical appraisal of research, you will probably be focusing on step 1, identifying the steps of the research process in the report.
q_0119.trap: (D) describes the experienced appraiser, who might perform two or three steps simultaneously. It is a real description in the chapter, just not of a beginner.

q_0120.stem: While analyzing interview data, a qualitative researcher documents every coding decision and the reasoning behind it. Which element of trustworthiness is she primarily supporting?
options: Credibility
Dependability
Transferability
Confirmability
q_0120.rationale: Dependability is the documentation of the steps taken and decisions made during analysis, and it is supported by the audit trail, the researchers' record of the analysis process.
q_0120.trap: (D) is the immediate neighbor and the next event in the sequence. Documenting the decisions is dependability; other researchers reading that record and agreeing is confirmability.

q_0121.stem: An independent research team reviews the audit trail of a completed qualitative study and agrees that the authors' conclusions are logical. Which element of trustworthiness has been demonstrated?
options: Credibility
Dependability
Transferability
Confirmability
q_0121.rationale: Confirmability is the extent to which other researchers can review the audit trail and agree that the authors' conclusions are logical.
q_0121.trap: This is the mirror of the dependability item, and (A) pulls because agreement sounds like believability. Credibility is the reader's confidence that the results reflect the views of the participants, not another team's endorsement of the reasoning.

q_0122.stem: A nurse on a rural home health team reads a qualitative study of rural family caregivers and wants to use its findings. Which statement about applying them is correct?
options: The findings are not generalizable, but they may be transferable to other settings with similar participants
The findings are generalizable because the researchers reached data saturation
The findings may not be applied outside the setting in which the study was conducted
The findings are generalizable only if the study also reported statistical significance
q_0122.rationale: Qualitative findings are not generalizable but are transferable or applicable in other settings with similar participants.
q_0122.trap: (C) overcorrects the rule everyone memorizes. "Not generalizable" does not mean "not usable" — the chapter's word is transferable, to settings and participants like the ones studied.

q_0123.stem: Which statements about trustworthiness in qualitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Trustworthiness is the extent to which a study is dependable, confirmable, credible, and transferable
Confirmability means the researcher returns to the participants to confirm that the findings are correct
Credibility is the reader's confidence that the results reflect the views of the participants
Dependability is supported by the researchers' audit trail
When findings are appraised to be confirmable and dependable, they have more credibility
q_0123.rationale: Trustworthiness is the determination that a qualitative study is rigorous and of high quality, meaning it is dependable, confirmable, credible, and transferable, and findings appraised as confirmable and dependable carry more credibility.
q_0123.trap: (B) describes member checking, not confirmability. Confirmability as defined here is about other researchers reviewing the audit trail, not about the participants ratifying the results.

q_0124.stem: A nurse comfortable with quantitative terms asks which element of trustworthiness plays the role that reliability plays in quantitative research. Which answer is correct?
options: Credibility
Transferability
Dependability
Trustworthiness as a whole
q_0124.rationale: Dependability, along with confirmability, is the qualitative analogue of reliability; credibility corresponds to validity, and transferability takes the place of generalizability.
q_0124.trap: (A) is the reflex because credibility sounds like results you can rely on. Credibility maps to validity. If the stem says reliability, the answer is dependability or confirmability.

q_0125.stem: An appraiser finds that a qualitative study's stated purpose does not match the research questions it asks. How should this finding be characterized?
options: A weakness, because logical inconsistency is a common flaw in qualitative research just as it is in quantitative research
A neutral observation, because qualitative research has fewer rules than quantitative research
A strength, because a qualitative purpose is expected to evolve during data collection
A weakness only if the researchers also failed to report an audit trail
q_0125.rationale: Common weaknesses in qualitative studies are logical inconsistencies and improperly applied methods, the same as in quantitative research, and the logical links among study elements are critical to the credibility of the study.
q_0125.trap: (B) leans on a true statement to reach a wrong conclusion. Qualitative research does have fewer rules, which is why appraising it can seem daunting, but that does not exempt purpose, research questions, and method from having to line up.

q_0126.stem: In appraising a hermeneutic phenomenological study, reviewers noted that the researchers cited Max van Manen but never cited Heidegger. Why does this count as an appraisal finding?
options: Van Manen is not recognized as an expert in hermeneutic phenomenology
A study must cite at least two methodologists to be considered rigorous
Citing a contemporary expert instead of the originator invalidates the study's findings
Heidegger originated hermeneutic phenomenology, and consistency with experts in the method used is part of the appraisal
q_0126.rationale: Van Manen is a commonly cited contemporary expert in hermeneutic phenomenology, but the researchers did not cite Heidegger, the originator; guidance from an expert in the method matters, and areas of consistency are strengths whereas areas of inconsistency may indicate weaknesses.
q_0126.trap: (C) overstates a real finding into a fatal one. This is a documented weakness in one section of the appraisal, not grounds to discard the study.

q_0127.stem: In a study appraised in the chapter, participants completed a quality-of-life scale as a pretest, received a 4-week transition-to-care intervention, and then completed the same scale as a posttest. The appraisal judged the design weak. What was the stated reason?
options: The same instrument was administered twice, which invalidates the posttest scores
There was only one group and no separate comparison group, so the change from pretest to posttest could have been caused by extraneous variables
The intervention lasted only 4 weeks, which is too short to change quality of life
The researcher's credentials did not include preparation in the study's clinical area
q_0127.rationale: The design was judged weak because there was only one group and no separate comparison group to determine whether the treatment was effective or whether the change from pretest to posttest was caused by extraneous variables.
q_0127.trap: (D) inverts the chapter's own note on author expertise. The researcher was a DNP-prepared family nurse practitioner with clinical and research experience in that area, and the design was still judged weak — expertise does not rescue a design.

q_0128.stem: A nurse manager states that the unit's new fall-prevention protocol is evidence-based because it was drawn entirely from the most recent meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Which response best reflects the chapter's definition of evidence-based practice?
options: Evidence-based practice requires that only findings from meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials be used
Evidence-based practice requires that expert clinical opinion take precedence over published research findings
Evidence-based practice requires integrating the best research evidence with clinical expertise, patient circumstances, and patient values
Evidence-based practice requires that each unit generate its own research before changing a protocol
q_0128.rationale: EBP is defined as a complex phenomenon that requires integration of the best research evidence with clinical expertise, patient circumstances, and patient values in the delivery of quality, safe, cost-effective care.
q_0128.trap: (A) sounds rigorous and does name the strongest evidence source, but research evidence is only one of the four elements. A protocol built from evidence alone, with no attention to clinical expertise, patient circumstances, or patient values, is not EBP.

q_0129.stem: A chief nursing officer is building the case for investing in an evidence-based practice program. Which statements about the benefits and institutional drivers of EBP are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The greatest benefits of EBP are improved outcomes for patients, providers, and healthcare agencies
Magnet status is approved through the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
EBP improves nurses' satisfaction and facilitates achievement of accreditation requirements
The Joint Commission revised its accreditation criteria to emphasize patient care outcomes achieved through EBP
Agencies seeking or maintaining Magnet status must document research-related outcomes
q_0129.rationale: The greatest benefits of EBP are improved outcomes for patients, providers, and healthcare agencies; leaders recognize that EBP promotes quality outcomes, improves nurses' satisfaction, and facilitates achievement of accreditation requirements. Magnet status is approved through the American Nurses Credentialing Center.
q_0129.trap: AHRQ is real in this chapter and is easy to reach for, but its role here is funding the evidence-based practice centers, not conferring Magnet status. Magnet runs through the ANCC.

q_0130.stem: A staff nurse objects that evidence-based guidelines cannot account for the patient in front of her. Which statement identifies the challenge she is naming along with the chapter's recommended response?
options: Nursing has few systematic reviews compared with medicine and psychology, so the response is to require randomized controlled trials before any guideline is adopted
Research evidence is generated from population data and applied to individual patients, so poor outcomes under a guideline should be reported and, if possible, published as a case study
Guidelines should be applied uniformly to all patients regardless of circumstances or values, so individual variation is not a concern
Research evidence is generated from individual case studies and applied to populations, so poor outcomes should be managed by discontinuing the guideline on the unit
q_0130.rationale: Evidence is generated based on population data and then applied in practice to individual patients, who respond in unique ways or have unique circumstances and values. Patients with poor outcomes under a guideline should be reported and, if possible, published as a case study, and the NIH supports translational research to improve use of evidence across patient populations and settings.
q_0130.trap: (C) is the reflex answer for anyone who reads evidence-based as protocol-driven, but uniform application regardless of patient circumstances contradicts both this challenge and the definition of EBP. (A) names a genuine challenge from the chapter and attaches the wrong response to it.

q_0131.stem: A committee is grading the evidence it has gathered on a wound-care intervention. Which source provides the strongest evidence?
options: A single randomized controlled trial with a large sample
A meta-synthesis of qualitative studies of patients' wound-care experiences
A mixed-methods systematic review of intervention and descriptive studies
A systematic review that includes a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
q_0131.rationale: The strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews that include meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.
q_0131.trap: (A) is tempting because the RCT is the strongest individual design, so students pick the design rather than the synthesis. A synthesis of RCTs outranks any single trial.

q_0132.stem: Which statements about sources of evidence for changing practice are consistent with the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews that include meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials
Meta-syntheses provide important evidence for changing practice
Only meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials may be used to develop research-based protocols
Mixed-methods systematic reviews provide important evidence for changing practice
Individual studies also provide important evidence for changing practice
q_0132.rationale: The chapter names systematic reviews containing meta-analyses of RCTs as the strongest evidence but explicitly states that meta-syntheses, mixed-methods systematic reviews, and individual studies also provide important evidence for changing practice.
q_0132.trap: (C) overstates the text. Ranking meta-analysis highest is not the same as excluding everything else, and the chapter goes further: research evidence can be combined with other sources of knowledge such as theories, scientific principles, expert opinion, and case reports to build research-based protocols. Expert opinion is weakest on its own but legitimate as a supplement.

q_0133.stem: In the chapter's PICO question on IM injection technique, the statement "IM injection given with 5 to 10 seconds of aspiration in all sites, regardless of age and volume" occupies which position?
options: P, the population
I, the intervention
C, the comparison intervention
O, the outcome
q_0133.rationale: The comparison intervention is the practice being measured against, which here is aspirating 5 to 10 seconds in all sites regardless of age and volume. The intervention is IM injection given without aspiration in the right site based on volume of medication and age.
q_0133.trap: Aspirating feels like the thing being done, so students slot it into I. In this question the comparison is the older outgoing practice and the intervention is the newer no-aspiration technique. The outcome is IM injection of vaccine without complications.

q_0134.stem: A nurse is administering a vaccine into an adult patient's deltoid. Based on the current evidence in the chapter, what should the nurse do about aspiration?
options: Aspirate for 5 to 10 seconds before injecting
Do not aspirate, because aspiration is recommended only for the dorsogluteal site
Aspirate for 5 to 10 seconds only if the volume exceeds 2 mL
Do not aspirate, because aspiration is no longer recommended at any injection site
q_0134.rationale: Current evidence supports no aspiration in the deltoid, ventrogluteal, and vastus lateralis sites, and aspiration only in the dorsogluteal site because of the close proximity of the gluteal artery.
q_0134.trap: (D) overcorrects. The dorsogluteal exception survives, though researchers recommend that the dorsogluteal site not be used if possible. (A) is the older guideline that this chapter uses as its example of practice lagging behind evidence.

q_0135.stem: Which statements about IM injection site selection are consistent with the chapter's clinical practice guideline? Select all that apply.
options: The vastus lateralis is the preferred site for infants
The ventrogluteal or deltoid site is appropriate for adults
The dorsogluteal site is preferred for adults because it tolerates large volumes
Aspiration for 5 to 10 seconds is required in the vastus lateralis in infants
Large volumes of 2 to 5 mL should be given in the ventrogluteal site in adults
q_0135.rationale: Infants receive injections in the vastus lateralis; toddlers and children in the vastus lateralis or deltoid; adults in the ventrogluteal or deltoid. Large volumes of 2 to 5 mL go in the ventrogluteal site for adults, and small volumes of 2 mL or less go in the deltoid for toddlers, children, and adults.
q_0135.trap: (C) is the specific practice error the chapter documents nurses still making. Nurses over-used the dorsogluteal site despite evidence favoring the ventrogluteal. (D) applies the outdated aspiration rule to a site where current evidence says not to aspirate.

q_0136.stem: A study by Thomas and colleagues reported what finding about aspiration practice, and what point does the chapter use it to make?
options: 90% of nurses were still aspirating after IM injections 74% of the time, showing that the guideline itself was flawed
74% of nurses had adopted the no-aspiration guideline within one year, showing that dissemination in nursing is efficient
74% of nurses reported complications from IM injections, showing the need for a new comparison intervention
74% of nurses were still aspirating after IM injections 90% of the time, showing that evidence existing is not the same as evidence being used
q_0136.rationale: 74% of nurses were still aspirating after IM injections 90% of the time, and researchers therefore recommended additional education in nursing programs and continuing education. This is the chapter's central point about the gap between available evidence and used evidence.
q_0136.trap: (A) inverts the two percentages. 74% is the proportion of nurses; 90% is how often those nurses aspirated.

q_0137.stem: A nurse using the Stetler Model critically appraises the retrieved reports and finds only three small, methodologically weak studies. According to the model, what happens next?
options: The nurse proceeds to comparative evaluation and weighs feasibility despite the weak evidence
The nurse combines the weak studies into a meta-analysis to strengthen them
The findings are considered inadequate for use in practice and the process stops
The nurse proceeds to translation and applies the findings on a trial basis
q_0137.rationale: In Phase II, Validation, the reports are critically appraised for scientific soundness. If the studies are limited in number, weak, or both, the findings are considered inadequate for use in practice and the process stops.
q_0137.trap: (A) reflects the reflex that a model is a checklist you always run to the end. Stetler builds in a stop. (B) borrows a true statement from Phase II, that a systematic review, meta-analysis, or meta-synthesis greatly strengthens the evidence, and misapplies it as a way around a failed appraisal.

q_0138.stem: After reading a synthesis on delirium, a nurse changes no order and no procedure, but now understands why her older postoperative patients become confused and analyzes her unit's practice dynamics differently. Under the Stetler Model, this is which kind of application?
options: Cognitive
Instrumental
Symbolic
Comparative
q_0138.rationale: Phase IV, Translation/Application, describes cognitive, instrumental, and symbolic application. Cognitive application means the research base is a means of modifying a way of thinking or one's appreciation of an issue, such as improving understanding of a situation or allowing analysis of practice dynamics.
q_0138.trap: (D) is not a kind of application at all. Comparative evaluation is the name of Phase III, and reusing that word as an application type is the easiest way to be pulled off the three real options.

q_0139.stem: Which items are the four parts of Phase III, Comparative Evaluation/Decision Making, in the Stetler Model? Select all that apply.
options: Substantiation of the evidence
Pilot testing of the research-based protocol
Fit of the evidence with the healthcare setting
Feasibility of using the findings
Concerns with current practice
q_0139.rationale: Phase III has four parts: substantiation of the evidence, fit of the evidence with the healthcare setting, feasibility of using the findings, and concerns with current practice.
q_0139.trap: (B) belongs to the Iowa Model, where research-based protocols are pilot-tested before adoption. Importing an Iowa step into a Stetler phase is the most common error on this content.

q_0140.stem: A nurse assessing feasibility under the Stetler Model is applying the model's three Rs. What are they?
options: Relevance, reliability, and rigor
Research, review, and revision
Results, reporting, and replication
Risks, resources, and readiness
q_0140.rationale: Feasibility is assessed as potential risks, resources needed, and readiness of those involved.
q_0140.trap: The three Rs are the feasibility test only, which is one of the four parts of Phase III. They are not a summary of the whole model.

q_0141.stem: An evidence-based practice team finds sound evidence supporting a change, but the change is complex and would involve pharmacy, respiratory therapy, and nursing, and coordinating it will take considerable time. Which Phase III decision fits this situation?
options: To consider using the research evidence
To use the research evidence
Not to use the research evidence
To return to Phase II for revalidation
q_0141.rationale: Phase III allows three decisions: to use the evidence, to consider using it, or not to use it. To consider using it applies when a change is complex and involves multiple disciplines, so more time is needed to coordinate.
q_0141.trap: Students who remember only a use or do-not-use binary force this item into (B) or (C). Not to use is reserved for evidence that is not strong, or for risks or costs of change that are too high in comparison with the benefits.

q_0142.stem: A hospital's risk-management reports show a cluster of medication errors on night shift, and the unit council decides to search the literature. In the Iowa Model, this beginning is best described as which of the following?
options: A knowledge-focused opportunity
A problem-focused trigger
Stetler Phase I preparation
An expanded philosophy of care
q_0142.rationale: Problem-focused triggers are clinical problems and data from risk management, process improvement, benchmarking, and financial reports.
q_0142.trap: (C) is the near-neighbor across models. An individual nurse deciding whether to apply findings is Stetler; a trigger arising from agency risk-management data is Iowa.

q_0143.stem: Which of the following would the Iowa Model classify as knowledge-focused opportunities? Select all that apply.
options: New research findings published on an intervention the unit uses
A change in national agency standards and guidelines
Benchmarking data showing the unit's catheter-associated infection rate is above its peers
An updated professional model of care, which is a Magnet recognition requirement
A question raised by the institutional standards' committee
q_0143.rationale: Knowledge-focused opportunities include new research findings, changes in national agency or organizational standards and guidelines, an expanded philosophy of care, an updated professional model of care (a Magnet recognition requirement), and questions from the institutional standards' committee.
q_0143.trap: (C) is benchmarking data, which the chapter lists as a problem-focused trigger alongside risk management, process improvement, and financial reports. Sorting a given example into the right kind of trigger is the whole point of this distinction.

q_0144.stem: An Iowa Model team has confirmed that its topic is an agency priority and has developed a research-based protocol for oral care in ventilated patients. What comes next, before the protocol is adopted?
options: Implement the protocol agency-wide and monitor outcomes through quality improvement
Submit the protocol to the institutional standards' committee for symbolic approval
Conduct additional studies, because a protocol cannot be built from existing evidence
Pilot-test the protocol and evaluate its impact on patient care, personnel, and the agency
q_0144.rationale: Research-based protocols, algorithms, guidelines, and policies are pilot-tested and then evaluated for impact on patient care, personnel, and the agency. If outcomes are favorable, the change is adopted, integrated, and sustained, with key outcomes monitored through quality improvement.
q_0144.trap: (A) skips the pilot. Agency-wide rollout and QI monitoring are what follow a favorable pilot, not what replace it. (C) applies only when the evidence found is inadequate, which is not the case here.

q_0145.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Stetler Model from the Iowa Model?
options: Stetler is a user-initiated, conscious critical-thinking process organized in five phases, while Iowa is an agency-level model that begins with triggering issues or opportunities
Stetler is an agency-level model organized around triggers, while Iowa is an individual nurse's critical-thinking process
Stetler applies only at the institutional level, while Iowa applies only to individual practitioners
Both models require pilot testing before any decision about using the evidence is made
q_0145.rationale: The intent of the Stetler Model is to make using research evidence in practice a conscious, critical thinking process that is initiated by the user, organized in five phases. The Iowa Model promotes the implementation of EBP by nurses in clinical agencies and begins with triggering issues or opportunities.
q_0145.trap: (C) half-remembers a real detail and inverts it. Stetler evidence can be used at the institutional level, producing policies, algorithms, procedures, protocols, and formal programs, or at the individual level by RNs, educators, and policy makers. It is not restricted to institutions.

q_0146.stem: A research team states that it will use whatever combination of methods best answers the clinic's question rather than committing in advance to an objective or a subjective worldview. Which philosophical position does this describe?
options: Postpositivism
Constructivism
Positivism
Pragmatism
q_0146.rationale: Pragmatism focuses on solving problems by whatever methods fit the problem or question; researchers have exchanged the dichotomy of positivism and constructivism for the middle ground of pragmatism.
q_0146.trap: Postpositivism is the objective view of quantitative researchers and constructivism the subjective view of qualitative researchers. Mixed methods is explicitly neither.

q_0147.stem: A clinic manager concerned about missed follow-up appointments works with a researcher who runs focus groups and administers an exit survey. Which statement best explains the choice of design?
options: The goal was to obtain the information they needed to improve the attendance rate, which is consistent with a pragmatic approach
Focus groups are required before any survey instrument may be administered
Qualitative data are considered more trustworthy than survey data in clinic settings
A mixed methods design was needed to satisfy the constructivist requirements of the study
q_0147.rationale: Pragmatists want to obtain the information they believe they need to resolve an issue, and the chapter names improving the attendance rate as the goal that made mixed methods the fitting choice.
q_0147.trap: (D) misassigns the philosophy. Constructivism is the subjective view of qualitative researchers, and a mixed methods study is neither constructivist nor postpositivistic.

q_0148.stem: Which statements describe why researchers combine quantitative and qualitative methods in one study? Select all that apply.
options: The strengths of one method can compensate for the possible limitations of the other
The strengths of each method interact in a complementary way
Methods are chosen to fit the problem or question rather than a fixed worldview
Mixing methods removes the need for the study to take any philosophical position
Mixing methods converts subjective qualitative findings into objective facts
q_0148.rationale: The chapter frames the rationale two ways — one method's strengths compensate for the other's possible limitations, or, stated positively, the strengths of each method interact in a complementary way — under the pragmatic principle of fitting methods to the question.
q_0148.trap: (D) is wrong because pragmatism is itself the position taken. (E) confuses data conversion, an integration technique, with a change in the nature of the findings.

q_0149.stem: A team knows little about how adolescents with cystic fibrosis judge the quality of their healthcare services. They interview 25 adolescents and young adults, content-analyze the transcripts, convert the determinants they identify into questionnaire items, and survey 113 respondents. Which design is this?
options: Convergent concurrent
Exploratory sequential
Explanatory sequential
Parallel
q_0149.rationale: An exploratory sequential strategy begins with the collection and analysis of qualitative data, followed by the collection of quantitative data, and is often selected for underresearched topics so the first phase can inform the quantitative phase.
q_0149.trap: Explanatory sequential is the reflex answer for anyone who treats explore and explain as interchangeable. Exploratory means the qualitative phase comes first.

q_0150.stem: Researchers evaluating an intensive outpatient PTSD program measure symptom change in 30 women and 18 men with a mean age of 43.48 years, then interview participants about which parts of the treatment they found helpful. Which design is this?
options: Explanatory sequential
Exploratory sequential
Convergent concurrent
Parallel
q_0150.rationale: In an explanatory sequential strategy the researcher collects and analyzes quantitative data and then collects and analyzes qualitative data to explain the quantitative findings.
q_0150.trap: This is the mirror of the cystic fibrosis item. Anchor on the word explain — the numbers already exist and the qualitative arm explains them, so quantitative came first.

q_0151.stem: The qualitative arm of the explanatory sequential PTSD study used grounded theory coding. What was the stated reason?
options: The researchers lacked resources for a comparison or control group
The goal of the qualitative arm was to generate a tentative theory
Grounded theory is required whenever quantitative data are collected first
Grounded theory produces countable codes suitable for conversion to quantitative data
q_0151.rationale: The qualitative arm used grounded theory coding because the goal was to generate a tentative theory.
q_0151.trap: (A) is true of that study — the missing control group is why qualitative data were added to supplement the quantitative estimates of treatment effects — but it does not explain the choice of grounded theory coding in particular.

q_0152.stem: In the PICU family-stress study, parents were interviewed and completed quantitative stress measures during a single interaction, and the transcripts were not analyzed before the quantitative phase. Why is the design classified as concurrent rather than sequential?
options: Because the qualitative component was emphasized over the quantitative
Because only nine parents from eight families were enrolled
Because the sequence of analysis, not the sequence of contact, determines the design
Because both components addressed the same research question
q_0152.rationale: The interviews came first chronologically, but the transcripts were not analyzed before the quantitative phase and both types of data were collected during one interaction, which is what makes the design concurrent.
q_0152.trap: (A) is a true statement about that study — the qualitative arm was emphasized and the quantitative findings were used to enrich the description — but emphasis is not what classifies the design.

q_0153.stem: A researcher collects survey scores and interview narratives from a single sample during the same period and combines them only after each has been analyzed separately. Which statement about this study is accurate?
options: It is an explanatory sequential design, because the survey was analyzed first
It is an exploratory sequential design, because the interviews informed the survey
It is a convergent concurrent design, and integration must occur during data collection
It is a convergent concurrent design, and integration occurs during the interpretation phase
q_0153.rationale: A convergent concurrent design uses a single sample, or two samples from the same population, and integration happens after the data are analyzed, during the interpretation phase.
q_0153.trap: (C) is the near miss. Concurrent refers to when the data are collected, not to when the two arms are brought together.

q_0154.stem: In a convergent concurrent study, the qualitative and quantitative arms yield the same findings. What is this called, and what does it mean?
options: Cross-validation, which means the two samples came from the same population
Convergence, which strengthens the evidence
Corroboration, which indicates the study should be repeated sequentially
Congruence, which confirms that the sample was representative
q_0154.rationale: When the findings from the qualitative and quantitative methods yield the same findings, that is convergence, and it strengthens the evidence.
q_0154.trap: Confirm, cross-validate, and corroborate are the stated purposes for selecting the design; convergence is the name for the result when the two arms agree.

q_0155.stem: A convergent concurrent study's quantitative and qualitative findings do not agree. How does the chapter say researchers should treat this result?
options: As a failure of the design that requires the study to be repeated
As evidence that the qualitative arm introduced bias
As an opportunity to provide a broader description of the problem
As grounds for reporting only the quantitative findings
q_0155.rationale: Different findings are not a failure; researchers may be able to use them to provide a broader description of the problem.
q_0155.trap: Divergence is not invalidation. Any option calling non-matching results invalid contradicts the chapter.

q_0156.stem: Which statements about the three mixed methods designs are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: A convergent concurrent design is selected to confirm, cross-validate, or corroborate findings
The convergent concurrent design is also called a parallel design
An exploratory sequential design is often selected for underresearched topics
In an explanatory sequential design, qualitative data are collected to explain the quantitative findings
In an exploratory sequential design, the quantitative phase is completed before the qualitative phase is designed
q_0156.rationale: Convergent concurrent, also called parallel, runs both arms at once to cross-validate; exploratory sequential runs qualitative first for underresearched topics; explanatory sequential runs quantitative first and uses qualitative data to explain the results.
q_0156.trap: (E) inverts the exploratory sequential design. It describes explanatory sequential, where phase one is quantitative.

q_0157.stem: Which statements describe the cystic fibrosis study used to illustrate the exploratory sequential design? Select all that apply.
options: Interviews were conducted with 25 adolescents and young adults with cystic fibrosis
Four determinants of quality identified by content analysis were transformed into questionnaire items
The final questionnaire contained 113 items
A panel of 10 experts rated the items for clarity and relevance
The reported content validity was 0.91
q_0157.rationale: Content analysis of interviews with 25 participants produced four determinants of quality, each becoming an individual questionnaire item; a panel of 10 experts rated clarity and relevance for a content validity of 0.91.
q_0157.trap: (C) swaps the instrument length with the sample size. The questionnaire had 24 items and went to 113 participants.

q_0158.stem: A mixed methods team plans to decide how to combine its quantitative and qualitative findings after both data sets have been collected and analyzed. What does the chapter say about that plan?
options: It is appropriate, because integration cannot be planned before the data are seen
It is appropriate only in convergent concurrent designs
Integration should be handled by the qualitative arm, which interprets meaning
Integration is the critical phase and should be given significant thought during development of the study, ideally in the proposal
q_0158.rationale: The capacity of mixed methods designs to answer the research questions depends on effective methods for integrating the data, so integration is the critical phase and should be planned during study development.
q_0158.trap: In a convergent design integration does occur after both arms are analyzed, which makes (A) and (B) feel right. Performing integration late is not the same as planning it late.

q_0159.stem: Which of the following are strategies the chapter names for integrating data in a mixed methods study? Select all that apply.
options: Building the second phase on the findings of the first
Discarding the arm whose findings are weaker
Expanding the view of a phenomenon
Counting qualitative codes and converting them to quantitative data
Strengthening support by interpreting the findings together
q_0159.rationale: The three named integration strategies are building the second phase on the first, expanding the view of a phenomenon, and strengthening support by interpreting the findings together; some researchers also convert data, counting qualitative codes or converting quantitative data into conceptual ideas or themes.
q_0159.trap: (B) contradicts the chapter's handling of divergent findings, which are used to broaden the description rather than to disqualify an arm.

q_0160.stem: Two teams report that their mixed methods studies cost more than a single-method study would have. One ran both arms at the same time; the other ran the qualitative phase first. Which explanation of their different burdens is accurate?
options: The concurrent team needed more elapsed time; the sequential team needed additional personnel
Both teams needed additional personnel, and neither needed more time than a single-method study
The concurrent team needed additional personnel to conduct both arms at the same time; the sequential team needed more elapsed time because phase one had to be completed and analyzed first
Neither design requires more resources than a single-method study once the proposal is funded
q_0160.rationale: Because of the complexity of concurrent designs, additional personnel are needed to conduct all aspects of both arms at the same time, whereas in sequential designs phase one must be completed and analyzed before phase two can be developed or revised.
q_0160.trap: (A) is the straight inversion of the two burdens. Mixed methods studies also require a time commitment that may exceed single-method studies — one team collected data for 4 years — and additional time often translates into a need for greater financial support.

q_0161.stem: A hospital system asks a researcher to determine how patients' health status changed as a result of the nursing care they received. Which methodology is being described?
options: Outcomes research, a rigorous scientific method focused on the end results of patient care
An explanatory sequential mixed methods study
A quality improvement audit of individual nurses' documentation
Comparative effectiveness research comparing two nursing interventions
q_0161.rationale: Outcomes research is a rigorous scientific method focused on the end results of patient care; in nursing it focuses on how a patient's health status changes as a result of the nursing care received or the nursing services delivered.
q_0161.trap: (C) is the reflex for anyone who equates outcomes with chart review. Outcomes research does not examine care at the individual nurse level. Comparative effectiveness research is a real term here, but it names AHRQ's current initiative rather than this study.

q_0162.stem: A researcher studies end results for patients with chronic conditions for whom cure is not always possible. According to AHRQ, which end results are relevant?
options: Cure rate, remission duration, and relapse rate
Structure, process, and outcome
Quality of life, functioning, symptom management, and mortality
Cost per case, length of stay, and readmission rate
q_0162.rationale: AHRQ frames end results as effects people experience and care about, such as a change in their ability to function; for individuals with chronic conditions these include quality of life, functioning, symptom management, and mortality.
q_0162.trap: (D) names economic measures. Economic efficiency is what draws policy makers and insurers to outcomes research, but it is not AHRQ's list of end results.

q_0163.stem: Which study description matches the level of analysis used in outcomes research?
options: Evaluating one nurse's effect on her six assigned patients
Evaluating all of the nursing care provided to patients in a particular ICU
Evaluating one patient's physiological response to a single intervention
Evaluating the documentation accuracy of one unit's charge nurse
q_0163.rationale: Outcomes studies do not examine patient care at the individual nurse or individual patient level; they might instead examine all the nursing care provided to patients in a particular ICU.
q_0163.trap: One of the chapter's own open questions is how to distinguish care provided by nurses from care provided by other professionals — a problem that only exists because the unit of analysis is the aggregate, not the individual.

q_0164.stem: Which statements describe how outcomes research differs from the other methodologies in this text? Select all that apply.
options: Studies are more complex in design, population, settings, and data analyses
Care is examined at the level of the individual nurse and the individual patient
Research teams often include disciplines such as economics and public health
Researchers use a unique theoretical framework
Much of the momentum comes from policy makers, insurers, and the public
q_0164.rationale: Outcomes studies are more complex in design, population, settings, and data analyses, draw on a mix of disciplines including economics and public health, use a unique theoretical framework, and are driven by policy makers, insurers, and the public who base payment on economic efficiency.
q_0164.trap: (B) inverts the level of analysis, which is the aggregate rather than the individual.

q_0165.stem: A researcher catalogs the nursing units, hospitals, and home health agencies where patients received care, along with each organization's leadership and decision-making processes. Within Donabedian's framework, which focus of evaluation is this?
options: Process
Structure
Outcome
Quality
q_0165.rationale: Structure covers the elements of organization and administration, as well as provider and patient characteristics, that guide the processes of care; nursing units, hospitals, and home health agencies are the chapter's examples.
q_0165.trap: (D) is the overriding construct of Donabedian's theory, not one of its three foci. The three foci are structure, process, and outcome.

q_0166.stem: A study documents the practice style nurses use for wound care and whether the unit's standard of care was followed. Which focus of evaluation does this represent?
options: Structure
Outcome
Process
Nursing-sensitive outcome
q_0166.rationale: Process is how care is provided, such as practice style or standard of care.
q_0166.trap: This is the mirror of the structure item. Sort by whether the element describes the setting and its organization (structure) or how care is actually delivered (process).

q_0167.stem: A student claims that most published outcomes studies examine structure, process, and outcome together. Which response is accurate?
options: Correct, because Donabedian's theory is the dominating framework for outcomes research
Correct, because NDNQI participation requires all three
Incorrect, because the theory calls for structure and outcome only
Incorrect, because researchers have had little success including all three simultaneously
q_0167.rationale: A complete quality outcomes study requires simultaneous inclusion of all three and examination of the relationships among them, but researchers have had little success accomplishing this theoretical goal; the funding and cooperation required have not yet been realized.
q_0167.trap: (A) is the reflex, and its premise is true — the theory does dominate outcomes research — which is exactly why students assume complete studies are the norm.

q_0168.stem: The chapter relies on the World Health Organization's definition of quality of care. Why?
options: Because Donabedian's definition applies only to the structure of care
Because the NQF adopted the WHO definition as its national standard
Because quality is not a central construct in Donabedian's theory
Because Donabedian never defined the concept himself, although quality is the overriding construct of his theory
q_0168.rationale: Although quality is the overriding construct of Donabedian's theory, he never actually defined the concept, so the WHO definition is used — the extent to which healthcare services improve desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge.
q_0168.trap: (C) inverts the point. Quality is precisely the overriding construct, which is what makes the missing definition worth noticing.

q_0169.stem: Donabedian's cube depicts which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: The cost of care delivered
Health
The subjects of care
The providers of care
Physical, psychological, and social function
q_0169.rationale: The cube has three dimensions — health, the subjects of care, and the providers of care — and incorporates three aspects of health: physical function, psychological function, and social function.
q_0169.trap: Economic efficiency is what draws payers to outcomes research, but cost is not one of the cube's dimensions.

q_0170.stem: A hospital cites its Magnet designation and its nurses' autonomy in clinical practice as reasons its patients do well. How does the chapter classify these two features?
options: Structural variables, because they are elements of organization that guide the processes of care
Process variables, because they describe how nurses deliver care
Nursing-sensitive patient outcomes, because they are influenced by nursing decisions
Nursing interventions, because they reflect the care delivered by nurses
q_0170.rationale: The organization of nursing care and nursing leadership affect nursing practice and in turn patient outcomes; autonomy in clinical nursing practice is a structural variable recognized as critically important, and Magnet designation is an identified autonomy-enabling structure, verifiable through the ANCC.
q_0170.trap: (D) names a real category from this chapter — nursing interventions are things like a falls risk assessment or a pressure ulcer risk assessment — but autonomy sounds like something nurses do, which is why students file it under process.

q_0171.stem: A researcher studying nursing services variables would examine which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Staffing levels and skill mix
Assignment patterns such as primary nursing, functional assignments, and team nursing
Patients' quality of life six months after discharge
Shift patterns and the ratio of full-time to part-time nurses
Cohesion and communication among nursing staff and between nurses and physicians
q_0171.rationale: Nursing services is a general concept referring to the organization and administration of nursing activities, and the variables studied include skill mix and personnel configuration, staffing levels, assignment patterns, shift patterns, education and experience levels, full-time to part-time ratios, leadership, cohesion and communication, and clinical care maps.
q_0171.trap: (C) is a distal outcome, not a nursing services variable. Nursing services describes the arrangement of care, not the end result of it.

q_0172.stem: A nurse manager states that her unit's lower fall rate proves that nursing care caused the improvement. Which statement about nursing-sensitive patient outcomes corrects her?
options: The outcome is influenced by nursing care decisions and actions, but it may be associated with nursing rather than caused by it
The outcome is caused by nursing care by definition, so her claim is accurate
The outcome is distal, so it cannot be linked to nursing at all
The outcome is a structural variable, so it reflects staffing rather than care
q_0172.rationale: Nursing-sensitive patient outcomes are considered sensitive because they are influenced by nursing care decisions and actions; an outcome may not be caused by nursing but is associated with nursing.
q_0172.trap: The definition deliberately hedges — influenced by and associated with, never caused by. An option asserting nursing causation overstates what the term supports.

q_0173.stem: In the chapter's definition of nursing-sensitive outcomes, the term nursing may refer to which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: The individual nurse
Nurses as a working group
The approach to nursing practice
The physician-directed plan of care
The nursing unit or institution that determines numbers of nurses, salaries, and educational level
q_0173.rationale: Nursing in this definition may mean the individual nurse, nurses as a working group, the approach to nursing practice, or the nursing unit or institution that determines numbers of nurses, salaries, and educational level.
q_0173.trap: The breadth of the term is the point. Reading it as only the individual nurse contradicts the aggregate level at which outcomes research operates.

q_0174.stem: An outcomes study measures patients' signs and symptoms of disease at the completion of a nursing intervention. How is this outcome classified?
options: Distal, because it is measured at the end of the intervention
Proximal, because it is close to the delivery of care
Adverse, because symptoms indicate injury from care
Structural, because symptom control depends on staffing levels
q_0174.rationale: A proximal outcome is close to the delivery of care, and signs and symptoms of disease are the chapter's example.
q_0174.trap: (A) treats timing of measurement as the criterion. Proximity refers to closeness to the care delivered, not to the calendar.

q_0175.stem: An outcomes study measures patients' quality of life one year after discharge. Which statement about this outcome is accurate?
options: It is proximal, because quality of life is a nursing-sensitive measure
It is proximal, because it was measured on patients who received nursing care
It is distal, and it is easier to attribute to nursing than symptom measures are
It is distal, and it is more influenced by external nontreatment factors
q_0175.rationale: A distal outcome is removed from proximity to the care or service received and is more influenced by external nontreatment or nonintervention factors; quality of life is the chapter's example.
q_0175.trap: (C) inverts attribution. Being more influenced by external factors is exactly what makes distal outcomes harder, not easier, to attribute to nursing.

q_0176.stem: A nurse researcher wants a published classification that identifies nurse-sensitive outcomes as proximal or distal. Which resource should she use?
options: The Nursing Outcomes Classification
The National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
The National Guideline Clearinghouse
The National Quality Forum measure portfolio
q_0176.rationale: The Nursing Outcomes Classification identifies proximal and distal nurse-sensitive outcomes for research and practice.
q_0176.trap: NDNQI houses data on nursing-sensitive quality indicators and the National Guideline Clearinghouse summarizes evidence-based clinical practice guidelines. Neither sorts outcomes by proximity to care.

q_0177.subtopic: adverse outcomes and standards of care
q_0177.stem: During an admission for pneumonia, a patient develops a central line infection that prolongs the hospital stay. Under the chapter's definition, how is this best classified?
options: A distal outcome, because it developed after admission
A process measure, because it reflects how care was provided
An adverse outcome, because it results from medical management or a complication rather than the underlying disease
A structural variable, because infection rates depend on staffing
q_0177.rationale: An adverse outcome is a consequence of injury caused by medical management or complication rather than by the underlying disease itself, and generally includes prolonged health care, resulting disability, or death.
q_0177.trap: Deterioration caused by the pneumonia itself would not qualify. The injury has to come from the management or a complication, not from disease progression.

q_0178.subtopic: adverse outcomes and standards of care
q_0178.stem: A researcher evaluating the process of care needs the term for the norm against which quality of care is judged. Which term applies?
options: Practice pattern
Practice style
Functional status
Standard of care
q_0178.rationale: A standard of care is a norm on which quality of care is judged.
q_0178.trap: Practice pattern is described as a concept closely related to practice style, and both describe how care is actually delivered rather than the norm used to judge it. Functional status is a multidimensional construct measured as an outcome.

q_0179.stem: A researcher beginning to evaluate the structure of care identifies and describes its elements. Which elements does the chapter name? Select all that apply.
options: Patients' symptom management after discharge
Leadership
Organizational hierarchy
Decision-making processes and the distribution of power
Financial management
q_0179.rationale: Evaluating structure begins by identifying and describing the elements of the structure using administration and management theories; the elements named are leadership, organizational hierarchy, decision-making processes, distribution of power, and financial management.
q_0179.trap: (A) is an end result and belongs to the outcome focus, not the structure focus.

q_0180.stem: Choosing an instrument for an outcomes study, a researcher asks whether it will register improvement after the intervention. Which measurement property is she evaluating?
options: Sensitivity to change
Content validity
Convergence
Functional status
q_0180.rationale: Sensitivity to change is an important measurement property in outcomes research because researchers are often interested in evaluating how outcomes change in response to healthcare interventions.
q_0180.trap: Content validity is what the expert panel established for the cystic fibrosis questionnaire at 0.91; it addresses whether items represent the concept, not whether the instrument detects change over time.

q_0181.stem: A quality committee needs to consult the national standard-setting organization for healthcare performance measures. Which organization is it, and when was it founded?
options: AHRQ, part of DHHS
