The National Quality Forum, founded in 1999
PCORI, funded through the Recovery Act of 2009
NDNQI, whose database was funded in 1998
q_0181.rationale: The National Quality Forum, founded in 1999, is the national standard-setting organization for healthcare performance measures, with a portfolio of performance measures, serious reportable events, and preferred practices.
q_0181.trap: About one-third of the NQF's measures are patient outcomes such as mortality, readmissions, health functioning, depression, and experience of care. Note also that the NQF holds that quality is as much about influencing positive outcomes as about avoiding negative ones, even though most measures in use focus on failure to meet expected standards.

q_0182.stem: Which organization was created to produce evidence-based information from research guided by patients, caregivers, and the broader healthcare community, and how was it funded?
options: AHRQ, whose number one funding priority is supporting the implementation of PCOR
The National Quality Forum, the national standard-setting body for performance measures
PCORI, funded through the Recovery Act of 2009, with $473 million designated for patient-centered outcomes research
NDNQI, launched by an ANA plan in 1994
q_0182.rationale: PCORI was funded via the Recovery Act of 2009, which designated $473 million for patient-centered outcomes research, and it helps people make informed healthcare decisions through research guided by patients, caregivers, and the broader healthcare community.
q_0182.trap: (A) is tempting because AHRQ's number one funding priority really is improving healthcare quality by supporting the implementation of PCOR, and its current initiative is comparative effectiveness research. AHRQ funds the work; PCORI is the body created to produce it.

q_0183.stem: Which measures were among the nursing-sensitive measures submitted by the ANA under NDNQI? Select all that apply.
options: Nursing staff skill mix
Hospital 30-day mortality rate
Central line-associated bloodstream infection rate
Ventilator-associated pneumonia rate
RN practice environment scale
q_0183.rationale: The ANA's list — the first nationally standardized performance measures of nursing-sensitive outcomes in acute care hospitals — includes nursing staff skill mix, nursing care hours per patient day, catheter-associated urinary tract infection rate, central line-associated bloodstream infection rate, fall and injury rates, hospital- and unit-acquired pressure ulcer rates, nurse turnover rate, the RN practice environment scale, and ventilator-associated pneumonia rate.
q_0183.trap: (B) belongs to the NQF's outcome measures, not the ANA's nursing-sensitive set. Note the lineage: the ANA worked with the American Academy of Nursing Expert Panel on Quality Health Care, used Donabedian's theory as the project framework, and first called the indicators the ANA Nursing Care Report Card, which could facilitate benchmarking across hospitals.

q_0184.stem: A nurse researcher enrolls 480 patients across six medical units and records the frequency of falls, the time of day each fall occurred, and the characteristics of the patients who fell. No intervention is delivered and the units operate as they normally do. Which type of quantitative research is this?
options: Correlational
Descriptive
Quasi-experimental
Experimental
q_0184.rationale: Descriptive research is the exploration and description of phenomena in real-life situations, giving an accurate account of the characteristics of particular individuals, situations, or groups using numbers. It is usually conducted with large numbers of participants in natural settings with no manipulation.
q_0184.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because several variables are being measured at once. Correlational research requires that the study systematically investigate the relationship between those variables, not merely count and categorize them.

q_0185.stem: Which of the following are outcomes of descriptive research as the chapter describes them? Select all that apply.
options: Identification and description of concepts
Determination of the degree and strength of the relationship between two variables
Identification of possible relationships
Development of hypotheses that provide a basis for future quantitative research
Determination that one variable causes a change in another
q_0185.rationale: The chapter gives three outcomes of descriptive studies: identification and description of concepts, identification of possible relationships, and development of hypotheses that provide a basis for future quantitative research.
q_0185.trap: (B) belongs to correlational research, which measures variables and then applies correlational statistics to determine the degree and type of relationship. Descriptive research identifies only possible relationships.

q_0186.stem: A nurse implements a structured early-mobility protocol on one postoperative unit and compares outcomes with a unit receiving usual care. Participants could not be randomly selected because staffing patterns determined which unit each patient entered. Which type of quantitative research is this?
options: Descriptive
Correlational
Quasi-experimental
Experimental
q_0186.rationale: Quasi-experimental research implements an intervention to examine causal relationships but has less control over the implementation of the intervention, the management of the setting, and/or the selection of participants. Inability to randomly select participants points to quasi-experimental.
q_0186.trap: (D) is the reflex answer because an intervention is present. Both quasi-experimental and experimental studies involve interventions; the level of control, not the presence of an intervention, decides which one it is.

q_0187.stem: Which statements about the four types of quantitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Descriptive and correlational studies are typically designed with minimal researcher control
Both quasi-experimental and experimental studies involve implementing an intervention
Experimental research is the most highly controlled of the four types
When little knowledge is available about a phenomenon, experimental studies are conducted first in order to establish control
Descriptive and correlational studies are frequently conducted to provide a basis for quasi-experimental and experimental studies
q_0187.rationale: Descriptive and correlational research are conducted with minimal control, both quasi-experimental and experimental research implement interventions, and experimental research is the highly controlled investigation conducted to predict and control phenomena. When little knowledge is available, descriptive studies are conducted first and provide a basis for correlational and then for the more highly controlled designs.
q_0187.trap: (D) reverses the progression. The four types build on one another from the least controlled to the most controlled, so descriptive work comes first when little is known.

q_0188.stem: Why does the chapter state that nurse researchers conduct more quasi-experimental studies than experimental studies?
options: Quasi-experimental designs provide stronger evidence of causality than experimental designs
Experimental designs cannot examine the effect of one variable on another
Quasi-experimental designs do not require an intervention, which makes them easier to run in practice
In clinical settings researchers frequently cannot select participants randomly or control certain variables related to the intervention or the setting
q_0188.rationale: When studying human behavior, especially in clinical settings, researchers frequently are unable to select participants randomly or to control certain variables related to the intervention or setting, so nurse researchers conduct more quasi-experimental than experimental studies.
q_0188.trap: (A) inverts the hierarchy. Quasi-experimental studies dominate nursing because of feasibility, not because they are the stronger design; the experimental design carries the highest control.

q_0189.stem: A study reports that as smoking pack-years increase, life span decreases. How is this relationship best described?
options: A positive relationship, because both variables were measured with precision
A weak relationship, because the direction is negative
A negative relationship, because the variables vary in opposite directions
No relationship, because the two variables move in different directions
q_0189.rationale: A negative relationship means the variables vary in opposite directions, so that as one increases the other decreases. This is the chapter's own smoking and life-span example.
q_0189.trap: (B) is the classic misread. Negative names the direction of the relationship, not its weakness; a value near negative 1 is a strong relationship.

q_0190.stem: A study finds that the more minutes people exercise each week, the greater their bone density. How is this relationship best described?
options: A positive relationship, because the variables vary together
A positive relationship, because the health outcome is a desirable one
A negative relationship, because exercise reduces the rate of bone loss
A causal relationship, because exercise preceded the change in bone density
q_0190.rationale: A positive relationship means the variables vary together, both increasing or both decreasing. This is the chapter's exercise and bone-density example.
q_0190.trap: (B) is the mirror image of the smoking item's trap. Positive and negative name direction only; they do not mean the finding is good news or bad news.

q_0191.stem: Two correlational findings are reported from the same study: variable pair 1 has a value of negative 0.86 and variable pair 2 has a value of positive 0.14. Which interpretation is accurate?
options: Pair 2 has the stronger relationship because its value is positive
Pair 1 shows no relationship because its value falls below zero
Both values fall outside the range possible for a correlational value
Pair 1 has the stronger relationship, and pair 2 is close to showing no relationship
q_0191.rationale: Correlational values range from negative 1, a perfect negative relationship, to positive 1, a perfect positive relationship, with 0 indicating no relationship. Negative 0.86 is near a perfect negative relationship, while positive 0.14 sits close to zero.
q_0191.trap: (B) treats a negative value as an absence of relationship. It is 0, not any negative number, that indicates no relationship.

q_0192.stem: Which statements about correlational research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is the systematic investigation of relationships between or among variables
Its primary intent is to determine whether one variable causes a change in another
Its findings generate hypotheses that are then tested in quasi-experimental and experimental studies
It uses correlational statistics to determine the degree and the type of relationship present
It is usually conducted with minimal researcher control
q_0192.rationale: Correlational research systematically investigates relationships between or among variables, measures those variables in a sample and applies correlational statistics to determine strength and type of relationship, is designed with minimal control, and generates hypotheses for the causal designs.
q_0192.trap: (B) is the single highest-yield distractor in this chapter. The primary intent of correlational studies is to explain the nature of relationships in the real world, not to determine cause and effect.

q_0193.stem: Wacker et al. (2016) studied the muscle and bone pathology of rickets in mice in a laboratory. How is this study classified?
options: Basic research, because it pursues knowledge for its own sake and works toward general scientific principles
Applied research, because rickets is a clinical condition that nurses treat
Applied research, because the investigators used an experimental design
Basic research, because studies using animals cannot include an intervention
q_0193.rationale: Basic, or pure or bench, research is scientific investigation conducted for the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake, typically laboratory work with animals or humans on physiological functioning, genetics, or pathological processes. The mouse rickets study is the chapter's example of a basic experimental study.
q_0193.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because the topic sounds clinical. Classification follows the purpose of the knowledge being generated, not whether the disease appears in practice.

q_0194.stem: A nurse conducts a study comparing two catheter-care protocols to determine which one reduces catheter-associated infections on her unit. How is this study classified, and what is its aim?
options: Basic research, aimed at establishing general scientific principles
Basic research, aimed at the pleasure of learning and finding truth
Applied research, aimed at describing phenomena in real-life situations without changing them
Applied research, aimed at solving problems and making decisions about outcomes in real-life practice
q_0194.rationale: Applied, or practical, research generates knowledge that will directly influence or improve clinical practice, with the aim of solving problems, making decisions, and predicting or controlling outcomes in real-life practice settings.
q_0194.trap: (C) attaches a descriptive-research purpose to the applied label. Applied names the use to which the knowledge is put; it does not name the study type or the level of control.

q_0195.stem: A researcher chooses to record heart rate with a cardiac monitor rather than palpating the radial pulse for 30 seconds and writing the value on a data sheet. Which element of a rigorous study is being strengthened, and what does strengthening it make possible?
options: Control, which allows the researcher to manipulate the study setting
Precision, which supports transparency and therefore replication
Rigor, which is achieved primarily by increasing the size of the sample
Intervention fidelity, which supports consistent implementation of the intervention
q_0195.rationale: Precision encompasses accuracy, detail, and order and is most explicitly demonstrated in the measurement or quantification of the study variables. The chapter uses this exact monitor-versus-palpation contrast, and notes that precision enables transparency, which enables replication.
q_0195.trap: (D) is plausible because fidelity also concerns consistency, but intervention fidelity is the detailed development and consistent implementation of the intervention, not the way an outcome variable is measured.

q_0196.stem: A researcher studying the effect of relaxation therapy on incisional pain enrolls only patients who have abdominal incisions and who are receiving one type of intravenous pain medication. What is the researcher doing?
options: Establishing intervention fidelity
Operationally defining the dependent variable
Controlling extraneous variables that could interfere with understanding the relationships among the study variables
Obtaining a random sample of postoperative patients
q_0196.rationale: Extraneous variables can interfere with obtaining a clear understanding of the relationships among the study variables. In this worked example the type of surgical incision and the time, amount, and type of pain medication must be controlled, which the researcher accomplishes through the selection criteria.
q_0196.trap: (D) confuses narrowing the sample for control with random selection. Restricting who is eligible controls extraneous variables; it does not make the resulting sample random.

q_0197.stem: Which statement about extraneous variables and rigor is accurate?
options: Extraneous variables occur only in experimental studies, where an intervention is delivered
Extraneous variables exist in all studies, and descriptive and correlational studies are rigorously conducted even though they are designed with minimal control
A tightly controlled design eliminates extraneous variables from a study entirely
Descriptive studies cannot be considered rigorous, because the researcher exercises minimal control
q_0197.rationale: Extraneous variables exist in all studies and can interfere with understanding the relationships among the study variables. Descriptive and correlational studies are rigorously conducted but are often designed with minimal researcher control.
q_0197.trap: (D) equates low control with low rigor. Rigor is the striving for excellence through discipline, adherence to detail, precision, and accuracy, and it is expected of every quantitative design regardless of how much control the design permits.

q_0198.stem: Which statements about control and design in quantitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Control is the imposing of rules by researchers to decrease the possibility of error
Design is the set of rules used to achieve control in research
A design is a blueprint for the conduct of a study that maximizes control over factors that could interfere with the study's desired outcome
Design refers strictly to the plan for collecting data from participants
Quantitative studies range from uncontrolled to highly controlled
q_0198.rationale: Control is the imposing of rules to decrease the possibility of error, which increases the probability that the findings accurately reflect reality. The rules used to achieve control are the design, defined also as a blueprint that maximizes control, and studies range from uncontrolled to highly controlled.
q_0198.trap: (D) is too narrow to be the chapter's definition. Data collection is one part of a design, but the chapter defines design by control, not by data collection.

q_0199.stem: A nurse researcher measures and interviews participants in their own homes and deliberately changes nothing about the home environment. Which setting is this, and which types of study typically use it?
options: Natural or field setting, typically used for descriptive and correlational studies
Partially controlled setting, typically used for descriptive and correlational studies
Highly controlled setting, typically used for bench and experimental studies
Natural or field setting, typically used for experimental studies
q_0199.rationale: A natural or field setting is an uncontrolled real-life situation or environment that the researcher does not manipulate or change, and descriptive and correlational studies are commonly conducted in natural settings.
q_0199.trap: (D) pairs the correct setting with the wrong study type. Experimental research requires a level of control that a natural setting by definition does not provide.

q_0200.stem: A study is conducted in a research center built solely for the purpose of conducting research, where temperature, lighting, and participant activity are all regulated by the investigators. Which setting is this?
options: Natural setting
Field setting
Partially controlled setting
Highly controlled setting
q_0200.rationale: A highly controlled setting is an artificially constructed environment developed for the sole purpose of conducting research, such as a laboratory, research center, or test unit, and it is where bench and experimental studies are conducted.
q_0200.trap: (C) is the near neighbor and the mirror image of this item. A partially controlled setting is a real environment that the researcher has manipulated or modified in some way, not one constructed for research from the beginning.

q_0201.stem: Liao et al. (2017) recruited older adults through convenience sampling and then randomly placed each participant into either an exercise intervention group or a usual-activity group. Which statement about this study is accurate?
options: The sample must have been randomly selected, because random assignment was used
The sample was obtained nonrandomly, and the design was strengthened by the random assignment
The study lacked control, because a nonrandom sample cannot be used in an intervention study
The random assignment converted the study environment into a highly controlled setting
q_0201.rationale: The sample of older adults was obtained by nonrandom convenience sampling, and the design was strengthened by the random assignment of those adults to the exercise intervention or usual activity.
q_0201.trap: (A) is the inversion the chapter warns about directly. Random assignment to groups says nothing about how the sample was selected; nonrandom selection combined with random assignment is a real and common design in nursing research.

q_0202.stem: Which statements about sampling in quantitative nursing research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Sampling is the process of selecting participants who are representative of the population being studied
In random sampling, each member of the population is selected independently and has an equal chance of being included
A population is a subset of the sample that is selected for a particular study
Quantitative nursing studies often are conducted with nonrandom samples, because randomly selected samples are very difficult to obtain
Randomly assigning participants to intervention and control groups increases control and rigor and decreases bias
q_0202.rationale: Sampling selects participants representative of the population; random sampling gives each member an independent and equal chance of inclusion; nursing studies often use nonrandom samples, and participants selected nonrandomly are often randomly assigned to groups to increase control and rigor and decrease bias.
q_0202.trap: (C) reverses the two terms. The population is all the elements that meet the criteria for inclusion, and the sample is the subset of that population whose members are the participants.

q_0203.stem: Moon et al. (2017) built a level-of-care variable as the sum of five questions about chores, shopping, personal care, getting around the home, and transportation, each scored from 1, meaning rarely, to 4, meaning every day. What kind of definition is this?
options: A conceptual definition, because it was drawn from the study framework
A conceptual definition, because it names the components that make up the concept
An operational definition, because it identifies the population of interest
An operational definition, because it specifies how the variable can be measured
q_0203.rationale: An operational definition is developed so that the variable can be measured or an intervention implemented in a study, and scoring, coding, and summing items is measurement.
q_0203.trap: (B) is tempting because the five questions do enumerate the components of caregiving, but attaching scores and summing them is measurement. If a definition names numbers, scales, coding, or instruments, it is operational.

q_0204.stem: A researcher states that primary stressors are the care recipient's dementia status, the level of care the caregiver provides, and whether that care is given on a regular schedule, taking that meaning from a theorist's work. What kind of definition is this, and what does it do?
options: A conceptual definition, which gives the variable theoretical meaning and links the study framework to the study variables
An operational definition, which makes the variable measurable within the study
A conceptual definition, which specifies the instrument used to measure the variable
An operational definition, which is derived from a theorist's definition or a concept analysis
q_0204.rationale: A conceptual definition provides a variable or concept with theoretical meaning, is derived from a theorist's definition or a concept analysis, and links the study framework to the study variables.
q_0204.trap: (C) is the mirror-image error to the previous item. It carries the conceptual label but describes operational work, and naming an instrument is always operational no matter which label the option attaches to it.

q_0205.stem: Which statements accurately describe how the research process differs from the nursing process? Select all that apply.
options: The research process focuses on large groups, whereas the nursing process focuses on a specific patient and family
The research process requires greater precision, rigor, and control
The research process has weaker theoretical underpinnings, because it is driven by collected data rather than by theory
The research process is more complex and involves the rigorous application of a variety of research methods
Research outcomes are shared widely through presentations and publications and can be synthesized across studies into evidence for practice
q_0205.rationale: The research process is more complex, focuses on large groups rather than an individual patient and family, demands greater precision, rigor, and control, and produces outcomes that are shared widely and synthesized across studies into evidence.
q_0205.trap: (C) inverts the theory dimension. The research process has much stronger theoretical underpinnings than the nursing process, with all steps logically linked to each other and to the study's theoretical foundations.

q_0206.stem: A nurse educator notices that new graduates are leaving her unit within six months and conducts a qualitative study to promote understanding of the experience from the perspective of the nurses living it and, if possible, to solve the problem. Which approach is this?
options: Grounded theory research
Descriptive phenomenological research
Exploratory-descriptive qualitative research
Ethnographic research
q_0206.rationale: Exploratory-descriptive qualitative research is conducted to provide information that will promote understanding of an experience from the perspective of the persons living the experience and possibly solve a problem. It addresses an issue or problem in need of a solution and understanding.
q_0206.trap: Every qualitative approach studies experience from the participant's perspective, so that phrase alone does not decide it. The give-away is the intent to solve a problem, which no other approach in this chapter claims as an outcome.

q_0207.stem: Which pairings of a qualitative approach with its origin or its intended outcome are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Phenomenological research comes from philosophy and yields a composite of the essence of the experience
Grounded theory research comes from sociology and yields a theory with relational statements between concepts
Ethnographic research comes from anthropology and yields a picture of the culture as a whole
Exploratory-descriptive qualitative research comes from psychology and yields a validated instrument
Each approach is based on a philosophical orientation that influences the interpretation of the data
q_0207.rationale: The chapter assigns phenomenology to philosophy, grounded theory to sociology by way of symbolic interaction, and ethnography to anthropology, and states that each approach is based on a philosophical orientation that influences interpretation of the data.
q_0207.trap: (D) is the fabricated pairing. The fact bank leaves the discipline cell blank for exploratory-descriptive work, and its outcome is understanding and possibly a solution, never an instrument.

q_0208.stem: A researcher studies how nurses and families negotiate goals of care in the ICU, an area in which little previous research has been conducted, and ends the report with a diagram of concepts linked by relational statements. Which approach is this, and what does grounded refer to?
options: Grounded theory; the theory was developed from the data the participants provided
Grounded theory; the study was grounded in an established theoretical framework that it then tested
Ethnography; the description was grounded in a year of immersion in the unit's culture
Interpretative phenomenology; the interpretation was grounded in a naive reading of the texts
q_0208.rationale: Grounded means the theory developed from the research, grounded in the real world and based on data provided by participants. Grounded theory is used most frequently in areas where little previous research has been conducted, and fully developed studies result in theoretical frameworks with relational statements between concepts, sometimes with a diagram.
q_0208.trap: (B) inverts the direction of the logic. Grounded theory is inductive: it produces a theory rather than testing one.

q_0209.stem: Most grounded theory methodology is based on which theory, and who developed it?
options: Hermeneutic theory, developed by Martin Heidegger
Symbolic interaction theory, developed by Glaser and Strauss
Phenomenological theory, developed by Edmund Husserl
Symbolic interaction theory, developed by George Herbert Mead
q_0209.rationale: Most grounded theory methodology is based on symbolic interaction theory, developed by the social psychologist George Herbert Mead in 1934, which explores how people define reality and how their beliefs are related to their actions.
q_0209.trap: (B) names the right theory with the wrong authors. Glaser and Strauss developed the grounded theory method itself in 1967, through interviews to understand the perspectives of persons who were dying.

q_0210.stem: An ethnographer joins a hospital night shift for a year and learns the staff's own terms, routines, and meanings as the staff themselves understand them, recognizing the uniqueness of each individual. Which approach is this, and is it the typical goal of ethnography?
options: An etic approach, and it is the typical goal
An emic approach, and it is the typical goal
An emic approach, but the etic approach is the typical goal
An etic approach, but the emic approach is the typical goal
q_0210.rationale: The emic approach studies behaviors from within the culture and recognizes the uniqueness of the individual, and it is the typical goal of ethnography. Ethnography requires immersion; early researchers spent a year or longer in another culture.
q_0210.trap: Morgan-Trimmer and Wood argue for using both emic and etic perspectives, which makes the two-sided options attractive, but that recommendation does not change which one the chapter names as typical.

q_0211.stem: A second researcher on the same night-shift study deliberately stands back and analyzes the unit's elements as a naive outsider would. This describes which approach?
options: Etic
Emic
Bracketing
Triangulation
q_0211.rationale: The etic approach views the culture as a naive outsider and analyzes its elements as a researcher.
q_0211.trap: (C) is tempting because bracketing also involves holding the researcher's own frame at a distance, but bracketing belongs to Husserlian phenomenology, not to ethnography, and the word naive appears in both definitions.

q_0212.stem: Which of the following would the chapter classify as material culture? Select all that apply.
options: Buildings used for cultural events
Symbolic meaning and social customs that become apparent only over time
Symbols
Family traditions
Networks of social relations
q_0212.rationale: Material culture is all created or constructed aspects of culture, including buildings for cultural events, symbols, family traditions, networks of social relations, and beliefs reflected in social and political institutions.
q_0212.trap: (B) is the nonmaterial half, which is symbolic meaning, social customs, and beliefs. Family traditions and social networks feel intangible, but the chapter lists both under material culture, so sorting by whether you can touch it will fail.

q_0213.stem: A researcher states that the aim of her study is to capture the experience of chemotherapy in its essence, without interpreting, explaining, or theorizing. Whose tradition is this, and which type of phenomenological research?
options: Heidegger; interpretative phenomenological research
Heidegger; hermeneutic phenomenological research
Husserl; descriptive phenomenological research
Mead; descriptive phenomenological research
q_0213.rationale: Husserl focused on the phenomenon itself and aimed to capture experience in its essence without interpreting, explaining, or theorizing. He supports descriptive phenomenological research, whose purpose is to describe experiences as they are lived, capturing the lived experience.

q_0214.stem: A study analyzes participants' interview texts beginning with a naive reading, looks for the hidden meaning in how participants gave meaning to their illness, and presents a rich word picture as interpreted by the researcher. This describes:
options: Descriptive phenomenological research consistent with Husserl
Interpretative phenomenological research using hermeneutics, consistent with Heidegger
Grounded theory using symbolic interaction, consistent with Mead
Ethnographic research using an emic approach, consistent with anthropology
q_0214.rationale: Interpretative phenomenological research is consistent with Heidegger and involves analyzing the data and presenting a rich word picture of the phenomenon as interpreted by the researcher. Hermeneutics is an interpretative method involving textual analysis that begins with a naive reading of the texts.
q_0214.trap: The phrase naive reading pulls toward Husserl, whose bracketing requirement is about describing the phenomenon in a naive way. But a naive reading of texts is the hermeneutic starting point, and hermeneutics is Heideggerian.

q_0215.stem: Before beginning interviews, a phenomenologist writes out her own assumptions about living with chronic pain and sets them aside so she can describe the phenomenon in a naive way. What is this, and whose requirement is it?
options: Triangulation; a requirement of ethnographic fieldwork
Bracketing; a requirement of Heidegger's interpretative phenomenology
Saturation; a requirement of grounded theory
Bracketing; a requirement of Husserl's descriptive phenomenology
q_0215.rationale: Bracketing is setting aside one's own biases and preconceptions in order to describe the phenomenon in a naive way, and it is a Husserl requirement supporting descriptive phenomenological research.
q_0215.trap: (B) is the classic swap the fact bank flags. Heidegger argued that it is impossible to set aside preconceptions and understand the world naively, so bracketing can never be attached to interpretative or hermeneutic work.

q_0216.stem: Which statements reflect Heidegger's position as the chapter presents it? Select all that apply.
options: The focus is how participants have interpreted or given meaning to their experiences
The analysis looks for the hidden meaning in participants' interpretations
Researchers must set aside their own biases before data collection begins
It is impossible to set aside preconceptions and understand the world naively
It supports interpretative phenomenological research
q_0216.rationale: Heidegger focused on how participants interpreted or gave meaning to their experiences and on the hidden meaning in those interpretations, argued that setting preconceptions aside is impossible, and supports interpretative phenomenological research.
q_0216.trap: (C) is Husserl's bracketing requirement, and selecting it is the single most predictable error in this chapter. Heidegger did not soften bracketing; he denied it was possible.

q_0217.stem: A researcher recruits eight nurses specifically because each one worked a mass-casualty event, rather than drawing names at random from the staff roster. What sampling method is this, and what is the stated justification?
options: Purposeful sampling; participants are recruited for their particular knowledge, experience, or views related to the study
Convenience sampling; participants are recruited because they are the most easily available
Random sampling; it reduces selection bias in qualitative work
Purposeful sampling; it guarantees the findings will apply to all emergency nurses
q_0217.rationale: Sampling in qualitative research is purposeful. The researcher recruits participants because of their particular knowledge, experience, or views related to the study.
q_0217.trap: (D) names the right method and attaches a quantitative justification. Purposeful sampling is chosen for depth of experience, not to make findings apply to a whole population.

q_0218.stem: A grounded theory team deliberately recruits participants who differ in age, role, and years of experience. What kind of sample is this, and why is it chosen?
options: A homogeneous sample, because the central focus is the phenomenon itself
A homogeneous sample, because grounded theory requires similarity to reach saturation faster
A heterogeneous sample, because participants with different characteristics support theory development
A heterogeneous sample, because saturation cannot be reached with similar participants
q_0218.rationale: Heterogeneous samples, in which participants have different characteristics, are used frequently for grounded theory to support theory development. Homogeneous samples, in which participants have similar characteristics, are used when the central focus is the phenomenon.
q_0218.trap: There is no blanket rule that qualitative samples must be homogeneous. Match the sample type to the method: phenomenon in focus means homogeneous, theory being built means heterogeneous.

q_0219.stem: A doctoral student's phenomenological study has enrolled nine participants, and the three most recent interviews produced nothing the earlier interviews had not already covered. What should the student conclude?
options: The sample is too small, because qualitative studies require more than 30 participants
Saturation has been reached, because additional participants are not providing new information
A power analysis is needed to confirm whether the minimum sample size has been met
Data collection must continue until the planned enrollment target is reached
q_0219.rationale: Saturation occurs when additional participants or data sources do not provide new information. Phenomenological studies typically use 10 or fewer participants if the topic is narrow and participants provide adequate data.
q_0219.trap: (D) defines saturation as hitting a planned number. Saturation is defined by no new information, not by a count, and the sizes the chapter gives are typical rather than rules.

q_0220.stem: Which statements about sample size in qualitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Phenomenological studies typically use 10 or fewer participants if the topic is narrow and participants provide adequate data
Grounded theory studies may require more than 30 participants to develop a robust theory
Sampling continues until saturation
Qualitative researchers deliberately recruit fewer participants but ensure that each one has experience with the research topic
A power analysis determines the minimum sample size for a qualitative study
q_0220.rationale: The chapter gives 10 or fewer as typical for phenomenology and more than 30 as possible for grounded theory, states that sampling continues until saturation, and notes that qualitative researchers deliberately recruit fewer participants while ensuring each has experience with the topic.
q_0220.trap: (E) is a quantitative tool. Power analysis determines the minimum sample size for a quantitative study; qualitative sample size is governed by saturation.

q_0221.stem: A quantitatively trained colleague criticizes a phenomenological study because the researcher became personally close to the participants over months of interviews. How does the chapter frame that involvement?
options: It is a source of bias in both quantitative and qualitative research
It is a threat to dependability that must be corrected with an audit trail
It is acceptable only if the researcher brackets the relationship after data collection
It is considered a source of bias in quantitative research but is thought by qualitative researchers to be a critical element of the research process
q_0221.rationale: One of the important differences between quantitative and qualitative research lies in the degree of involvement of the researcher with the participants; involvement considered a source of bias in quantitative research is thought by qualitative researchers to be a critical element of the research process. The researcher influences the people being studied and in turn is influenced by them.
q_0221.trap: (B) sounds rigorous and uses real vocabulary from the chapter, but the audit trail documents that methods were implemented appropriately. It is not a device for neutralizing researcher closeness.

q_0222.stem: Qualitative reports call the individuals studied participants rather than subjects. What reason does the chapter give?
options: They were not randomly assigned to groups
The researcher and participants carry out the study cooperatively
They provide narrative data rather than measured data
The sample is purposeful rather than representative
q_0222.rationale: The term participants is used because the researcher and participants carry out the study cooperatively.
q_0222.trap: (D) is a true statement about qualitative sampling but is not the reason the chapter gives for the terminology. The reason is the cooperative relationship, which fits with the researcher's involvement being treated as a critical element.

q_0223.stem: Which statements about qualitative data collection and analysis are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Data are collected through interviews, focus groups, observation, and examination of documents and media materials
Data are words and images instead of numbers
Interpretation is avoided so that the findings remain purely descriptive
A code is a symbol or abbreviation used to classify words or phrases in the data
Observation is a fundamental method of gathering data, especially for ethnographic studies
q_0223.rationale: Qualitative data are words and images rather than numbers, collected by interview, focus group, observation, and examination of documents and media; observation is fundamental, especially in ethnography. Analysis moves from codes to themes to interpretation.
q_0223.trap: (C) stops the analysis one step short. Interpretation asks what the findings mean and may focus on the usefulness of the findings for clinical practice or move toward theorizing.

q_0224.stem: Which statements about rigor in qualitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The degree of rigor is the extent to which the findings are dependable, confirmable, credible, and transferable
Rigor is established by demonstrating that the findings generalize to the target population
An audit trail is one way a researcher can assure a reader that the methods of the study were implemented appropriately
Rigor is assessed in relation to the detail built into the design, the carefulness of data collection, and the thoroughness of the analysis
Studies that are dependable and confirmable can be said to have truth, value, or credibility
q_0224.rationale: The chapter states that the extent to which findings are dependable, confirmable, credible, and transferable is the degree of rigor, assessed through design detail, careful data collection, and thorough analysis, with the audit trail assuring the reader that methods were implemented appropriately.
q_0224.trap: (B) imports the quantitative standard. Rigor in qualitative research is assessed differently precisely because the desired outcome is different.

q_0225.stem: A qualitative team interviews patients, interviews their family members, and reviews clinic documents, then converges these into one perspective on the topic. What is this strategy, and what does it support?
options: Triangulation, a strategy for credibility
Bracketing, a strategy for dependability
Saturation, a strategy for transferability
Methodological congruence, a strategy for confirmability
q_0225.rationale: Triangulation means the researchers use at least two different perspectives to converge into a unique perspective on the topic, and it is named among the credibility strategies along with engaging family members, using multiple sources, and linking codes and themes with exemplar quotations.
q_0225.trap: (D) borrows a real term from the chapter with the wrong meaning. Methodological congruence is the fit among purpose, questions, and methods that makes a study a cohesive whole, not a data-convergence strategy.

q_0226.stem: A nurse manager reads a qualitative study of burnout conducted in a 200-bed rural hospital and asks whether she can apply the findings on her own similar rural unit. Which criterion is she invoking?
options: Generalizability, the desired outcome for qualitative studies
Credibility, the truth value of the findings
Dependability, the appropriate implementation of the methods
Transferability, the applicability of the findings to similar individuals
q_0226.rationale: Transferability is the applicability of the findings to similar individuals and is the desired outcome for qualitative studies; findings cannot be generalized but may be applied in other contexts or with other participants.
q_0226.trap: (A) reverses the pair and mislabels it. Generalizability is not the desired outcome for qualitative studies at all.

q_0227.stem: A quantitative study draws a sample that is representative of the target population so its results apply to that population. Which term names that desired outcome, and to which type of research does the chapter assign it?
options: Transferability; qualitative research
Transferability; quantitative research
Generalizability; quantitative research
Generalizability; qualitative research
q_0227.rationale: Generalizability is a desired outcome for quantitative studies when the sample is representative of the target populations.
q_0227.trap: This is the mirror image of the transferability item, and the pair is the one the fact bank flags most explicitly. An option praising a qualitative study for being generalizable to the population contradicts the chapter outright.

q_0228.stem: A student argues that although the Nazi medical experiments were cruel, they at least produced valuable scientific data. How does the chapter characterize those experiments?
options: They were rigorously designed but conducted without consent
They were poorly conceived and conducted and generated little, if any, useful scientific knowledge
They produced hypothermia findings that remain scientifically useful
They were reviewed by an ethics committee before being carried out
q_0228.rationale: In addition to unjust selection of subjects, involuntary participation, and permanent damage including death, the experiments are described as poorly conceived and conducted, generating little, if any, useful scientific knowledge.
q_0228.trap: (A) is the reflex position that sound science and bad ethics can coexist here. The chapter denies the premise outright rather than weighing the data against the harm.

q_0229.stem: What finally brought the Tuskegee Syphilis Study to an end in 1972?
options: A Centers for Disease Control review concluded the study should be stopped
The Belmont Report made the design illegal
Public outrage after an account of the study appeared in the Washington Star
The institution's review committee withdrew its approval
q_0229.rationale: In 1969 the CDC reviewed the study and decided it should continue; the study stopped only after a 1972 account in the Washington Star sparked public outrage.
q_0229.trap: (A) inverts the record — the scientific review that did occur voted to continue the study. Any option crediting internal or scientific oversight with ending Tuskegee is wrong.

q_0230.stem: Which statements about the Tuskegee Syphilis Study are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The study ran 40 years, from 1932 to 1972
Subjects were informed of the purpose and procedures of the study at enrollment
Treatment was withheld even after penicillin was known to be an effective treatment in the 1940s
By 1936 the group with syphilis had developed more complications than the control group
Ten years later the death rate in the syphilis group was twice that of the control group
q_0230.rationale: The US Public Health Service study of the natural history of syphilis in black men ran from 1932 to 1972; deliberate steps were taken to deprive subjects of treatment after penicillin was known effective; by 1936 the syphilis group had more complications, and ten years later its death rate was twice the control group's.
q_0230.trap: (B) is tempting because reports on the study were published openly every four to six years. Publication in the literature is not disclosure to subjects — many were never informed, and some did not know they were subjects at all.

q_0231.subtopic: willowbrook and jewish chronic disease hospital
q_0231.stem: At Willowbrook, the institution was closed to new admissions because of overcrowding, but the research ward kept admitting, so parents could place their child only by agreeing to enrollment in the hepatitis study. Which violation does this arrangement describe?
options: Invasion of privacy
Breach of confidentiality
Falsification of data
Coerced consent involving a vulnerable population
q_0231.rationale: Parents could admit their children only if they were willing to give permission for the child to be in the study, which made the consent coercive and used a vulnerable population.
q_0231.trap: The harm students name first is the deliberate infection of children with hepatitis. The stem is describing the separate wrong — consent extracted as the price of admission.

q_0232.subtopic: willowbrook and jewish chronic disease hospital
q_0232.stem: In the Jewish Chronic Disease Hospital study of the 1960s, live cancer cells were injected into 22 patients who were not told they were in a study. Beyond violating self-determination and protection from harm, what additional failure occurred?
options: The study was never reviewed by the institution's research committee
The findings were never published in the scientific literature
The consent forms required subjects to waive their legal rights
The subjects were all children in an institution
q_0232.rationale: The study was never reviewed by the research committee, and the patients' own physicians were unaware that their patients were enrolled.
q_0232.trap: (D) belongs to Willowbrook. These four studies are routinely swapped, so anchor each to its one distinctive feature: Tuskegee withheld available treatment, Willowbrook coerced parental consent, Jewish Chronic Disease bypassed review entirely, the Nazi experiments were involuntary and lethal.

q_0233.stem: A committee drafts criteria requiring that a study be undertaken only when the knowledge cannot be gained any other way, that it build on previous work including animal experimentation, and that the anticipated results justify conducting it. These belong to which category of the Nuremberg Code?
options: Rationale for the study
Rights of human subjects
Risk avoidance
Resources
q_0233.rationale: The rationale-for-study category requires that the knowledge cannot be gained any other way, that the study be based on previous studies including animal experimentation and the natural history of the disease, that it be designed to yield results needed by society, and that anticipated results justify conducting it.
q_0233.trap: (C) risk avoidance covers avoiding unnecessary physical or mental suffering and terminating a study if the risk of harm increases. It is about conduct during the study, not about whether the study is justified in the first place.

q_0234.stem: A patient with advanced cancer enrolls in a trial of an investigational drug that may shrink her tumor. Under the distinction the Declaration of Helsinki set out to clarify, this is:
options: Nontherapeutic research, because the drug is still experimental
Therapeutic research, because she has an opportunity to receive a treatment that might have beneficial results
Exempt research, because she gave consent
Nontherapeutic research, because the findings will help future patients
q_0234.rationale: Therapeutic research provides patients with an opportunity to receive an experimental treatment that might have beneficial results, and clarifying this distinction was the major focus of the Declaration of Helsinki.
q_0234.trap: (A) treats "unproven" as the deciding feature. The distinction turns on whether the participants themselves might benefit, not on how well established the treatment is.

q_0235.stem: Healthy volunteers give repeated blood samples so researchers can map inflammatory biomarkers; nothing in the protocol is expected to change the volunteers' own health. This study is best classified as:
options: Therapeutic research, because the findings may eventually benefit these volunteers
Therapeutic research, because participation is voluntary
Nontherapeutic research, because it generates knowledge for science and is not expected to benefit those acting as participants
Nontherapeutic research, because the volunteers are healthy rather than ill
q_0235.rationale: Nontherapeutic research is conducted to generate knowledge for science; the results may help future patients but are not expected to benefit those acting as research participants.
q_0235.trap: This is the mirror of the previous item, and (D) is the dangerous option because it reaches the right label by the wrong route. Health status is not the criterion; a study can enroll sick patients and still be nontherapeutic.

q_0236.stem: Which statements about the major ethical standards are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The Nuremberg Code was released in 1949 after the Nuremberg Tribunals of German war crimes
The Declaration of Helsinki was developed in 1964 and built on the Nuremberg Code
The Common Rule was issued in 1949 and has not been revised since
The Belmont Report, published in 1979, was the first major US ethical guide
The commission that produced the Belmont Report was formed in response to the outcry over Tuskegee
q_0236.rationale: The Nuremberg Code followed the Nuremberg Tribunals in 1949, the Declaration of Helsinki built on it in 1964, and the Belmont Report of 1979 was the first major US ethical guide, written by the National Commission formed after the Tuskegee outcry.
q_0236.trap: (C) collapses two different documents. The Common Rule is the Code of Federal Regulations standard, named for the similarities among departments' CFR chapters, and it was most recently revised in 2017, effective January 2018.

q_0237.stem: A researcher restricts enrollment in a study of a new wound care protocol to privately insured patients and offers no scientific rationale for the restriction. Which ethical principle is violated?
options: Respect for persons
Beneficence
Justice
Autonomy
q_0237.rationale: Justice is the right to fair treatment, which includes access to the potential benefits of a study and not overexposure to its risks; inclusion and exclusion criteria must have scientific and/or logical explanations.
q_0237.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because uninsured patients are denied a possible good. A stem about unjustified inclusion or exclusion criteria is testing justice, not beneficence.

q_0238.stem: A study finds that enhanced diabetic education improved glucose control in the treatment group. At the end of the study the researcher offers the same education program to the control group. Which principle is she acting on?
options: Beneficence
Justice
Respect for persons
Self-determination
q_0238.rationale: A researcher guided by beneficence would provide the intervention for the subjects in the control group at the end of the study, consistent with doing good and, above all, doing no harm.
q_0238.trap: (B) is tempting because the act equalizes access, which sounds like fairness. The chapter names this exact scenario as its illustration of beneficence.

q_0239.stem: Which statements reflect the principle of beneficence as the chapter applies it? Select all that apply.
options: The researcher should do good and, above all, do no harm
It is the foundation for analyzing the benefits and risks of a study
Providing the effective intervention to the control group at the end of the study is an expression of it
Inclusion and exclusion criteria must have scientific or logical explanations
Maintaining the integrity of the study and disseminating the findings are part of it
q_0239.rationale: Beneficence encourages the researcher to do good and above all do no harm, is the foundation for analyzing benefits and risks, and extends to maintaining the integrity of the study and disseminating findings, because findings of poorly designed and implemented studies have no benefit.
q_0239.trap: (D) is justice, not beneficence. Note also that beneficence is broader than harm avoidance — a badly designed study is itself an ethical failure under this principle.

q_0240.stem: Six weeks into a 12-week trial, a participant tells the nurse she no longer wants to continue. The consent form she signed stated that she would forfeit her clinic follow-up appointments if she withdrew early. What is the correct evaluation?
options: She must complete the study because she gave consent at enrollment
Withdrawal is permitted only if the IRB approves it
The clause is acceptable because it protects the integrity of the study
The clause is improper; a subject may withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits
q_0240.rationale: The right to self-determination is based on respect for persons: a subject who consents and begins a study is allowed to withdraw at any time without penalty, and consent must state the right to refuse or withdraw without loss of benefits.
q_0240.trap: (C) treats controlling attrition as a legitimate competing interest. No design consideration overrides the right to withdraw, and no consent document can create that penalty.

q_0241.stem: Which of the following are among the five human rights that require protection in research? Select all that apply.
options: Self-determination
Privacy
Guaranteed access to the experimental treatment after the study ends
Anonymity and confidentiality
Fair selection and treatment
q_0241.rationale: The five human rights requiring protection are self-determination, privacy, anonymity and confidentiality, protection from discomfort and harm, and fair selection and treatment. The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses (2015) reiterates these rights.
q_0241.trap: (C) is a real obligation the chapter describes — beneficence supports offering the intervention to the control group afterward — but it is an application of a principle, not one of the five named rights.

q_0242.stem: A nurse manager gives a researcher a printout of patients' names, diagnoses, and payment histories, without the patients' knowledge, so the researcher can recruit for a study. What has occurred?
options: A breach of confidentiality, because raw study data were released
An acceptable use, because the information was already in the medical record
Broad consent, because the patients signed treatment consents at admission
An invasion of privacy, because private information was shared without the persons' knowledge
q_0242.rationale: Invasion of privacy occurs when private information is shared without a person's knowledge or against his or her will, and the HIPAA Privacy Rule protects identifiable information about a person's past or current health condition, the care received, and payment for health care received.
q_0242.trap: (A) is the near neighbor and the most common wrong choice. A breach of confidentiality is an unauthorized person gaining access to the raw research data; here no study data exist yet, and the wrong occurred at the moment existing private information was disclosed.

q_0243.stem: A nurse researcher collects signed consent forms, knows every participant by name, and stores coded data in a locked file. How should this study's data protection be described?
options: Complete anonymity, because names do not appear in the data file
Confidentiality, because the researcher is safely managing data whose sources she can identify
Complete anonymity, because the consent forms are stored separately from the data
Invasion of privacy, because the researcher knows the subjects' identities
q_0243.rationale: Confidentiality is the researcher's safe management of information or data shared by a subject so that the data are kept private from others; complete anonymity exists only when the researcher cannot link a subject's identity with her or his individual responses.
q_0243.trap: Calling a study with signed consent forms anonymous is the classic error. In most studies researchers know the identity of their subjects, which is why complete anonymity is uncommon.

q_0244.stem: Which situation meets the standard for complete anonymity?
options: Surveys arrive by mail with no identifiers, and the researcher cannot connect any response to a respondent
The researcher replaces each name with a code number that she is able to decode when needed
The researcher keeps a master list of names in a locked cabinet separate from the data
The researcher reports findings only for subgroups and never for individuals
q_0244.rationale: Complete anonymity exists when the researcher cannot link a subject's identity with her or his individual responses.
q_0244.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because coding feels like anonymizing, but a code the researcher can reverse preserves the link. That is confidentiality — safe management of identities the researcher knows.

q_0245.stem: A researcher conducts in-depth interviews with eight women about their experiences of intimate partner violence and plans to publish long verbatim quotes. Compared with a large quantitative survey study, the risk of a breach of confidentiality here is:
options: Lower, because results will be presented for the group rather than for individuals
Lower, because narrative data are less identifiable than numeric data
Unchanged, because both designs require the same safeguards
Higher, because the data come from fewer participants and long quotes are reported
q_0245.rationale: In quantitative studies results are presented for subgroups or groups and a breach is less likely; in qualitative studies a breach is more likely because the researcher gathers data from fewer participants and reports long quotes.
q_0245.trap: Students often assume the reverse, and (A) is dangerous because it states the quantitative case accurately — it just belongs to the comparison study, not this one. Confidentiality must be maintained during data collection, analysis, and reporting.

q_0246.stem: A biobank asks patients for permission to store, maintain, and use identifiable private information and biospecimens for future studies. Which elements must this broad consent include? Select all that apply.
options: Whether the analysis will include whole genome sequencing
A commitment to notify subjects about each specific future study conducted with their data
Whether biospecimens may be used for commercial profit and whether subjects will receive a share of any profits
The length of time the data will be kept, which may be indefinite
A statement that results will not be shared unless they are clinically relevant
q_0246.rationale: Beyond the standard consent components, broad consent must address commercial profit and profit sharing, whole genome sequencing, the types of research the data may be used for, the length of time data will be kept, and contact information.
q_0246.trap: (B) inverts the requirement. Broad consent states that subjects will not be informed about the specific studies later conducted with their information — that is precisely what makes the consent broad.

q_0247.stem: A patient signs a consent form after the researcher reads it aloud to her, but when the nurse asks what the study involves, the patient answers that she is "getting a new medicine that will fix my kidneys" — something the study does not offer. Which element of informed consent is deficient?
options: Disclosure
Competence
Comprehension
Voluntary agreement
q_0247.rationale: Comprehension is the extent to which the potential subject actually understands the information, and the researcher must take the time to teach the subjects about the study.
q_0247.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because the information clearly was delivered. Comprehension is a separate element from disclosure precisely because telling is not the same as understanding.

q_0248.stem: A researcher wants to enroll adults residing in a state psychiatric facility under court-ordered commitment. What does the chapter say about their capacity to give consent?
options: They may consent, because institutional residence does not affect legal competence
Persons with diminished autonomy because of legal or mental incompetence or confinement to an institution are not legally competent to consent
Consent is unnecessary because the facility administrator authorizes participation
Their consent is valid as long as the form is written in plain, understandable language
q_0248.rationale: Persons with diminished autonomy because of legal or mental incompetence or confinement to an institution are not legally competent to consent, and investigators must report the competence of subjects and the consent process used.
q_0248.trap: (D) swaps competence for comprehension. Readable language supports understanding, but competence is the prior question of whether the person is capable of weighing benefits and risks at all.

q_0249.subtopic: disclosure under the revised common rule
q_0249.stem: Under the 2017 revision of the Common Rule, how did the focus of disclosure in the consent process change?
options: From sharing every possible detail of a study to providing the information a reasonable person would need to make a decision
From a written consent document to an entirely verbal process
From disclosing risks to emphasizing anticipated benefits
From researcher-led disclosure to disclosure performed by the IRB
q_0249.rationale: The revision changed the focus of the consent process from sharing every possible detail of a study to providing the information that a reasonable person would need to make a decision, consistent with the revision's twin goals of enhancing subject protection and reducing administrative burden.
q_0249.trap: (B) mistakes less content for less documentation. The consent form remains a written document containing the elements of informed consent required by the Common Rule.

q_0250.stem: An IRB is reviewing a consent form for completeness. Which components must be present for the consent to be comprehensive? Select all that apply.
options: Purpose and procedures of the study and the expected length of involvement
A statement that the subject waives the right to sue the researcher for negligence
Benefits and the risks or discomforts of participating
Compensation for research-related injury and any alternative treatments
Contact persons and the right to refuse or withdraw without loss of benefits
q_0250.rationale: A comprehensive consent covers purpose and procedures, length of involvement, benefits and risks or discomforts, compensation for research-related injury, alternative treatments, confidentiality of records, contact persons, and the right to refuse or withdraw without loss of benefits.
q_0250.trap: (B) violates the requirement that consent be cautious — the subject does not waive any legal rights or release the researcher or funder from negligence. A form containing that waiver is invalid, not merely poorly worded.

q_0251.stem: A nurse plans an anonymous survey of staff attitudes, decides on her own that it qualifies as exempt, and begins collecting data without submitting anything to the IRB. What is the problem with what she did?
options: Surveys can never qualify for exemption from review
The IRB chairperson and/or committee, not the researcher, decides the level of review required for each study
Exempt studies still require continuing review every 12 months
Only federally funded studies may be classified as exempt
q_0251.rationale: The IRB chairperson and/or committee, not the researcher, decides the level of the review required for each study; the levels are exempt, expedited, and full.
q_0251.trap: (A) overcorrects. Surveys with unidentified subjects whose data are not linked to them are one of the listed exempt categories, so her conclusion may well have been right. The error is who made the determination.

q_0252.stem: An IRB classifies a nurse's study of an educational intervention as exempt. What follows from that classification?
options: The study must still undergo continuing review annually
The study may proceed without informed consent of any kind
No continuing review is required, and exempt status is a common outcome for studies conducted by nurses
The study must be re-registered with the Office of Human Research Protection each year
q_0252.rationale: Exempt studies pose no apparent risks, and once a study is exempt no continuing review is required, unlike other levels of review; studies conducted by nurses frequently are evaluated as being exempt from review.
q_0252.trap: Treating exempt status as unusual, or as evidence a corner was cut, misreads the chapter — the revised Common Rule deliberately broadened the types of study that qualify.

q_0253.stem: A researcher asks passersby in a public park to spend two minutes sorting neutral word cards, recording no identifying information. Which term describes this procedure in the exempt categories?
options: Nontherapeutic intervention
Expedited intervention
Minimal-risk therapeutic intervention
Benign behavioral intervention
q_0253.rationale: Benign behavioral interventions are short, noninvasive actions that are not expected to have a long-term adverse impact or to be embarrassing or offensive; studies using them with data not linked to subjects are among the exempt categories.
q_0253.trap: (B) borrows the vocabulary of review levels. Expedited names a level of IRB review, not a type of intervention, so it can never describe the procedure itself.

q_0254.stem: An institution is assembling an IRB. Which requirements apply to its membership? Select all that apply.
options: There must be at least five members
A member who submits a study for review may take part in the deliberations and the decision on it as long as the conflict is disclosed
At least one member must have scientific expertise
At least one member must be a community member without scientific training
At least one member must have no affiliation with the institution in any way
q_0254.rationale: An IRB has at least five members of varying cultural, economic, educational, gender, and racial backgrounds, including at least one scientist, at least one nonscientist community member, and one member unaffiliated with the institution, who may be the same person as the nonscientist.
q_0254.trap: (B) is wrong even with disclosure: a member who proposes a study cannot be involved in the deliberations and decision other than to provide information. Note also that an all-clinician IRB is noncompliant no matter how large it is.

q_0255.stem: A researcher discovers that an assistant transposed digits when entering 12 blood pressure values, corrects the dataset, and documents the correction. Does this meet the definition of research misconduct?
options: No, because misconduct does not include honest error and requires an intentional, significant departure from accepted practice
Yes, because the data as originally recorded did not accurately represent the research
Yes, because changing values already recorded in a dataset is falsification
No, because only the principal investigator can commit research misconduct
q_0255.rationale: Research misconduct is fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in processing, performing, or reviewing research or in reporting results; it does not include honest error or differences in opinion, and it is an intentional act involving a significant departure from accepted practice.
q_0255.trap: (C) recites the mechanism of falsification — changing or omitting data — while quietly dropping the intent requirement, which is exactly what makes it plausible.

q_0256.stem: A faculty member serves as a confidential peer reviewer for a colleague's grant proposal, then incorporates the colleague's novel design into her own proposal without credit. How is this classified?
options: Falsification, because she altered the research process
A difference of opinion rather than misconduct, because study designs are not owned
Plagiarism, because appropriating another's ideas or processes without credit includes material obtained through confidential peer review
Fabrication, because the design was not the product of her own work
q_0256.rationale: Plagiarism is the appropriation of another person's ideas, processes, results, or words without giving appropriate credit, including material obtained through confidential peer review of others' proposals and manuscripts.
q_0256.trap: Students associate plagiarism with copied published text, so unpublished ideas seen while reviewing feel like fair game. The peer-review clause is the least intuitive part of the ORI definition and the reason this scenario is testable.

q_0257.stem: Which statements about research misconduct are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The Office of Research Integrity, part of DHHS, defines and manages research misconduct
It comprises fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism
Honest error and differences in opinion are included within the definition
An allegation must be confirmed by a preponderance of evidence before action is taken
Research misconduct does occur in the nursing profession, and the principal investigator was usually identified as the responsible party
q_0257.rationale: ORI, within DHHS, defines and manages research misconduct as fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism; action requires confirmation by a preponderance of evidence. Research coordinators who reported misconduct often learned of it firsthand and usually identified the principal investigator as responsible.
q_0257.trap: (C) is the explicit exclusion, not an inclusion. Also resist concluding that nursing is unaffected because the seven ORI cases in 2016 were all laboratory cellular studies that rarely include nurse researchers — the chapter states directly that misconduct does occur in the profession, beginning with protocol and consent violations.

q_0258.stem: A study's introduction reads: "Little is known about how medical-surgical nurses recognize early sepsis in hospitalized older adults." The next paragraph reads: "The purpose of this study is to describe how medical-surgical nurses recognize early sepsis in adults older than 65." What does the first sentence represent?
options: The research purpose
The research problem
The research objective
The research topic
q_0258.rationale: The research problem is an area of concern in which there is a gap in the knowledge needed for nursing practice; the purpose is a clear concise statement of the specific goal or focus of a study.
q_0258.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because both sentences sit in the same introduction. The sentence naming what is not yet known is always the problem; the sentence naming what this particular study will do is the purpose.

q_0259.stem: Which statement correctly describes how a study's problem and purpose relate to each other?
options: The purpose identifies the gap in knowledge, and the problem narrows that gap to this study's goal
The problem and the purpose are two names for the same statement
The problem is the gap in knowledge, and it provides the basis for developing the purpose
The purpose is written first, and the problem is derived from it
q_0259.rationale: The problem is the area of concern in which there is a gap in knowledge, and the chapter states that the problem provides the basis for developing the research purpose.
q_0259.trap: (A) is the exact inversion of the pair and is the single most common error on this content. Direction of travel is problem to purpose, never the reverse.

q_0260.stem: Which considerations does the chapter list under the feasibility of a study problem? Select all that apply.
options: Researcher expertise
Application to nursing practice
Money commitment
Ethical considerations
Addressing nursing research priorities
q_0260.rationale: Feasibility is judged on researcher expertise, money commitment, and ethical considerations.
q_0260.trap: (B) and (E) are real criteria from this chapter, but they answer whether the problem is worth studying, not whether this researcher can actually carry it out. Application to practice, expanding previous research, and addressing nursing research priorities belong to the first question.

q_0261.stem: A study report includes the statement: "This study describes the coping strategies used by family caregivers of persons with dementia." Which element is this, and what identifies it?
options: A research question, because it names variables
A research objective, because it is a declarative statement expressed in the present tense
A hypothesis, because it names a population
The research problem, because it identifies what is not yet known
q_0261.rationale: A research objective, sometimes called an aim, is a clear, concise, declarative statement expressed in the present tense that identifies the goals of the study.
q_0261.trap: (C) is tempting because the statement names both variables and a population, but a hypothesis must predict an expected relationship between variables. Nothing here predicts anything.

q_0262.stem: The same report includes the statement: "What coping strategies do family caregivers of persons with dementia use?" Which element is this, and what identifies it?
options: A research objective, because objectives are interrogative
The research purpose, because it identifies the study's goal
A nondirectional hypothesis, because no direction is predicted
A research question, because it is an interrogative statement worded in the present tense
q_0262.rationale: A research question is a clear, concise, interrogative statement worded in the present tense that includes one or more variables and is expressed to guide the implementation of studies.
q_0262.trap: (A) swaps the grammatical forms, which is the whole point of this pair. Objective and question are separated by declarative versus interrogative, not by tense — both are present tense.

q_0263.stem: Which statements about research objectives are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Objectives are sometimes called aims
Qualitative objectives are narrower in focus and more concrete than quantitative objectives
Objectives are expressed in the present tense
Objectives may be written to determine differences between two or more existing groups
Quantitative objectives usually focus on one or two variables
q_0263.rationale: Objectives, sometimes called aims, are declarative present-tense statements that usually focus on one or two variables and may identify relationships or determine differences between existing groups such as females and males.
q_0263.trap: (B) inverts the qualitative contrast. Qualitative objectives are commonly broader in focus and include concepts that are more complex and abstract, not narrower and more concrete.

q_0264.stem: A researcher states: "Hours playing video games is related to body mass index in school-age children." How is this hypothesis classified?
options: Simple, associative, nondirectional
Simple, causal, directional
Complex, associative, nondirectional
Simple, associative, directional
q_0264.rationale: Two variables makes it simple; "is related to" proposes that the variables occur together without claiming that one causes the other; and no positive or negative nature is predicted.
