q_0264.trap: (D) is chosen by students who read any stated relationship as a direction. Direction requires words such as positive, negative, less, more, increase, decrease, greater, higher, or lower — none appears here.

q_0265.stem: A researcher states: "Participants who perform brisk walking exercise combined with music exhibit higher sleep quality scores than participants who perform brisk walking alone." How is this hypothesis classified?
options: Associative, simple, nondirectional
Causal, complex, directional
Causal, simple, nondirectional
Associative, complex, nondirectional
q_0265.rationale: The chapter classifies this hypothesis as causal, complex because it involves three variables, and directional in the positive sense because it predicts higher sleep quality scores.
q_0265.trap: (C) can be eliminated before you count anything. The chapter states that the independent variable increases or decreases each dependent variable, so all causal hypotheses are directional and "causal, nondirectional" is an impossible combination.

q_0266.stem: Which statements about classifying hypotheses are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: All causal hypotheses are directional
A hypothesis stating relationships among three or more variables is complex
A nondirectional hypothesis predicts a negative relationship
A complex hypothesis can be associative rather than causal
Words such as greater, less, increase, and decrease signal a directional hypothesis
q_0266.rationale: Every hypothesis is classified simultaneously on relationship type, number of variables, direction, and form; simple means two variables and complex means three or more, and all causal hypotheses are directional.
q_0266.trap: (C) confuses nondirectional with negative. A nondirectional hypothesis states only that a relationship exists and does not predict its nature at all; predicting a negative relationship is directional.

q_0267.stem: A researcher states: "Parents will be more likely to misperceive the weight status of younger children." Which classification does the chapter assign?
options: Simple, associative, nondirectional
Complex, causal, directional
Simple, associative, directional
Simple, causal, directional
q_0267.rationale: Two variables makes it simple, no cause and effect is proposed, and "more likely" paired with "younger" specifies the nature of the relationship; the chapter classifies it as directional and negative.
q_0267.trap: A directional hypothesis does not have to predict a positive relationship. Direction means the nature is specified, and this one is directional precisely because it predicts a negative relationship.

q_0268.stem: A published report states only a directional research hypothesis and then reports a t-test comparing group means. Which hypothesis was actually tested, and why?
options: The directional research hypothesis, because it is the one the researcher stated
Neither one; the t-test tests the level of significance rather than a hypothesis
The research hypothesis, because null hypotheses apply only to associative relationships
The statistical null hypothesis, which is implied because it is the converse of the research hypothesis
q_0268.rationale: Even if the null hypothesis is not stated, it is implied because it is the converse of the research hypothesis, and it is the statistical hypothesis that is tested to determine whether the independent variable produced a significant effect.
q_0268.trap: (A) is the reflex because the printed hypothesis is the only one visible. What is printed and what is tested are different things in every quantitative report.

q_0269.stem: A hypothesis proposes that perceived social support and medication adherence occur together in adults with heart failure, with no claim that either causes the other. Which analysis matches this hypothesis?
options: Correlational analyses examining the existence, type, and strength of the relationship
A t-test comparing experimental and comparison group means
An ANOVA comparing three treatment group means
A comparison of pretest and posttest means under an intervention protocol
q_0269.rationale: Associative hypotheses are tested with correlational analyses that examine the existence, type, and strength of the relationship, while causal hypotheses are tested with analyses of differences between means such as t-test or ANOVA.
q_0269.trap: (B) and (C) are the causal-hypothesis tools. Match the analysis to the relationship the hypothesis claims, not to how sophisticated the study looks.

q_0270.stem: Which elements should a clearly stated hypothesis include? Select all that apply.
options: The population to be studied
The instrument that will measure the dependent variable
The independent variables to be manipulated or measured
The proposed outcomes or dependent variables to be measured
The level of significance that will be used
q_0270.rationale: A clearly stated hypothesis includes the independent variables to be manipulated or measured, the proposed outcomes or dependent variables to be measured, and the population to be studied.
q_0270.trap: (B) and (E) look like rigor and are actually flaws. Naming an instrument limits the hypothesis to one study's measurement method, and determination of the level of significance is only a statistical technique applied to sample data.

q_0271.stem: A reviewer must flag one of these hypotheses as improperly written. Which one, and why?
options: "Postoperative anxiety, measured by the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, is lower in patients who receive guided imagery" — it names the measurement method
"Patients who receive guided imagery report lower postoperative anxiety than patients who receive standard care" — it predicts a direction
"Perceived stress is related to sleep quality in graduate nursing students" — it does not claim causation
"Nurses with higher workloads report more missed nursing care" — it uses the comparative word higher
q_0271.rationale: Methodological phrases such as "measured by," "in a random sample of," and "using ANOVA" are inappropriate in a hypothesis because they limit it to one study's measurement methods, sample, or analysis techniques.
q_0271.trap: (B) and (D) are correctly written directional hypotheses and (C) is a correctly written associative hypothesis. Predicting a direction and declining to claim causation are strengths, not defects.

q_0272.stem: A reviewer is judging whether a hypothesis is testable. Which feature is required?
options: It states whether the difference between the groups will be statistically significant
It names the sample and the analysis technique so the prediction can be checked
It predicts a relationship among variables that the data can support or not support
It is written in null form so that it can be rejected
q_0272.rationale: A testable hypothesis clearly predicts relationships among variables, contains variables that are measurable or able to be manipulated, and predicts a relationship that can be supported or not supported by the data.
q_0272.trap: (A) and (B) name the two things a hypothesis must not contain. (D) is unnecessary because the null hypothesis is implied as the converse of the research hypothesis whether or not it is written out.

q_0273.stem: A researcher is designing a quasi-experimental study testing whether a nurse-led education protocol reduces 30-day readmissions compared with usual care. What does the chapter say about hypotheses for a study like this?
options: Hypotheses are optional; research questions are preferred for intervention studies
Quasi-experimental and experimental studies should include hypotheses to predict the study outcomes
Hypotheses are required only when the sample has been randomly selected
Hypotheses are appropriate only for descriptive and correlational studies
q_0273.rationale: Quasi-experimental and experimental studies should include hypotheses to predict the study outcomes, and predictive correlational studies that measure independent variables to predict a dependent variable often include hypotheses.
q_0273.trap: (D) inverts the rule. Descriptive and correlational studies typically use objectives or questions, and hypotheses go on to shape the design, sampling method, data collection and analysis, and interpretation of findings.

q_0274.stem: A researcher assigns patients to either a nurse-led sleep hygiene protocol or usual care and measures sleep quality at 4 weeks. Which labeling is correct?
options: Sleep quality is the independent variable and the protocol is the dependent variable
Both are research variables because both are measured
The protocol is an extraneous variable and sleep quality is the dependent variable
The protocol is the independent variable and sleep quality is the dependent variable
q_0274.rationale: The independent variable is the intervention or treatment manipulated or varied by the researcher to create an effect on the dependent variable, and the dependent variable is the outcome the researcher wants to predict or explain.
q_0274.trap: (A) is the classic inversion. The independent variable — also called the intervention, treatment, or experimental variable — is what the researcher does, not what is measured as a result.

q_0275.stem: In a predictive correlational study, self-efficacy, social support, and health literacy are measured to predict medication adherence. Nothing is manipulated. What are the first three variables called?
options: Research variables, because none of them is manipulated
Extraneous variables, because they are not controlled
Independent variables, even though none of them is manipulated
Dependent variables, because all three are measured
q_0275.rationale: The chapter states explicitly that in predictive correlational studies, the variables measured to predict a single dependent variable are called independent variables.
q_0275.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because nothing is being manipulated. This chapter is clear that "independent variable" does not always mean "manipulated intervention," so any option asserting that an independent variable must be manipulated is too absolute for this content.

q_0276.stem: A nurse conducts a descriptive study measuring fatigue, appetite, and mood in patients receiving chemotherapy. No intervention is provided and no cause-and-effect relationship is examined. What are these three variables called?
options: Research variables
Independent variables
Dependent variables
Extraneous variables
q_0276.rationale: Research variables are the qualities, properties, or characteristics measured in a study as they exist in a natural setting without a treatment, and they appear in descriptive and correlational studies where no independent variables are manipulated.
q_0276.trap: (C) is tempting because the three variables are outcomes being measured. Calling them dependent variables implies their changes are presumed to be caused by an independent variable, and there is no independent variable here.

q_0277.stem: Which statements about extraneous variables are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: They exist in all studies
They are classified as recognized or unrecognized
They are classified as controlled or uncontrolled
They are absent from descriptive and correlational studies
They are a primary concern in intervention studies
q_0277.rationale: Extraneous variables exist in all studies and can affect the measurement of study variables and the relationships among them; they are classified as recognized or unrecognized and as controlled or uncontrolled, and they are a primary concern in intervention studies.
q_0277.trap: (D) confuses "primary concern in intervention studies" with "only present in intervention studies." Some extraneous variables are not recognized until a study is in progress or completed, and researchers control them through specific designs, intervention protocols, and sample criteria, with environmental control an extremely important part of experimental studies.

q_0278.stem: A student is appraising a research report published in a nursing journal and written by the three investigators who designed and conducted the study. How should the student classify this source?
options: A primary source, because it was written by the people who generated the ideas being reported
A secondary source, because it appears in a periodical rather than as the original data
A secondary source, because a journal editor and peer reviewers shaped the final text
A primary source only if the report includes the raw data set
q_0278.rationale: A primary source is written by the person who originated or is responsible for generating the ideas published, so a research report written by the researchers who conducted the study is a primary source.
q_0278.trap: Students routinely reclassify journal articles as secondary because they are published. Primary versus secondary turns on who generated the ideas, not on the format or the editorial process.

q_0279.stem: A review cites a textbook chapter in which the author paraphrases the work of several researchers and theorists and presents her own interpretation of what they wrote. What is the source type, and what risk does the chapter attach to it?
options: Primary source; the risk is that the author's credentials cannot be verified
Primary source; the risk is that book chapters are rarely peer-reviewed
Secondary source; the information may be a misinterpretation of the primary authors' thoughts
Secondary source; the information is by definition more than 5 years old
q_0279.rationale: A secondary source summarizes or quotes content from primary sources, and the chapter's stated risk is that the information may be a misinterpretation of the primary authors' thoughts.
q_0279.trap: (D) fuses two separate standards. Source type and currency are independent dimensions, so a secondary source can be brand new and still carry the misinterpretation risk.

q_0280.stem: A faculty reviewer questions a student's use of a secondary source. According to the chapter, which conditions justify citing one? Select all that apply.
options: The primary source cannot be located
The secondary source presents creative ideas not found in a primary source
The secondary source offers a unique organization of information not found in a primary source
The secondary source is written more clearly than the primary source
The secondary source was published more recently than the primary source
q_0280.rationale: Secondary sources are used only when primary sources cannot be located, or when the secondary source provides creative ideas or a unique organization of information not found in a primary source.
q_0280.trap: Readability and recency are not exemptions. Most references in a quality review are primary sources that are peer-reviewed, so the secondary source is a narrow exception rather than an interchangeable substitute.

q_0281.stem: An author submitted a manuscript to a publication editor, who identified scholars familiar with the topic to review it; those scholars advised on whether it was accurate, met quality standards, and was appropriate for the journal. What does completing this process establish about the article?
options: That it is a primary rather than a secondary source
That it reports data-based rather than theoretical knowledge
That it is current, having been published within the past 5 years
That it has undergone significant scrutiny and its content is considered trustworthy
q_0281.rationale: Peer review means the manuscript has undergone significant scrutiny and its content is considered trustworthy.
q_0281.trap: (A) is the reflex answer because quality reviews cite sources that are both primary and peer-reviewed. They are separate dimensions — a secondary source can be peer-reviewed, and a primary source can appear in an outlet that never reviewed it.

q_0282.stem: A student is sorting the sources cited in a review into empirical and theoretical literature. Which sources belong in the empirical category? Select all that apply.
options: A published report of a quasi-experimental study
An unpublished master's thesis reporting a completed research project
A doctoral dissertation reporting an original research project
A published concept analysis of the concept of hope
A conceptual framework proposed to explain self-care behavior
q_0282.rationale: Empirical literature is knowledge derived from research and is data-based, including published studies plus unpublished studies such as theses and dissertations. Concept analyses and conceptual frameworks are theoretical literature.
q_0282.trap: Excluding unpublished theses and dissertations from the empirical category is the common error — publication status does not decide it, data do. Keep the degrees straight as well: a thesis reports a master's project, a dissertation is the final requirement for a doctorate.

q_0283.stem: A researcher is developing the research framework for a planned study. Which body of literature provides the basis for that framework?
options: Theoretical literature — concept analyses, models, theories, and conceptual frameworks
Empirical literature — data-based reports of completed studies
Secondary sources that summarize several theorists at once
Unpublished theses and dissertations on the same topic
q_0283.rationale: Theoretical literature consists of concept analyses, models, theories, and conceptual frameworks that support a selected research problem and purpose, and it provides the basis for the research framework.
q_0283.trap: (B) is the reflex because empirical sources usually dominate the reference list. The framework is built from theoretical literature; the empirical literature documents what is known about the problem.

q_0284.stem: A faculty member tells a student that most of the sources in her synthesis paper must be current. How does the chapter define a current source?
options: Published within 2 years before publication of the manuscript
Published within 5 years before publication of the manuscript
Published within 10 years before publication of the manuscript
Published since the most recent revision of the relevant clinical guideline
q_0284.rationale: Current sources are those published within 5 years before publication of the manuscript.
q_0284.trap: Currency is a separate test from relevance. A source published last month with no direct bearing on the problem of concern is current but not relevant.

q_0285.stem: A peer reviewer criticizes a literature review for citing a 1967 study, calling it out of date. That study was the first study on the topic and signaled the beginning of a new way of thinking about it. What is the best appraisal of the criticism?
options: The criticism is correct; sources older than 5 years should be removed from the review
The criticism is correct unless the 1967 study has been replicated since
The criticism is unfounded; a review should be comprehensive as well as current, and seminal studies belong in it
The criticism is unfounded because the currency rule applies only to qualitative reviews
q_0285.rationale: Sources should be comprehensive as well as current, and because some problems have been studied for decades, reviews properly include seminal and landmark studies conducted years ago.
q_0285.trap: The 5-year rule is real, but it is a currency standard, not a ban. An old citation is not automatically a weakness if it is seminal or landmark.

q_0286.stem: A review describes one cited study as a significant research project that generated knowledge influencing the discipline and sometimes society as a whole, and notes that it has been replicated frequently. Which term names this kind of study?
options: A relevant study
A current source
A seminal study
A landmark study
q_0286.rationale: Landmark studies are significant research projects that have generated knowledge influencing a discipline and sometimes society as a whole, and they are frequently replicated or used as the basis for further studies.
q_0286.trap: (C) is the near-neighbor and the most-swapped pair in the chapter. Landmark means influential and discipline-shaping; seminal means first.

q_0287.stem: An author refers to a group of cited works as classic studies. Which term does the chapter treat as interchangeable, and what does that term denote?
options: Seminal studies — the first studies on a topic, which signaled the beginning of a new way of thinking
Landmark studies — studies that generated knowledge influencing an entire discipline
Relevant studies — studies with a direct bearing on the problem of concern
Empirical studies — studies whose knowledge is derived from data
q_0287.rationale: Seminal studies are the first studies on a particular topic that signaled the beginning of a new way of thinking, and they are sometimes called classic studies.
q_0287.trap: This is the mirror of the landmark item. Sort by the cue word in the stem: first or classic means seminal, influential or frequently replicated means landmark.

q_0288.stem: A student is appraising the reference list and scope of a published literature review. Which features indicate a sound review? Select all that apply.
options: Most of the references are primary sources that are peer-reviewed
The sources are relevant, having a direct bearing on the problem of concern
The review is broad enough for the reader to become familiar with the research problem
The review is narrow enough to include only the most relevant sources
Every source without exception was published within the past 5 years
q_0288.rationale: Most references in quality reviews are primary and peer-reviewed, relevant sources have a direct bearing on the problem, and the scope is broad enough to familiarize the reader yet narrow enough to include only the most relevant sources.
q_0288.trap: (E) turns a currency guideline into an absolute. Reviews must be comprehensive as well as current, which is exactly why seminal and landmark studies survive the 5-year cutoff.

q_0289.stem: According to the chapter, what does the literature review in a published research report do? Select all that apply.
options: Describes the current knowledge of a practice problem
Identifies the gaps in that knowledge base
Explains how the study being reported has contributed to building knowledge in the area
Establishes whether the study's findings reached statistical significance
Substitutes for the study's research framework
q_0289.rationale: A review in a published report describes current knowledge of a practice problem, identifies gaps in that knowledge base, and explains how the reported study contributed to building knowledge in the area.
q_0289.trap: (E) inverts the relationship. The framework is built from theoretical literature rather than replaced by the review, and both may be folded into the introduction without a separate heading.

q_0290.stem: A nurse wants to change a unit practice and asks a colleague where the process starts. What does the chapter identify as the first step in implementing evidence-based practice and identifying research problems?
options: Convening a practice council to select an outcome measure
Reviewing the literature
Selecting a research framework
Collecting baseline data on the unit
q_0290.rationale: Reviewing the literature is the first step in implementing evidence-based practice and in identifying research problems.
q_0290.trap: (D) is attractive because baseline data feel like step one on a quality-improvement project. The chapter puts the review first, before anything is measured or framed.

q_0291.topic: literature review timing by research type
q_0291.stem: A quantitative study report contains an extensive review written before data collection plus a shorter review of studies published since the study began 3 years earlier. How should this be appraised?
options: A flaw, because a report should present a single unified review
A flaw, because the later review should have replaced the earlier one rather than been added to it
A flaw, because it shows the researchers did not adequately plan the study
Appropriate, because the major review directs planning and execution and a limited review after completion identifies studies published since, especially when a year or longer has passed
q_0291.rationale: In quantitative research the major review is performed at the beginning to direct the planning and execution of the study, a limited review is conducted after completion — especially if a year or longer has passed — and both reviews appear in the report.
q_0291.trap: An option describing the review as happening only after data collection is describing the qualitative pattern, not the quantitative one.

q_0292.topic: literature review timing by research type
q_0292.stem: A phenomenological researcher deliberately delays the literature review until after data collection and initial analysis are complete. What is the best appraisal?
options: A weakness, because the review must always precede data collection
A weakness unique to phenomenology that reviewers should require the author to correct
Consistent with the approach, because reviewing early could bias data collection, data analysis, and findings
Acceptable only when fewer than five studies exist on the topic
q_0292.rationale: Phenomenologists are likely to delay the review until after data collection and initial analysis, because some qualitative researchers do not want their expectations about the topic to bias data collection, analysis, and findings.
q_0292.trap: Calling a delayed review sloppiness is the reflex error. Delaying it is a deliberate methodological choice that keeps the researcher open to participants' perspectives.

q_0293.topic: literature review timing by research type
q_0293.stem: Which statements about the timing of the literature review in qualitative research are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Phenomenologists are likely to delay the review until after data collection and initial analysis
Grounded theory researchers conduct a minimal review at the beginning, merely to be aware of what has been done and that a problem exists
In ethnography the review is handled similarly to the way it is handled in quantitative research
A deeper review may be omitted because qualitative studies are often conducted on topics about which we know very little
In grounded theory the early review is used to direct data collection and theory development
q_0293.rationale: Phenomenology delays the review, grounded theory does a minimal review at the beginning, ethnography resembles quantitative research, and a deeper review may be omitted because little literature exists on topics about which we know very little.
q_0293.trap: (E) reverses grounded theory's rule. The early review is explicitly not used to direct data collection or theory development; the literature is used afterward to explain, support, and extend the theory generated.

q_0294.stem: A nursing student needs clinical, theoretical, and research articles drawn from nursing and allied health journals. Which database is the best fit?
options: CINAHL
PsycARTICLES
PubMed
Academic Search Complete
q_0294.rationale: CINAHL indexes nursing and allied health journals and includes clinical, theoretical, and research articles, many in full text.
q_0294.trap: (C) is the reflex because PubMed is free and familiar. PubMed is free access to MEDLINE, which indexes biomedical journals deemed reputable by the National Library of Medicine — not a nursing-specific body of literature.

q_0295.stem: A student is planning a database search for a synthesis paper. Which actions and cautions match the chapter's guidance? Select all that apply.
options: Look beneath a useful article's abstract to see whether its search terms are listed, and reuse them as keywords
Consult a librarian, who is an information specialist and may make searching more effective
Assess sources retrieved through general search engines for quality, such as evidence of peer review
Review the abstracts to identify relevant studies before reading full articles
Treat Google Scholar results as equivalent to bibliographic database results, since both index scholarly work
q_0295.rationale: The chapter's process moves from selecting databases and search terms through searching, refining, reviewing abstracts to identify relevant studies, and reading the articles; it recommends reusing a good article's listed search terms and consulting a librarian.
q_0295.trap: (E) is tempting because general search engines do return scholarly publications. They may also return sources that are not reliable and may not be the most current, which is why the peer-review check is required.

q_0296.stem: A student's literature review is a series of paragraphs, each describing a single study, with no link drawn to the other studies being reviewed. What is the correct appraisal?
options: It is acceptable, because each study is described accurately and given its own paragraph
It does not provide evidence of adequate analysis or synthesis of the literature
It is acceptable as long as the studies are arranged chronologically
It is acceptable as long as every study cited is a current primary source
q_0296.rationale: The chapter states directly that a review consisting of paragraphs each describing a single study, with no link to other studies, does not provide evidence of adequate analysis or synthesis of the literature.
q_0296.trap: (D) is tempting because source quality is a separate standard the review may genuinely satisfy. Excellent sources arranged one per paragraph are still a summary; synthesis requires linking the studies to one another.

q_0297.subtopic: locating the review in the report
q_0297.stem: A student reports that a published quantitative article contains no literature review, because there is no heading labeled Review of Literature. What is the best response?
options: The student is correct; an article without that heading has no review
The student is correct unless the article reports a qualitative study
The review section may not be labeled and may be integrated into the introduction, as the framework may also be
The review was almost certainly moved to the discussion section instead
q_0297.rationale: The literature review section may not be labeled and may be integrated into the introduction, and the same is true of the framework; citations may appear in all sections of the report.
q_0297.trap: Judging a report by its headings is the reflex here, and (D) reinforces it by naming a real section with a different job — the discussion compares this study's findings with other studies' findings and states conclusions that synthesize previous research with the present findings. The absence of a labeled review section is a formatting choice, not evidence that the review was never done.

q_0298.stem: A theorist writes that adherence to medications improves clinical outcomes and reduces the development of complications, patient suffering, and healthcare costs. In this sentence, what is patient suffering?
options: A statement
A philosophy
An assumption
A concept
q_0298.rationale: Concepts abstractly describe and name an object, idea, experience, or phenomenon, giving it a separate identity or meaning, and they are the basic element of a theory. Adherence to medications, clinical outcomes, complications, patient suffering, and healthcare costs are all concepts here.
q_0298.trap: The sentence as a whole is the statement, because it expresses the relationships among the concepts. A single named idea inside it is a concept, not a statement.

q_0299.stem: Which characteristics describe concepts as the chapter defines them? Select all that apply.
options: They abstractly describe and name an object, idea, experience, or phenomenon
They are narrower and more measurable than variables
They provide what they name with a separate identity or meaning
They are the basic element of a theory
Each one must be defined by the theorist
q_0299.rationale: Concepts are the basic element of a theory, they name and describe abstractly, they give what they name a separate identity or meaning, and each must be defined by the theorist. Theories with clearly identified and defined concepts provide a stronger basis for a research framework.
q_0299.trap: (B) inverts the abstraction ladder. A variable is more specific than a concept, not the reverse.

q_0300.stem: A theorist opens a paper with the claim that people want to assume control of their own health problems and offers no supporting evidence for it. How should a reader classify that claim?
options: An assumption
A hypothesis to be tested in the study
A finding carried over from prior research
A specific proposition
q_0300.rationale: Assumptions are statements taken for granted or considered true even though they have not been scientifically tested, and this is the chapter's own example. You may doubt the truth of it, but theorists begin with assumptions, explicit or implicit.
q_0300.trap: Assumptions are never what the study tests. Calling one a hypothesis, or treating it as a finding, is the standard error on this term.

q_0301.stem: Which term names rational intellectual explorations of truths or principles of being, knowledge, or conduct?
options: Assumption
Theory
Philosophy
Research framework
q_0301.rationale: Philosophies are rational intellectual explorations of truths or principles of being, knowledge, or conduct, and they describe viewpoints on what reality is, how knowledge is developed, and which ethical values and principles should guide practice.

q_0302.stem: Which of the following are among nursing's metaparadigm concepts? Select all that apply.
options: Environment
Caring
Health
Adaptation
Person
q_0302.rationale: The metaparadigm concepts are person, environment, health, and nursing, described as the essence of nursing. Three of them appear here; nursing is the fourth.
q_0302.trap: Caring is Swanson's middle range theory and adaptation is the core concept of Roy's grand theory. Neither is a metaparadigm concept. There are four, and only these four.

q_0303.stem: A research team diagrams its framework with resources at the top, social support and household income beneath it, and emotional support beneath those. What is resources in this structure?
options: A concept
A construct
A variable
An operational definition
q_0303.rationale: A construct is a broader category or idea that may encompass several concepts. In the chapter's example the construct resources encompasses the concepts social support and household income.
q_0303.trap: Reversing construct and concept is the standard swap in this chapter. The construct is the broader of the two, and the concept sits inside it.

q_0304.stem: In that same framework, emotional support is scored by summing a three-item subscale of the Functional Social Support Questionnaire. What is emotional support?
options: The construct
The concept
The phenomenon
The variable
q_0304.rationale: A variable is defined so that it is measurable and its numerical values can vary from one instance to another, and it is more specific than a concept. Emotional support is the variable; the FSSQ subscale is the measurement method.
q_0304.trap: This is the mirror image of the construct item. Sort the three by breadth, not by which term appears in the sentence: construct is broadest, concept sits under it, variable is the narrow measurable one.

q_0305.stem: A nurse discusses the experience of chronic pain in general terms, apart from any specific patient. This way of thinking is best described as which of the following?
options: Concrete
Denotative
Abstract
Operational
q_0305.rationale: Abstract means the expression of an idea apart from any specific instance and focuses on a general view. Concrete refers to realities or actual instances and focuses on the particular.
q_0305.trap: Concrete is not a criticism and abstract is not a compliment. They describe level of generality, not quality of thinking.

q_0306.stem: A researcher defines home as including feelings of security, love, and comfort. A dictionary defines home as a dwelling in which a group of people live, who may or may not be related. Which statement is accurate?
options: The researcher's definition is denotative and therefore more precise
The researcher's definition is connotative and more comprehensive
The dictionary definition is the conceptual definition
The two definitions are interchangeable in a research report
q_0306.rationale: Conceptual definitions are connotative and are more comprehensive than a denotative dictionary definition, because they include associated meanings.
q_0306.trap: A conceptual definition is more comprehensive, not more precise. The narrower and more specific one is the dictionary definition.

q_0307.stem: What is the correct relationship between the conceptual and operational definitions of a study variable?
options: They are developed independently of one another
The operational definition comes from the theory and provides the basis for the conceptual definition
The conceptual definition comes from the theory and provides the basis for the operational definition
The conceptual definition is derived from the scoring rules of the measurement instrument
q_0307.rationale: The conceptual definition comes from a theory and provides the basis for the operational definition. The operational definition then states how the concept is manipulated or measured.
q_0307.trap: The dependency runs one way only. (B) is the reflex answer for students who remember that the operational definition is what appears in the methods section and assume the methods drive the theory.

q_0308.stem: A study's intervention is described as a 6-week mindfulness program delivered in weekly 60-minute groups. This description functions as which of the following?
options: The conceptual definition of mindfulness
The operational definition of the independent variable
A proposition of the framework
An assumption of the study
q_0308.rationale: An operational definition states how a concept is manipulated, for an intervention or independent variable, or measured, for a dependent or outcome variable.
q_0308.trap: The conceptual definition of mindfulness would come from the theory and describe what mindfulness means, not how many minutes the sessions ran.

q_0309.stem: Which statements about conceptual definitions are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: They are described as connotative
They state the specific method for assigning numerical values to the variable
They are more comprehensive than a denotative dictionary definition
They are drawn from a theory
They may be explicit or implicit in a published study
q_0309.rationale: Conceptual definitions are connotative, more comprehensive than a dictionary definition, drawn from theory, and may be explicit or implicit. The chapter warns that identifying the researcher's conceptual definitions is part of critically appraising a study.
q_0309.trap: (B) describes measurement, the specific method for assigning numerical values, which belongs to the operational definition rather than the conceptual one.

q_0310.stem: A student is appraising a quantitative study and wants to trace each study variable back through the framework. Which elements should ideally be identifiable for each variable? Select all that apply.
options: The concept the variable represents
A dictionary definition of the term
The conceptual definition of that concept
The operational definition
An untested assumption that supports the variable
q_0310.rationale: Each variable is ideally associated with a concept, a conceptual definition, and an operational definition, with the conceptual definition drawn from the theory.
q_0310.trap: (B) is denotative and is exactly what a conceptual definition is not. (E) confuses assumptions, which are global and untested, with the definitional chain attached to a variable.

q_0311.stem: A grand theory states that health-related quality of life is related to depression. A framework built on it states that among persons on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection, domains of health-related quality of life are related to depressive symptoms. The second statement is best labeled as which of the following?
options: A general proposition
A hypothesis
An assumption
A specific proposition
q_0311.rationale: General propositions are the relational statements found in more abstract theories, while a specific proposition states the relationship in a more narrow way, making it more concrete and testable. Specific propositions live in less abstract frameworks such as middle range theories.
q_0311.trap: It reads like a hypothesis because it names a population, but the chapter's hypothesis narrows further still, to African American persons and to named domains and symptom parameters.

q_0312.stem: Which statement is written at the lowest level of abstraction and is the one actually tested in the study?
options: Health-related quality of life is related to depression
Among persons on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection, domains of health-related quality of life are related to depressive symptoms

Among African American persons on antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection, poor physical functioning and increased role limitations are related to increased frequency and severity of depressive symptoms
People want to assume control of their own health problems
q_0312.rationale: Hypotheses are written at the lowest level of abstraction to be tested in a study, and they are developed from propositions in a grand or middle range theory.
q_0312.trap: (D) is the chapter's assumption example. Assumptions are taken as true without testing and are never the study's tested claim.

q_0313.stem: Which statements about propositions and hypotheses are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: A proposition is a label given to statements describing relationships among concepts
Hypotheses are more abstract than general propositions
Specific propositions in middle range theories may lead to hypotheses
Hypotheses are developed based on propositions from a grand or middle range theory
A specific proposition is more concrete and testable than a general proposition
q_0313.rationale: The order runs general proposition, then specific proposition, then hypothesis, in decreasing abstraction, and hypotheses are derived from propositions.
q_0313.trap: (B) inverts the hierarchy. Any option that places the hypothesis above the proposition in abstraction is wrong.

q_0314.stem: A single study finds support for one relational statement in a middle range theory. What conclusion is warranted?
options: One statement has been supported, and many studies are required to validate all the statements in a theory
The theory has been proven
The theory has been validated for that population
The theory should be reclassified as a grand theory
q_0314.rationale: Testing a theory involves determining the truth of each statement in it, and many studies are required to validate all the statements in a theory.
q_0314.trap: One supporting study never proves or validates a theory, no matter how well the study was conducted. The claim size has to match the number of statements tested.

q_0315.stem: When research tests a theory, what is it about the theory that is being tested?
options: Its concepts
Its assumptions
Its philosophy
Its statements of relationships
q_0315.rationale: The statements of relationships are what are tested through research.
q_0315.trap: Concepts are defined rather than tested, and assumptions are taken for granted precisely because they have not been scientifically tested.

q_0316.subtopic: grand, middle range, and practice theories
q_0316.stem: A theory addresses nursing actions and patient responses across multiple settings and sits at the most abstract level of theoretical thinking. Which level is this?
options: Grand nursing theory
Middle range theory
Practice theory
Scientific theory
q_0316.rationale: Grand nursing theories are the most abstract and encompass nursing actions and patient responses in multiple settings.
q_0316.trap: Early scholars called these conceptual models or conceptual frameworks. Recognizing that older label does not make them a different or less abstract level.

q_0317.subtopic: grand, middle range, and practice theories
q_0317.stem: A researcher wants a framework with clearly identified concepts, definitions of those concepts, and relational statements, and notes that this level is the one most commonly applied as a framework in nursing studies. Which level fits?
options: Middle range theory
Grand nursing theory
Practice theory
Philosophy
q_0317.rationale: Middle range theories are less abstract and narrower in scope, are more closely linked to clinical practice and research, and are more commonly applied as frameworks in nursing studies because they have clearly identified concepts, definitions of concepts, and relational statements.
q_0317.trap: Grand theories are the better known names, so they are the reflex answer. Fame is not the criterion; usable concepts, definitions, and relational statements are.

q_0318.subtopic: grand, middle range, and practice theories
q_0318.stem: Why are middle range theories also called substantive theories?
options: They have been substantiated by more research than grand theories
They substitute for a grand theory when none exists for the topic
They contain a larger number of concepts than grand theories do
They are closer to the substance of clinical practice
q_0318.rationale: Middle range theories are called substantive theories because they are closer to the substance of clinical practice.
q_0318.trap: Substantive sounds like substantiated, which is where (A) comes from, but the word points at clinical substance, not at accumulated evidence.

q_0319.subtopic: grand, middle range, and practice theories
q_0319.stem: Which description of practice theories is accurate?
options: They are a type of middle range theory designed to propose specific approaches to particular nursing practice situations
They are a fourth, independent level that is more abstract than middle range theories
They are another name for grand nursing theories
They are theories derived from physiology, genetics, and physics
q_0319.rationale: Practice theories, also called situation-specific theories, are a type of middle range theory that are more specific and are designed to propose specific approaches to particular nursing practice situations.
q_0319.trap: Practice theories are a subtype of middle range, not a separate fourth level, and they are the most specific rather than the most abstract. (D) describes scientific theory.

q_0320.stem: From which sources may a middle range theory emerge? Select all that apply.
options: A grounded theory study
The four metaparadigm concepts
Deduction from a grand nursing theory
A synthesis of the literature on a particular topic
A dictionary definition of the central concept
q_0320.rationale: Middle range theories may emerge from a grounded theory study, be deduced from a grand nursing theory, or be created through a synthesis of the literature on a particular topic.
q_0320.trap: An option requiring that middle range theories always derive from a grand theory is too narrow. Deduction is one of three routes, not the only one.

q_0321.stem: Which of these are named in the chapter as middle range theories with ongoing use? Select all that apply.
options: Uncertainty in illness (Mishel)
Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing (Orem)
Comfort (Kolcaba)
Transitions (Meleis)
Unpleasant symptoms (Lenz et al.)
q_0321.rationale: The chapter's list of middle range theories in ongoing use includes caring, comfort, inner strength, nursing intellectual capital, self-transcendence, transitions, uncertainty in illness, unpleasant symptoms, and women's anger.
q_0321.trap: Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing is one of the four grand nursing theories, not a middle range theory. It is the theorist name most likely to be pulled into the middle range list.

q_0322.stem: A nurse assesses a patient's responses to focal, contextual, and residual stimuli and plans care aimed at returning the patient to homeostasis and promoting growth. Which grand theory is guiding this nurse?
options: Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing
Rogers' Science of Unitary Human Beings
Roy's Adaptation Model
King's Theory of Goal Attainment
q_0322.rationale: In Roy and Andrews' Adaptation Model, people adapt to focal, contextual, and residual stimuli using processes and systems that are partly automatic and partly learned, with the goal of returning to homeostasis and promoting growth.
q_0322.trap: The three kinds of stimuli are the giveaway and belong to Roy alone. No other grand theory in the chapter uses focal, contextual, and residual.

q_0323.stem: A nurse evaluates how a patient's developmental stage, current disease, and available resources have reduced her ability to care for herself, and then provides care in proportion to her remaining capacity. Which theory is guiding this nurse?
options: Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing
Roy's Adaptation Model
King's Theory of Goal Attainment
Rogers' Science of Unitary Human Beings
q_0323.rationale: In Orem's theory the ability to self-care is affected by developmental stage, presence of disease, and available resources and may result in a self-care deficit, and nursing provides care in proportion to the person's self-care capacity.
q_0323.trap: Developmental stage and resources also sound like contextual factors, which pulls toward Roy. The deciding feature is that the nursing dose is scaled to the patient's self-care capacity.

q_0324.stem: A nurse describes the patient and the environment as energy fields interacting as open systems and looks for the patterns those fields produce. Which theory is this?
options: Roy's Adaptation Model
Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing
King's Theory of Goal Attainment
Rogers' Science of Unitary Human Beings
q_0324.rationale: Rogers' Science of Unitary Human Beings holds that persons and environment are energy fields interacting as open systems, and that the fields produce patterns usable for identification.
q_0324.trap: Open systems appear in King's work as well, which is where the confusion starts. Energy fields and patterns are what mark the answer as Rogers.

q_0325.stem: A nurse and a patient sit down together, agree on goals for discharge, and the nurse then educates, supports, and guides the patient toward them. Which theory is this?
options: Roy's Adaptation Model
King's Theory of Goal Attainment
Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory of Nursing
Rogers' Science of Unitary Human Beings
q_0325.rationale: In King's Theory of Goal Attainment, persons within systems are goal-oriented, the nurse and patient set mutually agreed-upon goals, and through interaction the nurse educates, supports, and guides.
q_0325.trap: Orem is the near-neighbor any time the nurse's role is described as supportive. The deciding feature here is that the goals are set mutually by nurse and patient, not scaled to a self-care deficit.

q_0326.subtopic: programs of research around a grand theory
q_0326.stem: Which statements about building nursing knowledge around a grand theory are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It requires an organized program of research and a group of scholars
The Roy Adaptation Association analyzes, critiques, and synthesizes the English-language studies based on the model
The International Orem Society publishes the journal Nursing Science Quarterly
The Roy Adaptation Model has been in use for over 25 years
The Society of Rogerian Scholars publishes the journal Visions
q_0326.rationale: Building knowledge around a grand theory requires an organized program of research and a group of scholars, and the chapter names the Roy Adaptation Association, the Society of Rogerian Scholars with its journal Visions, and the International Orem Society.
q_0326.trap: The International Orem Society's journal is Self-Care, Dependent-Care, and Nursing. Nursing Science Quarterly is not the journal the chapter attaches to any of these societies.

q_0327.stem: Which statements accurately describe a research framework? Select all that apply.
options: It is an abstract and logical structure of meaning
It may be a portion of a theory
It is developed after data analysis to explain unexpected results
It guides the development of the study
It enables the researcher to link the findings to nursing's body of knowledge
q_0327.rationale: A research framework is an abstract and logical structure of meaning, such as a portion of a theory, which guides the development of the study and enables the researcher to link the findings to nursing's body of knowledge.
q_0327.trap: (C) reverses the timing. A framework is in place to guide the study, not assembled afterward to account for results.

q_0328.stem: How does the chapter characterize a clearly expressed framework in a quantitative study?
options: One indication of a well-developed quantitative study
A requirement for institutional review board approval
Evidence that the underlying theory has been validated
A feature unique to physiological studies
q_0328.rationale: A clearly expressed framework is one indication of a well-developed quantitative study.
q_0328.trap: A clear framework says something about the quality of the study's development. It says nothing about whether the theory itself has been validated, which would take many studies.

q_0329.stem: A student appraising a quantitative article cannot find any section naming a theory or framework. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The study has no framework
The study must actually be qualitative
The framework must be a scientific theory drawn from physiology
The framework is implicit, because every quantitative study has an implicit or explicit framework
q_0329.rationale: Every quantitative study has an implicit or explicit framework, whether the focus is physiological, psychological, social, or cultural. The appraisal question is not whether a framework exists but whether it is explicit and how well developed it is.
q_0329.trap: (A) is the reflex answer and it is wrong by the chapter's own rule. There is no such thing as a quantitative study with no framework.

q_0330.stem: A study's introduction notes that earlier work linked the variables but never explains why they should be related, and no framework section follows. What does the chapter recommend the reader do?
options: Reject the study as unappraisable
Extract the implicit framework from the text and, if it helps, draw a model of how the variables are linked
Substitute a grand nursing theory of the reader's own choosing
Treat the literature review as the study's operational definitions
q_0330.rationale: In most cases a careful reader can extract an implicit framework from the text, and when researchers do not clearly describe the framework you may want to draw a model, which helps you visualize the framework and how the variables are linked.
q_0330.trap: This is the classic implicit-framework signature: the linkage appears in the introduction or literature review and then the researcher stops without developing it into a framework.

q_0331.stem: What is the consequence of a researcher leaving the framework implicit?
options: It invalidates the study's statistical results
It converts the study into a qualitative design
It provides limited guidance for the development and conduct of the study and limits the contribution of the findings to nursing knowledge
It means the study's hypotheses cannot be tested
q_0331.rationale: Implicit frameworks provide limited guidance for the development and conduct of a study and limit the contribution of the study findings to nursing knowledge.
q_0331.trap: An implicit framework weakens guidance and contribution. It does not make the statistics invalid or change the design, so options that escalate to invalidation overshoot.

q_0332.stem: In a diagram of a study's framework, an arrow drawn from one concept to another is a graphic illustration of what?
options: A statistical correlation found in the study's data
A relational statement, or proposition, of the theory
A causal pathway already proven by prior research
An operational definition of the concept
q_0332.rationale: A model is a diagram with the concepts and relationships graphically displayed, it includes all the major concepts in a research framework, and each linkage shown by an arrow is a graphic illustration of a relational statement, or proposition, of the theory.
q_0332.trap: An arrow is a claim from the theory, not a finding from the data. Reading arrows as correlations or as proven causation is the standard misread.

q_0333.stem: Which of the following are identified as sources of research frameworks? Select all that apply.
options: Grand nursing theories
Middle range theories from nursing and from other professions
The study's data analysis plan
Syntheses of concepts and relationships from more than one theory
Syntheses of research findings
q_0333.rationale: The four sources are grand nursing theories, middle range theories from nursing and other professions, syntheses of concepts and relationships from more than one theory, and syntheses of research findings.
q_0333.trap: Middle range theories borrowed from other professions count. Restricting frameworks to nursing-only theories drops a legitimate source.

q_0334.stem: A researcher combines concepts from two different theories with findings from several published studies to build a framework for one particular study. What is this framework called?
options: A grand theory
A scientific theory
A tentative theory
A practice theory
q_0334.rationale: A tentative theory is a newly proposed framework, often a synthesis of concepts from more than one theory or of research findings, and it is usually developed for a particular study.
q_0334.trap: Synthesizing across theories does not produce a grand theory. Tentative theories are built for one study rather than for a program of research across settings.

q_0335.stem: A study of a cooling protocol's effect on cerebral perfusion draws its framework from pathophysiology and physics. This framework is best described as which of the following?
options: A grand nursing theory
A scientific theory
A tentative theory
A practice theory
q_0335.rationale: Frameworks for physiological studies come from physiology, genetics, pathophysiology, and physics, and are scientific theories, which have extensive research evidence to support their claims, concepts clearly linked to study variables, and valid and reliable methods for measuring each concept.
q_0335.trap: A framework that is not a nursing theory is still a framework. Physiological studies are exactly the case students use to argue, wrongly, that a study has no framework.

q_0336.stem: A reviewer reads this purpose statement: "to determine the effect of a nurse-led sleep hygiene protocol on the incidence of ICU delirium." Using the chapter's appraisal question, how should the reviewer classify what this study is doing?
options: Describing variables as they exist
Examining relationships among variables
Examining causality
Testing a proposed model of relationships
q_0336.rationale: In critical appraisal, determine whether the study's purpose is to examine causality, examine relationships, or describe variables; the purpose statement and the framework's propositions usually reveal which. Determining the effect of an intervention on an outcome is causality.
q_0336.trap: (B) is the reflex whenever two variables share a sentence. A relationship purpose asks whether variables vary together; a causal purpose asks whether one produces the other.

q_0337.stem: Which statement reflects this chapter's position on causality in nursing phenomena?
options: A well-developed theory identifies every element involved in causing a particular outcome
A multicausal perspective includes fewer variables so the true cause can be isolated
Absolute causality is the standard that quantitative designs are built to achieve
Very few phenomena in nursing can be clearly linked to a single cause and a single effect
q_0337.rationale: The chapter states that very few phenomena in nursing can be clearly linked to a single cause and a single effect, and that studies taking a multicausal perspective include more variables.
q_0337.trap: (B) inverts the text, since multicausality adds variables rather than stripping them out. (C) ignores probability, which addresses relative rather than absolute causality: a cause probably will result in a specific effect.

q_0338.stem: Beyond calling a research design a blueprint, the chapter's fuller definition specifies that the design does what?
options: Establishes the conceptual definitions of the study variables
Maximizes control over factors that could interfere with the validity of the findings
Guarantees that the findings can be generalized to the target population
Determines which statistical tests will reach significance
q_0338.rationale: A research design is a blueprint for conducting a quantitative study that maximizes control over factors that could interfere with the validity of the findings.
q_0338.trap: (C) overstates. Generalization is external validity, and it is usually narrower for a single study than for multiple replications using different samples and settings.

q_0339.stem: Which statements about bias reflect what this chapter says? Select all that apply.
options: Bias is a slant or deviation from the true or expected
A study that used random assignment can be appraised as free of bias
The composition of the sample and the groups that are formed are potential sources of bias
Not all biases can be identified from the published study report
The environment and the data collection process are potential sources of bias
q_0339.rationale: Bias is a slant or deviation from the true or expected that distorts findings from what they would have been without it. Named sources include researcher attitudes or motivations, the environment, selection of participants, sample composition, the groups formed, measurement methods, the data collection process, and statistical analyses.
q_0339.trap: (B) is the overreach the chapter warns against directly. The article may not provide sufficient detail about methods to detect possible biases, so no appraisal can declare a study bias-free.

q_0340.stem: A researcher measures fall rates on three medical-surgical units over one quarter and reports how the units differ. No intervention is delivered and no relationships are tested. Which design is this?
options: Simple descriptive
Comparative descriptive
Descriptive correlational
Predictive correlational
q_0340.rationale: A comparative descriptive design describes and compares variables across groups; a simple descriptive design only describes variables as they exist.
q_0340.trap: (A) is chosen because nothing was manipulated, but the absence of an intervention is not what separates these two. The comparison across the three units is what moves it from simple to comparative descriptive.

q_0341.stem: A researcher measures resilience and burnout scores in staff nurses at one time point and reports how strongly the two are related. There is no attempt to forecast one score from the other. Which design is this?
options: Descriptive correlational
Predictive correlational
Model testing
Comparative descriptive
q_0341.rationale: A descriptive correlational design describes relationships among variables, whereas a predictive correlational design measures independent variables in order to predict a dependent variable.
q_0341.trap: (B) is the reflex whenever a correlation coefficient appears. Prediction requires that independent variables be measured to predict a dependent variable, not merely that a relationship be described.

q_0342.stem: Which statements about the chapter's design families are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: A predictive correlational design measures independent variables to predict a dependent variable
A model testing design tests a proposed model of relationships
A descriptive correlational design tests the effect of an intervention
A simple descriptive design describes variables as they exist
A comparative descriptive design describes and compares variables across groups
q_0342.rationale: The chapter's families are simple descriptive, comparative descriptive, descriptive correlational, predictive correlational, model testing, and quasi-experimental or experimental designs, which test the effect of an intervention.
q_0342.trap: (C) hands the intervention-testing job to a correlational design. Only quasi-experimental and experimental designs test the effect of an intervention, because only they involve manipulation.

q_0343.stem: Postoperative patients are assigned to receive either guided imagery or usual care, and pain scores are compared. Which element distinguishes this family of designs from descriptive and correlational designs?
options: Prospective data collection
Use of more than one measurement method
A large sample size
Manipulation of the independent variable
q_0343.rationale: Manipulation is a form of control generally used in quasi-experimental and experimental studies, which are the designs that test the effect of an intervention.
q_0343.trap: (A) is true of many experiments but does not define them. Descriptive and correlational studies can also collect data looking forward, so time orientation never settles the design family.

q_0344.stem: Which statements about designs that examine causality are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Descriptive and correlational designs also test the effect of an intervention
Manipulation is a form of control generally used in quasi-experimental and experimental studies
A randomized controlled trial is a type of experimental design often considered one of the strongest designs to examine cause and effect
Internal validity is a concern in all studies but is a major focus in studies examining causality
Random assignment decreases the selection threat
q_0344.rationale: Manipulation is generally used in quasi-experimental and experimental studies; the RCT is an experimental design often considered one of the strongest for examining cause and effect; internal validity is a concern in all studies but a major focus in causal studies; and random assignment decreases the selection threat.
q_0344.trap: (D) looks too generous to be keyed, which is why students drop it. Any option restricting internal validity to experimental designs is too narrow, and so is any answer key that leaves this statement out.

q_0345.stem: One researcher enrolls patients at the time of catheter insertion and follows them forward for 30 days to record infections. A second researcher pulls last year's charts to identify who developed an infection after insertion. These two approaches are, respectively:
options: Prospective and retrospective
Retrospective and prospective
Experimental and quasi-experimental
Descriptive and correlational
q_0345.rationale: Prospective means looking forward; retrospective means looking backward, usually in relation to time.
q_0345.trap: The data source does not decide this. A chart review can serve either direction, so what settles it is whether the look runs forward from enrollment or backward from the outcome.

q_0346.stem: A researcher studying postoperative pain uses a 0-to-10 numeric rating scale as the only measure of pain. Which threat to construct validity does this illustrate?
options: Inadequate definition of the construct
Unreliable measurement method
Mono-operation bias
Experimenter expectancy
q_0346.rationale: Mono-operation bias occurs when only one method of measurement is used to assess a construct, so fewer dimensions of the construct are measured; construct validity greatly improves with more than one instrument.
q_0346.trap: (B) belongs to statistical conclusion validity and concerns whether a measure gives the same result each time. A single measure can be perfectly reliable and still produce mono-operation bias, because the problem is the count of methods, not their consistency.

q_0347.stem: Following the chapter's own pain example, which measures would strengthen construct validity when pain is the dependent variable? Select all that apply.
options: A pain rating scale
Verbal reports from the patient
Physical responses such as increased pulse, blood pressure, and respirations
Observed behaviors such as crying, grimacing, guarding, and pulling away
The number of persons approached who declined to participate
q_0347.rationale: The chapter's mono-operation example names a pain rating scale, verbal reports, physical responses including increased pulse, blood pressure, and respirations, and observed behaviors including crying, grimacing, guarding, and pulling away.
q_0347.trap: (E) is the refusal rate. It must be reported, but it belongs to external validity as part of the interaction of selection and intervention, not to measuring the construct.

q_0348.stem: The principal investigator of a new mobility protocol believes strongly in the protocol and personally collects all outcome data. Which threat is this, and what is the chapter's fix?
options: An internal validity threat (selection); randomly assign participants to groups
A statistical conclusion validity threat (low power); increase the sample size
An external validity threat (interaction of setting and intervention); add more study sites
A construct validity threat (experimenter expectancy); blind the data collectors to group assignment
q_0348.rationale: Experimenter expectancy, the Rosenthal effect, means the expectancies of the researcher can bias the data. Using nonbiased data collectors or those blinded to group assignment increases construct design validity, and some researchers choose not to be involved in data collection at all.
q_0348.trap: (A) is the common misfile. This text classifies the Rosenthal effect as a construct validity threat, even though it sounds like a rival explanation for the finding and therefore feels like internal validity.

q_0349.stem: Day-shift nurses receive a new handoff protocol and night-shift nurses serve as the comparison group, because randomizing individual nurses was not feasible. Which internal validity threat is most prominent?
options: History
Maturation
Selection
Mono-operation bias
q_0349.rationale: Selection is the process whereby participants are chosen to take part and how they are grouped within a study. It is more likely to occur in studies in which randomization is not possible, and random assignment decreases the threat.
q_0349.trap: (A) requires an unrelated event occurring during the study. Here the problem exists before the first data point, in how the two groups were formed.

q_0350.stem: Which statements about attrition as a threat to internal validity are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Attrition is participants dropping out of a study before it is completed
Attrition is harmless as long as the number of dropouts is the same in each group
It is a threat when the dropouts differ in type from those who remain
It is a threat when there is a difference in the number and type of dropouts between groups
Attrition greater than 25% could affect the accuracy of the results
q_0350.rationale: Attrition is participants dropping out before completion. It threatens internal validity when dropouts differ in type from those who remain, or when the number and type of dropouts differ between groups, and attrition greater than 25% could affect the accuracy of results.
q_0350.trap: (B) is the count-only reflex. Equal numbers do not settle it, because attrition is a threat mainly on account of who leaves; equal counts of very different people still bias the comparison.

q_0351.stem: During a 12-month cardiac rehabilitation support study, several of the nurses who deliver the program quit. Which internal validity threat does this illustrate?
options: Maturation
History
Attrition
Selection
q_0351.rationale: History is an event that is not related to the planned study but occurs during the time of the study; the chapter's own example is several nurses quitting during a cardiac rehabilitation support study.
q_0351.trap: (C) is the reflex because someone left. Attrition refers to participants dropping out, not staff departing, and staff leaving is an external event acting on the study.

q_0352.stem: Over an 18-month longitudinal study with repeated measures, participants become stronger and more experienced at the study tasks in ways the researchers neither planned nor noticed. Which threat is this, and where is it most likely?
options: History; most likely in cross-sectional studies
Selection; most likely when randomization is used
Attrition; most likely when the study period is short
Maturation; most likely in longitudinal studies with repeated measures
q_0352.rationale: Maturation is growing older, wiser, stronger, hungrier, more tired, or more experienced during the study; the changes are unplanned and unrecognized, and maturation is more likely in longitudinal studies with repeated measures.
q_0352.trap: History and maturation are routinely swapped. History is an external event that happens to the study; maturation is change occurring inside the participants themselves.

q_0353.stem: A published study reports that 39% of those approached declined to participate. Which threat does this raise, and to which type of design validity?
options: Interaction of selection and intervention; external validity
Selection; internal validity
Attrition; internal validity
Interaction of history and intervention; external validity
q_0353.rationale: A high refusal rate limits the sample in non-obvious ways. With 39% declining, those enrolled may be volunteers, do-gooders, or those with nothing better to do, so generalizing to all nurses or patients is not justified, and researchers must report the refusal rate.
q_0353.trap: (B) wins on the shared word. The plain selection threat concerns how enrolled participants were chosen and grouped and is an internal validity problem; the refusal rate concerns who never entered at all and is an external validity problem.

q_0354.stem: Which statements about external validity are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: With the most serious threat, the findings would be meaningful only for the group studied
Generalization is usually narrower for a single study than for multiple replications using different samples, populations, and settings
Hospitals seeking Magnet designation may welcome nursing studies while others resist, so the two types of setting may differ in important ways
Replicating a study during various time periods allows the findings to be generalized to the future
Choosing instruments that are valid and reliable but have fewer items decreases participant burden and helps reduce the selection threat
q_0354.rationale: With the most serious threat, findings would be meaningful only for the group studied; generalization is narrower for a single study than for multiple replications; the Magnet example illustrates interaction of setting and intervention; and shorter valid and reliable instruments reduce participant burden and help reduce the selection threat.
q_0354.trap: (D) overshoots the chapter's own caution. Logically one can never generalize to the future; replicating during various time periods strengthens the usefulness of findings over time but licenses no claim about it.

q_0355.stem: Three patients die from dialysis equipment failure during a study of a support intervention for patients receiving dialysis. Which external validity threat does this create for the published findings?
options: Interaction of selection and intervention
Interaction of setting and intervention
Interaction of history and intervention
Maturation
q_0355.rationale: Interaction of history and intervention means the circumstances at the time the study was conducted affect generalization; the chapter's example is exactly this dialysis equipment failure during a dialysis support study.
q_0355.trap: History appears in both validity lists, so read what the item is asking. As a plain internal validity threat, history asks whether the event explains the result; as an interaction with intervention, it asks whether those circumstances make the findings ungeneralizable to other times.

q_0356.subtopic: statistical power and Type II error
q_0356.stem: A study with 18 participants per group finds no significant difference between the intervention and comparison groups. Which threat is most likely, and which error does it produce?
options: Low statistical power; Type II error
Low statistical power; Type I error
Unreliable measurement methods; Type I error
Extraneous variances in the setting; Type I error
q_0356.rationale: Low statistical power increases the probability of concluding there is no significant relationship or difference when actually there is one, which is a Type II error. It is most likely when the sample size is small or the power of the statistical test is low.
q_0356.trap: (B) keeps the right threat and swaps the error. Low power means missing a real effect, which is Type II; nothing about a small sample manufactures a false positive.

q_0357.subtopic: statistical power and Type II error
q_0357.stem: Which of the following is a Type II error as this chapter defines it?
options: Concluding there is a significant difference when in fact there is not one
Concluding there is no significant relationship or difference when actually there is one
Using only one method of measurement to assess a construct
Generalizing findings beyond the sample that was studied
q_0357.rationale: A Type II error is concluding there is no significant relationship or difference when actually there is one, and low statistical power increases its probability.
q_0357.trap: (A) is the mirror-image error and reads as the more familiar mistake. Sort it by what was missed: a stem describing a false alarm points the other way, while a stem describing a small sample and a null result points to Type II.

q_0358.stem: A physiological instrument gives the same reading each time the same variable is measured under the same conditions. Which appraisal statement is accurate?
options: The measure is valid, because consistency establishes accuracy
The measure demonstrates construct validity, because it matches the conceptual definition
The measure demonstrates intervention fidelity
The measure is reliable, and a physiological measure that measures consistently is described as precise
q_0358.rationale: A measure is reliable if it gives the same result each time the same situation or variable is measured, and physiological measures that measure consistently are precise, as with a thermometer showing the same reading on repeat testing.
q_0358.trap: (A) equates consistency with accuracy, which is the single most common inversion here. A consistently wrong scale is still reliable; reliability is sameness of result, not truth of result.

q_0359.stem: Which of the following are threats to statistical conclusion validity as this chapter lists them? Select all that apply.
options: Low statistical power
Unreliable measurement methods
Interaction of setting and intervention
Limited intervention fidelity
Extraneous variances in the setting
q_0359.rationale: The chapter lists low statistical power, unreliable measurement methods, limited intervention fidelity, and extraneous variances in the setting. Limited fidelity matters because when administration varies from one person to another, the chance of detecting a true difference decreases, so data collectors must be trained for consistency.
